intro:
**The Assembly of the Prophets and the Approaching Reckoning**

Al-Anbiyāʾ, "The Prophets," is the twenty-first chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 112 verses of late-to-mid Makkan revelation. It takes its name from its glorious, panoramic assembly of sixteen named prophetic figures—along with Maryam—marching in a single, unbroken spiritual chain across verses 48–91. In classical hadith literature, Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ is grouped alongside the earliest treasures of revelation: ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd famously stated in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (4994) that *“Banī Isrā'īl (al-Isrāʾ), al-Kahf, Maryam, Ṭā-Hā. Al-Anbiyāʾ are among the ancient treasures (*min al-ʿitāq al-uwal*) and they are of my earliest acquisitions.”* Emerging from the intense intellectual clashes of the Makkan period, Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ confronts human heedlessness with volcanic urgency: opening with the terrifying announcement that human reckoning has drawn dangerously near while mankind turns away in heedless play, and culminating in the magnificent declaration that the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ is sent as nothing less than an all-encompassing mercy to all creation (*Raḥmatan li-l-ʿālamīn*, 21:107).

**The Grand Prophetic Procession and Thematic Arc**

The architecture of Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ moves from cosmic physics to prophetic history, and from the crucible of suffering to Last-Day fulfillment. The opening movement (1–47) establishes the proximity of the Judgment, shows the absurdity of polytheism (arguing that had there been gods other than Allah in heaven and earth, both would have been corrupted and ruined, 21:22), and presents profound cosmic signs: the heavens and earth joined together before being violently split apart, all living matter created from water (21:30), firm mountains stabilizing the crust, and every celestial sphere swimming in its appointed orbit (*kullun fī falakin yasbaḥūn*). The second movement (48–91) unfolds the glorious roll-call of the prophets, illustrating how each responded to intense existential crises: Moses and Aaron receiving the Criterion (*al-Furqān*); Abraham smashing the idols of his people, surviving the raging furnace transformed by divine command into coolness and peace (*kūnī bardan wa-salāmā*, 21:69); Isaac and Jacob gifted as leaders guiding by divine command; Lot delivered from the vile city; Noah saved from the great distress while his mockers drowned; David and Solomon gifted with wisdom, understanding the speech of birds and winds. The mountains glorifying God with David; Job (*Ayyūb*) calling out in the depths of disease and poverty: *“Adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful,”* whereupon his health and family were restored; Ishmael, Idrīs, and Dhū al-Kifl praised for unyielding patience; Jonah (*Dhū al-Nūn*) crying out from the triple darkness of the night, the sea, and the belly of the whale: *“There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers,”* an immortal prayer guaranteed to deliver believers from distress (21:87); Zechariah crying out in loneliness, gifted John; and Maryam who guarded her chastity, into whom the divine spirit was breathed. The third movement (92–112) unites all these diverse messengers into a single spiritual fraternity: *“Indeed, this community of yours is one single community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me”* (21:92). It warns of the breaching of Gog and Magog (*Ya'jūj wa-Ma'jūj*), describes the sky being rolled up on the Last Day like a scribe rolling up a scroll, confirms that the righteous servants shall inherit the earth (21:105), and closes with the universal prophetic charter: *“And We have not sent you, [O Muḥammad], except as a mercy to the worlds”* (21:107).

Whenever a new reminder from the Most Compassionate was recited, they listened to it while amusing themselves, whispering conspiratorially: *“Is this man anything more than a human being like yourselves? Will you then surrender to sorcery with your eyes wide open?”* (21:2–3).

verses.1:
> ˹The time of˺ people’s judgment has drawn near, yet they are heedlessly turning away

**The Reckoning That Comes Closer the More One Strays**

The opening of al-Anbiyāʾ announces a temporal paradox: the reckoning draws near precisely because people turn away. The Arabic verb *iqtaraba* — to draw near, to come close — places the hearer inside a process already in motion. The reckoning is not a future appointment that one awaits; it is a present pressure that one ignores. Every additional hour of heedlessness is a hour closer to the hour that heedlessness can no longer evade. The classical commentators cited in the source for this verse (al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Zamakhsharī) record the observation that *iqtaraba* ordinarily describes someone who has covered more than half the distance and is therefore closer to the arrival than to the start. Used of the Day of Judgment, the verb converts cosmic future into imminent present.

The pairing of the two halves of the verse is a single moral claim, not two. The reckoning is near; people turn away heedlessly. The nearness is fixed; the turning is chosen. The contrast means that the alarming fact is not the closeness of the reckoning but the leisure with which the addressees meet it. The same pairing returns in 70:6–7, where the deniers see the hour as far off while God sees it as near. There is no contradiction: the distance is measured in calendar years, the proximity in moral weight. A thing can be centuries away in time and already pressing on the conscience of anyone who has stopped to think.

**Reckoning as a Qur'anic Architectural Term**

The word *ḥisāb* — reckoning, account — is one of the Book's central architectural terms. It names the operation by which every deed, intention, and word is entered, weighed, and returned to its owner. The same root appears at 38:16, 40:28, and elsewhere to designate the Day itself, suggesting that for the Qur'an, the Day of Judgment and the operation of accounting are not two things but one. The classical commentators add an observation worth keeping: although the reckoning is announced as near, the precise moment is not given. The Qur'an insists on the fact of the reckoning without disclosing the hour, because disclosure would collapse moral seriousness into arithmetic. If people knew the day, every act in its shadow would be a forced move.
verses.2:
> Whatever new reminder comes to them from their Lord, they only listen to it jokingly

**Play as the Chosen Posture of Those Who Refuse**

The verse pairs with 21:1 to form a single moral statement. The reckoning draws near; people turn away heedlessly; and the form that turning takes is play. The Arabic *laʿib* — play, sport, amusement — names a deliberate downgrading of seriousness. Whatever new reminder descends, they receive it not as a summons but as a performance. The verse is not accusing the audience of being uninformed; it accuses them of being misinformed on purpose. They know that the message is a message; they have decided to treat it as entertainment.

The commentators note that *laʿib* in the Qur'an is associated with a settled state of *ghaflah* — heedlessness. The same pairing appears at 6:91, 43:83, 52:12, and 70:42. To treat revelation as play is therefore not a casual reaction; it is the consistent outward gesture of a particular inward condition. The condition cannot be cured by louder announcements, because the louder the announcement, the more elaborate the play. The Qur'an often responds to this dynamic by intensifying the warning rather than softening it — a counter-intuitive move, but one consistent with the verse's own logic. Play is met, in the Qur'an's rhetoric, with a severity that refuses to play along.

**From Jesting to Refusal — the Grammar of Turning Away**

Classical Arabic syntax places *laʿibīn* — jokingly, in play — in the accusative as a *ḥāl*, a state of being. They listen *while* they are in a state of play. The construction is significant: it tells us that the play is not a momentary lapse but the condition under which the listening occurs. They are not people who listen first and then make jokes afterward; they are people whose listening and whose joking are simultaneous.

The Qur'an names this dynamic in its own vocabulary — *laʿawa* — turning away, treating the message as something that one hears and passes by. The grammatical pairing of *laʿibīn* (joking) with *wa hum fī ghaflah* (in heedlessness) in the verses just before shows that play, in this phrase, is the surface expression of a deeper refusal.

**A Closing Image of the Receiver Taken Captive**

The closing image the verse leaves is of a person who has been captured by the very posture he chose. To listen jokingly is to train the heart to take every fresh reminder as another item in the same repertoire. Over time, the play hardens; what began as a way of keeping distance becomes the very mechanism by which the heart refuses any approach. The Qur'an elsewhere calls this hardening *qaswa* — a heart sealed off from the kind of attention that would let the reminder through (2:74). The verse at 21:2 is the first step toward that seal. The community that hears a fresh reminder and turns it into amusement has begun the process by which no further reminder will be able to reach it. The Qur'an's warning is, in this sense, both descriptive and predictive.
verses.3:
> with their hearts ˹totally˺ distracted. The evildoers would converse secretly, ˹saying,˺ “Is this ˹one˺ not human like yourselves? Would you fall for ˹this˺ witchcraft, even though you can ˹clearly˺ see?”

**The Visible — As the Limit of What They Will Admit**

The verse ends the question with *wa antum tubṣirūn* — even while you see. The phrase is decisive. The audience has eyes; they can see him; the seeing ought to be a witness. But they have converted the seeing into evidence against him. To see a man is to know he is a man, and to know he is a man is to know he cannot be the bearer of revelation. The argument is the oldest objection to prophecy in the Qur'an: *Why has no treasure been granted to him, or a garden for him to eat from?* (25:8); *If only an angel were sent down with him!* (6:8). The objection recurs because it is the natural objection of a mind that has decided in advance what a messenger must look like.

The Qur'an's response to this objection across the sūrahs is to insist that messengers are sent in the form of their addressees (21:7). The choice is not a deficiency; it is a condition of legibility. A messenger from outside the human form could not be tested, could not be opposed, could not be refused on the basis of a free decision. The secret counsellors of 21:3 want a messenger who cannot be refused. The form of the question reveals what kind of messenger they would accept: one whose refusal would be impossible because the credentials would be physically coercive. *Tubṣirūn* — you see — exposes the limit of their empiricism. They will only believe what they can see; they have ruled out in advance that what they see might be the form of what they cannot.

**The Hearts That Distract Themselves**

The opening of the verse — *their hearts distracted* — uses the verb *shaghal*, the root from which *shaghl* (occupation, pre-occupation) comes. The hearts are not empty; they are full of something else. Distraction is not absence of mind; it is presence of a different mind. The audience is thinking about something else while the reminder is being delivered. The Qur'an names the something else in 63:9: *Do not let your wealth and your children distract you from the remembrance of Allah* (63:9). The distraction has a content; it is the cares of the world, the business of trade, the management of households. The hearts are not vacant. They are at work on something other than what is being addressed.

**Witchcraft As the Decided Diagnosis**

The secret counsel chooses the word *siḥr* — witchcraft, sorcery — to describe what the messenger brings. The choice is significant. The Qur'an elsewhere records that the same accusation was made against Moses (7:109; 26:35) and against earlier messengers. Witchcraft is not a natural category of dismissal; it is a category that mixes marvel with menace. To call a message witchcraft is to concede that something is happening while denying that the something is from God. The conference is not denying that the recitation is striking; it is denying that the striking is real. The verses deliver a verdict that the audience will not yet speak aloud.
verses.4:
> The Prophet responded, “My Lord ˹fully˺ knows every word spoken in the heavens and the earth. For He is the All-Hearing, All-Knowing.”

**A Short Reply to a Long Conference**

The previous verse records a secret conference; this verse records an one-sentence reply. The disproportion is the point. The audience has accused; the Prophet answers in a single sentence that does not address the accusation directly. He does not defend himself against the charge of being a human like themselves; he does not argue with the diagnosis of witchcraft; he does not answer the implicit demand for visible credentials. He says: my Lord knows every word spoken in the heavens and the earth, and He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

The asymmetry is the whole theology of prophecy. The accusation is from below; the response is from above. The conference of 21:3 argued from the visible to dismiss the invisible; the reply of 21:4 invokes the One who sees what is spoken in both realms and therefore is not dependent on the verdict of the conference. The Prophet's reply is not a defense; it is a transference of jurisdiction. He declines to litigate his own case in a court that has already decided it, and he cites instead the court that has not.

**Why the Reply Cites Hearing and Knowing, Not Speaking**

The verse names two divine attributes — Hearing and Knowing — but does not name Speaking. The omission is telling. The audience has accused the Prophet of fabricating speech; the Prophet's response cites the One who hears everything. The shift is from the speaker's claim to the hearer's record. Whatever is said in the heavens and the earth, including this accusation and this recitation, has already been entered into a book (10:61; 27:75). The divine Hearing is not passive reception; it is the taking of testimony. The conference has spoken; the testimony is taken.

**A Reply That Includes the Accusers**

This implicit verdict is what gives the verse its quiet force. The conference of 21:3 was self-congratulatory; the conference imagined itself as the private jury that would settle the question of the Prophet. The verse tells the hearer that the conference is itself on trial. *Every word spoken* — including the conference's words — has been heard. The hearer is being asked to imagine his own whispering as it sounds in the divine register. The hearing is not the angelic recording of moralists; it is the testimony of One whose Knowledge is commensurate with His Hearing. The whisper will not be the final word because the whisper has already been heard by One whose hearing is total.
verses.5:
> Yet they say, “This ˹Quran˺ is a set of confused dreams! No, he has fabricated it! No, he must be a poet! So let him bring us a ˹tangible˺ sign like those ˹prophets˺ sent before.”

**The Demand for a Tangible Sign**

After three diagnoses, the verse records a demand: *fa lītīnā bi-āyatin kama al-arṣalu al-awwalūn* — so let him bring us a sign like those sent before. The demand is the operative one; the three diagnoses are its rhetorical setup. The audience is willing to grant the possibility that the recitation is *something*; they are not willing to grant that it is enough. Whatever the recitation is — dreams, fabrication, poetry — it lacks what earlier prophets had: the visible, coercive, externally verifiable sign.

The pattern repeats. Pharaoh demanded a sign of Moses and was given nine (7:133); the people of Salih demanded a she-camel (7:73); the Quraysh demanded a fountain, a garden, an angel (25:7–8). The common element is the demand that the sign be of the kind that bypasses the freedom of the hearer. A sign that admits no refusal is the only sign the audience will accept. The request is not for evidence; the request is for compulsion.

**Why the Qur'an Records These Objections at Length**

A reader might expect the Qur'an to interrupt the objections with a quick rebuttal. It does not. It records the full range of objections and then, in 21:6, gives an one-sentence response. The disproportion is intentional. The Qur'an wants its audience to see the full catalogue of refusal so that the response can be understood as a response to the whole pattern, not to any particular objection. The objections are not the result of careful investigation; they are the by-products of a refusal to investigate.

**The "Signs Like Those Sent Before"**

This is also the only objection that reveals the audience's anxiety. They are not, in this verse, accusing the Prophet of being a fraud; they are asking him to produce a coercive proof. The request assumes that they would accept the message if the sign were given. But the Qur'an, in verses that follow, will not give the requested sign, because to give it would be to confirm the very ontology the audience has constructed — an ontology in which God coerces assent. The Qur'an's reply, in 21:6, is a refusal grounded not in inability but in principle.
verses.6:
> Not a ˹single˺ society We destroyed before them ever believed ˹after receiving the signs˺. Will these ˹pagans˺ then believe

**"Will These Then Believe?" — The Rhetorical Turn**

The closing question is rhetorical but it is also a concession. The Qur'an is not denying that the audience *could* believe. It is denying that the *demand* for a sign, understood as a precondition for belief, is itself a sign of belief. A community that says "we will believe only when we see" is a community that has already refused to believe without seeing. The request reveals the will; the will is the obstacle. The verse addresses the obstacle, not the request.

**The Audience as the Possible Exception**

The argument is the architecture of the entire sūrah's argument against the Meccan audience. Throughout al-Anbiyāʾ, the Qur'an returns to the pattern: a demand, a reminder of historical pattern, a refusal to repeat what has not worked. The sūrah's audience is invited, by the cumulative pressure of these reminders, to be the exception on the right side rather than on the wrong side. The closing question of 21:6 is the first move in a long argument that the Qur'an will make in many forms.
verses.7:
> We did not send ˹messengers˺ before you ˹O Prophet˺ except mere men inspired by Us. If you ˹polytheists˺ do not know ˹this already˺, then ask those who have knowledge ˹of the Scriptures˺

**The Qur'an's Defence of Its Own Messenger**

The verse is doing work that the audience had asked the Prophet to do for himself in 21:4 and 21:5. The audience had questioned his credentials; the Qur'an now supplies the credentials. The Prophet is not asked to argue his case; the case is argued for him. The argument is religious, historical, and grammatical. The Prophet is a man because messengers have always been men. The form is consistent with what the People of the Book would confirm. The inspiration is cast upon him from above; he did not generate it. Each of these is an answer to a separate objection raised in the preceding verses. The Prophet's defence is woven into the structure of the sūrah's argument, not left to him to deliver.

**Why Not Angels — And Why the Verse Says So**

If the audience had wanted a non-human messenger, the consequence would have been the abolition of the test. A messenger who is visibly distinct from the audience — an angel, a thunder-bearing apparition — would coerce assent. The hearer would not choose; the hearer would be overwhelmed. The Qur'an elsewhere makes the same argument: *Had We sent an angel, the matter would have been decided and they would have had no respite* (32:18). The structure of the test requires a messenger the addressees can refuse. The form of the messenger is therefore the form of the test itself.

**The Qur'an's Defence of Its Own Messenger**

The verse therefore also teaches a lesson about prophetic speech. A messenger's authority is not the authority of his own defence; it is the authority of the message that defends him. The audience has asked the Prophet to defend himself; the Qur'an refuses the format of the question. The defence is given by the One who sent him, and the defence is given in the form of the verse: short, declarative, and based on a record the audience already has.
verses.8:
> We did not give those messengers ˹supernatural˺ bodies that did not need food, nor were they immortal

**Why the Audience Wanted the Messengers to Be Otherwise**

The Meccan audience had wanted, in 21:5, a tangible sign like the earlier prophets. They had wanted, in 21:3, a non-human messenger whose credentials would be visible. The Qur'an now says that what the audience wants is precisely what the messengers were not. The negation is therefore not an admission; it is a refusal. The audience has asked for the impossible, and the impossibility is now identified as a refusal rather than a failure.

**The Qur'an's Rejection of the Apotheosis of Messengers**

This verse is a guardrail for the rest of the sūrah's account of prophets. The sūrah will narrate Abraham, Moses, David, Solomon, Job, Jonah, Zachariah, Mary, and others. Each is treated as a human figure with a specific test, a specific vocation, and a specific outcome. The verse at 21:8 tells the reader in advance that none of these figures is to be deified. They ate food; they died; their significance is in what they were given to convey and in what they chose to do with the conveyance. The biographical material that follows is to be read as the history of obedient humans, not as the history of beings who had crossed out of the human condition.

**The Verse As a Rule for Reading the Rest of the Sūrah**

The reader who has read 21:8 will not be tempted to read the prophet narratives of al-Anbiyāʾ as mythic biographies of demigods. The prophets are men; the men ate; the men died. The verses that follow will narrate specific historical and human tests. The verse at 21:8 is the antecedent of every story that follows. It places the reader in the correct interpretive frame before the stories begin: these are not the stories of beings who escaped the human condition; these are the stories of beings who bore it with extraordinary fidelity and were given, in return, the mission that ordinary men could not bear.

This framing is part of the sūrah's argument. The audience had asked for an inhuman messenger. The sūrah's answer, given across multiple verses, is that the inhuman messenger would have been useless. The audience is being given a sūrah full of men, and the men are the answer to their request. The audience will recognise, by the end of the sūrah, that the men were enough.
verses.9:
> Then We fulfilled Our promise to them, saving them along with whoever We willed and destroying the transgressors

**The Distribution of Mercy and Judgment**

The verse names two acts together: saving and destroying. The pairing is essential. A Qur'anic theology that spoke only of mercy would lose the sharpness of the test; a Qur'anic theology that spoke only of destruction would lose the meaning of the calling. The messengers are saved because they bore the message; the transgressors are destroyed because they refused it. Between these two groups are those whose salvation is not automatic — *man nashāʾu* — those whom God wills to save. The middle term is not an euphemism; it is a recognition that salvation is not determined by membership in any visible category. It is determined by the divine will working through the conditions of the test.

The verse therefore refuses two simplifications. The first is that salvation is automatic for the messengers and their communities; the verse says *man nashāʾu*, whoever We willed, not whoever was with them. The second is that destruction is automatic for those who oppose; the verse says *al-mujrimīn*, the criminals, the doers of harm. The qualification matters. The destruction that came upon the communities was not punishment for refusal as such; it was punishment for the specific acts by which the refusal was enacted. The Qur'an elsewhere insists that *lā takūnu kal-ladhīna ẓalamū* — do not be like those who did wrong (2:254). The wrong is specified; the destruction is attached to the specified wrong.

**The Grammar of "Then" — Time, Sequence, and Fulfillment**

The verse begins with *thumma* — then. The particle marks sequence and elevation. The *thumma* of 21:9 is the *thumma* that, in Arabic rhetoric, signals both temporal succession and a kind of escalation. The fulfilment came; it came at the proper time; it came after a delay enough to constitute a real test. The delay is part of the fulfilment; it is not a postponement.
verses.10:
> We have surely revealed to you a Book, in which there is glory for you. Will you not then understand

The previous verses narrated the history of earlier messengers; this verse pivots to the present. The Qur'an has been recording what happened to Noah, Abraham, Moses, and the rest; it now turns to the audience of Muhammad and says: we have revealed to you a Book.

The description — *in which there is glory for you* — names the content of the Book from the audience's perspective. The question — *will you not then understand?* — is the rhetorical close that turns the verse into an appeal.

**"Glory for You" — The Meaning of the Qur'an for Its Audience**

The Arabic *fīhi majjukum* — in it is your glory, your honour, your dignity — names the function of the Book from the inside of the community. The audience is told that the Book is not only a warning or an indictment; it is the source of their honour. The word *maji* or *majj* is rare in the Qur'an; its appearance here attaches the entire vocabulary of dignity to the recited text. The audience's prestige, the verse says, is not in their ancestry, their wealth, or their numbers. It is in the Book.

**"We Have Surely Revealed" — The Divine Voice in the First Person**

The verse returns to the divine first person plural — *we have revealed*. This is the first time in the sūrah since 21:5 that God has spoken in the first person about the Book itself. The earlier verses had the Prophet speaking (21:4) or had third-person narration (21:6–9). The shift back to the first person plural signals that the Book is being spoken of as the direct object of the divine act. The Book is not a human product; the Book is what God has revealed.

**Glory As a Technical Term**

The word *majj* — glory, honour — is one of the Qur'an's terms for the kind of dignity that comes from being chosen by God for a particular role. The children of Israel were given *maǧd* at 4:54 — *and He gave them a kingdom and great wisdom*. The same root appears in the prayer of Solomon at 27:15 — *and He gave me a kingdom and a speech of clarity*. The vocabulary is consistent: *majd* is not biological or political; it is the gift of a position before God. The verse tells the audience of the Qur'an that the Book is the source of this kind of dignity. They are being made, by the Book, into a people with a role. The role is the content of the glory.
verses.11:
> ˹Imagine˺ how many societies of wrongdoers We have destroyed, raising up other people after them

**The Commentators' Identification of a Specific People**

The verse's deeper claim is that destruction is not the end of the story. After the destruction comes the raising of another people. The replacement is a divine act; the people are not raised by themselves. The verse therefore refuses both the despair that comes from seeing wrongdoing flourish and the complacency that comes from imagining that wrongdoing is permanent. The shattering is real, and the replacement is also real. The one is the consequence of moral failure; the other is the consequence of divine patience.

**A Question That Asks the Audience to Count**

The verse opens with an interjection — *wa kam qaṣamnā* — usually translated "and how many" but carrying in Arabic the sense of "how many have We shattered." The verb *qaṣaʿa* is violent. It means to shatter, to break into pieces, to demolish. The verse does not say that the communities were dismissed, or dismissed gently; it says they were shattered. The choice of verb is the choice of what happened to them. Communities built on wrongdoing do not leave the field quietly; they are broken open.

**The Commentators' Identification of a Specific People**

The classical commentators, including al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī, mentioned a specific people they connected with the verse: the people of Ḥadūr in Yemen, to whom a prophet was sent and who rejected him. The identification is not certain; the verse itself does not name the community. The general statement is firmer than the particular identification, and the Qur'an elsewhere gives examples without tying them to a single place. The function of the specific identification in the commentary is to remind the reader that the abstract claim of the verse has a concrete historical referent; the destruction is not a theoretical event.

**A Verse That the Reading Community Must Inhabit**

The verse is also a interpretive instruction. By asking the audience to imagine the number of destroyed communities, the verse trains them to read their own moment as one entry in a longer list. The audience is not to imagine themselves at the beginning of history, with all the options still open; they are to imagine themselves in the middle of a long sequence, with the past as a witness to what comes of the choices they will make. The imagining is not idle. It is an exercise in moral location. The audience is being asked to find themselves in the sequence.

The verse is one of many in the Qur'an that read the present through the past. *How many a town have We destroyed* — the phrasing recurs at 6:6, 7:4, 17:17, 19:98, 28:58, 38:3, 50:36. The repetition is not redundancy; it is the consistent application of a method. The Qur'an reads history as a single body of evidence, and each verse that mentions the destruction of past communities is a reminder that the evidence is cumulative. The audience is asked to weigh the present against the cumulative evidence. The weighing has a predictable outcome: the present is reminded that it is not the first generation to face the test, and that previous generations have, in the main, failed it.
verses.12:
> When the wrongdoers sensed ˹the arrival of˺ Our torment, they started to run away from their cities

**A Reading That Combines External and Internal Peril**

The classical commentators, including al-Ṭabarī, read *ḥassaū ba'sanā* as "when they sensed Our might" — that is, when they perceived the imminent destruction *before* it arrived. The reading is important. The verse is not saying that the wrongdoers were hit and then ran; it is saying that they perceived the coming blow and tried to escape it. The wilful had finally been replaced by the involuntary. They had refused the warnings; now they sense the consequence.

**"From Their Cities" — The Loss of Place**

This is one of the recurring features of the Qur'an's Last-Day language. The promise of a settled life in a built environment is real; the threat of the loss of that life is also real; the two are not contradictory. The same verse that speaks of building cities and enjoying their fruits (28:57–58) speaks of being driven out of them. The cities are not the permanent possession of anyone; they are entrusted, and the trust can be revoked. The verse at 21:12 records the moment of revocation for the wrongdoers. The audience of the Qur'an is invited to recognise that the same revocation is always one bad decision away.

**The Verse That Prepares for the Mockery of 21:13**

The next verse will mock the wrongdoers by inviting them to return to their luxuries. The present verse prepares for that mockery by establishing that the wrongdoers are now in flight. The contrast is the contrast of someone running for his life being invited, with a smile, to go home. The verse at 21:12 makes the contrast possible by showing the audience the flight; without the flight, the mockery at 21:13 would be cruel without being ironic. With the flight, the mockery becomes a poetic image of the futility of the escape. The two verses together perform the Qur'an's habitual move: it shows the seriousness of the situation by one rhetorical figure, and it deepens that seriousness by an ironic counter-figure. The audience is asked to feel both the gravity and the irony; the gravity is the more important, but the irony sharpens it.
verses.13:
> ˹They were told,˺ “Do not run away! Return to your luxuries and your homes, so you may be questioned ˹about your fate˺.”

**A Voice That Speaks from Inside the Punishment**

The previous verse described the flight of the wrongdoers; this verse records what was said to them as they fled. The voice is unnamed. The commentators record that it could be the angels, or it could be God. The grammatical alternative matters less than the rhetorical effect: the voice comes from the inside of the destruction, addressing those who are trying to flee it. The voice does not say "you cannot escape"; it says "return to what you had.".

**"So You May Be Questioned" — The Closed Circuit of Account**

The phrase *laʾallakum tusʾalūn* — so that you may be questioned — is one of the Qur'an's most carefully chosen expressions. The verb *suʾāl* can mean to be asked, to be questioned, or to be held accountable. The form *tusʾalūn* is in the passive; the questioner is not named. The audience is asked to consider who would be doing the questioning. The implied agent is God; the implied forum is the reckoning that the opening verse of the sūrah announced. The flight was a try to escape that reckoning; the command to return is an invitation to enter it.

The phrase *laʾallakum* — perhaps, so that — adds an ironic distance. The Qur'an often uses this particle to mark an outcome that has been determined but is being presented in softened form. The wrongdoers will be questioned; the question is whether they will be questioned now or later. The flight delays nothing. The questioning is already in motion.
verses.14:
> They cried, “Woe to us! We have surely been wrongdoers.”

**Why the Confession Comes Too Late**

The verse is read by al-Qurṭubī as the confession made when the angels began to carry out the punishment. The timing is the entire point. The wrongdoers had refused to confess when confession would have changed the outcome; they confess when the outcome is no longer in question. The Qur'an elsewhere calls this *istighātha baʿd al-amr* — calling for help after the matter has been decided (40:66). The confession is real; the time for it has passed. The verse therefore does not promise that confession is enough; it records that confession, even at the last moment, still does what confession does. It acknowledges the truth of what happened.

**The Word "Woe" — An Interjection with Weight**

The Arabic *wayl* is one of the Qur'an's heaviest words of distress. It is sometimes translated "woe," sometimes "alas," and sometimes left untranslated because no English word carries the same finality. The form *waylanā* — woe to us — extends the interjection from a single object to the speakers themselves. The wrongdoers are saying "woe to us." They are the objects of the woe they are naming; they are the targets of the distress they are expressing. The interjection collapses the distance between the speaker and the topic of the speech. The wrongdoers are not commenting on their situation; they are entering it.

**The Verse's Call to a Different Kind of Confession**

The audience of the Qur'an reads 21:14 as a record of a confession that did not save. The verse is therefore a call to a different kind of confession — one made before the punishment, before the angels begin to carry out the sentence, before the time for confession has run out. The Qur'an makes this kind of confession available. The audience is invited to make it. The making is the alternative to the cry of 21:14.
verses.15:
> They kept repeating their cry until We mowed them down, ˹leaving them˺ lifeless

**"Leaving Them Lifeless" — Khāmidīn and the Word for Stilled**

The Arabic *khāmidīn* is a rare and powerful word. It names a kind of stillness that is more than motionlessness. The same root is used for an extinguished flame, for a settled dust, for the silence of a thing that has finished its active motion. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verb *khamada* can also mean simply to die. The verse therefore does not say that the wrongdoers were slain in the violence of an attack; it says that they were left in a stillness that is itself a form of death. The stillness is the final state of those who have been mowed down; they are not moving any more.

The translation's "lifeless" captures this. The wrongdoers are not described as bodies; they are described as the absence of life.

**The Closing Question — "Divine Amusement?"**

The question *afa-lāhin* is sharp because the previous verses of the sūrah have already addressed the audience's accusation of play. The audience had said in 21:2 that they listened to the message *laʿiban* — in play. The Qur'an will return to the theme in 21:16: *We did not create the heavens and the earth in play* (21:16). The closing question of 21:15 therefore connects the audience's earlier accusation with the present destruction. The destruction was not play; the audience's accusation that the message was play is being returned to them. The verse names the connection without spelling it out. The audience is left to do the work of recognising that the accusation they had made against the message is precisely the accusation they cannot make against God.

**A Verse That Reframes the Audience's Accusation**

The audience had accused the Prophet of producing confused dreams, fabricated speech, and poetry (21:5). The Qur'an now reframes that accusation. The Prophet is not the one whose work is in question; the audience's own framework is in question. The audience had assumed that the message was a kind of entertainment; the verse says that entertainment is precisely what God does not produce. The destruction of the wrongdoers is not entertainment; the creation of the heavens and the earth (which the next verse will name) is not entertainment. The only entertainment in the sequence is the entertainment the audience had imagined the message to be. The audience is being asked to recognise the inversion: they had accused the message of being play; the verdict at 21:15 is that play is the wrong word for what has happened.

The verse is also a warning about the cost of the cry. The wrongdoers cried until they were cut down. The cry was real, but the cry was too late. The verse is therefore a call to make a different kind of cry — one that comes before the cutting, in the time when cries can still be heard. The closing question — *afa-lāhin* — invites the reader to enter the time when cries are still heard, and to cry then, in the way that is appropriate to the situation. The verse's invitation is not casual; it is the closing of a long argument that has been running since 21:1.
verses.16:
> We did not create the heavens and the earth and everything in between for sport

**Not in Sport — The Reframing of Creation**

The verse answers, with the divine voice, the question that closed the previous verse. *Mā khalaqnā al-samāwāti wa al-arḍa wa mā baynahumā lāʿibīn* — We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them as ones who play. The verb *khalaqa* is the Qur'an's standard verb for creation; the negative *lāʿibīn* — as players, in sport — is the same word that has appeared in 21:2 and 21:15. The repetition is the point. The audience had accused the message of being play; the Qur'an now says that creation is not play.

The verse therefore refuses two uses of the word. It refuses to apply *laʿib* to the divine act, and it refuses to allow the audience's previous use of the word to remain uncontested. The word has now been defined in the strongest possible way: it is the wrong word for what God does. The audience's earlier accusation was therefore not a description; it was a category mistake. The verse does not say the audience is mistaken about a fact; it says they have applied a word that does not fit.

**The Argumentative Edge That Does Not Need to be Spoken**

The verse's argumentative edge is silent but precise. The audience had been treating the message as play (21:2). The audience's framework cannot coherently treat creation as serious and the message as sport. The verse forces the audience to choose. The choice is not between the message and creation; the choice is between a coherent worldview and an incoherent one.

This is the work that the verse does without saying it explicitly. The Qur'an rarely needs to spell out the implication of its claims; the claims are usually tight enough that the implications follow. The audience is invited to do the inference. The inference is not difficult. The audience that refuses to do it is the audience that is already hardened, and the verse has not been written for hardened audiences to comfort them.

**Connection to the Larger Argument of the Sūrah**

The verse is the centre of a passage that runs from 21:1 to 21:30. The passage is the sūrah's argument against the Meccan audience's refusal of the message. The argument moves from accusation (21:2–5) to historical reminder (21:6–9) to direct address (21:10) to narrative of destruction (21:11–15). The verse at 21:16 is the pivot. After the verse, the argument turns to the metaphysical foundations of the message — creation, divine purpose, the nature of God. The shift is deliberate. The historical argument has reached its climax in the destruction of the wrongdoers; the next step is to ground the message in the structure of creation itself.

The verse is therefore not just one argumentative move among many; it is the move that allows the rest of the argument to happen. The audience is told that the world is not play. From this foundation, the audience can be told about the purpose of creation, about the responsibility of human beings, about the impossibility of polytheism, and about the necessity of worship. Each of these arguments depends on the foundation that the verse at 21:16 has laid. The verse is the floor on which the rest of the argument walks.
verses.17:
> Had We intended to take ˹some˺ amusement, We could have found it in Our presence, if that had been Our Will

**A Conditional That Denies Its Own Condition**

The verse is a conditional statement whose condition is denied. *Law aradnā a nattakhidha lahwān* — if We had wanted to take amusement — is the structure of a hypothesis that is then refused. The Qur'an uses this structure throughout to make claims about divine action by specifying what would not have been done. Here, the claim is that God does not take amusement. The denial of the condition is the teaching of the verse.

The verb *ittakhadha* — to take, to acquire, to adopt — is the same verb used elsewhere for taking a consort, taking a child, taking a partner. The word *lahw* in the verse means diversion, play, amusement, the kind of activity one undertakes to escape more serious things. The Qur'an's choice of *ittakhadha lahwān* — to take amusement as one would take a companion — emphasises that amusement is treated here as a thing one might have done. The verse says: this is not something we have done.

**"In Our Presence" — The Location of the Hypothetical Amusement**

The second half of the verse says *la-ijtadaynāhu min ladunnā* — we would have found it from what is with Us, in Our presence. The hypothetical amusement, had it been sought, would not have been sought in creation. It would have been sought in something closer to God. The commentators have read this in several ways. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as saying that if God had wanted to play, He would not have created the world at all; the world is not the place of divine play. Other commentators read it as a reference to the kinds of companions and consorts that the polytheists imagined God had — the consort, the child, the partner.

**The Verse's Place in the Anti-Polytheistic Argument**

The verse is part of a passage that will culminate in the radical monotheistic claims of 21:21–23. The progression is deliberate: creation is not play (21:16). If it had been play, it would not have required the world (21:17). The truth is that truth is hurled against falsehood and falsehood is crushed (21:18). The beings in the heavens and the earth belong to God (21:19). The beings near God do not tire of worshipping Him (21:20); the gods imagined on earth cannot raise the dead (21:21); if there were other gods, the heavens and earth would be corrupted (21:22); God cannot be questioned, but all others will be questioned (21:23). The verse at 21:17 is therefore one move in a longer argument that is dismantling the polytheistic framework piece by piece.

The dismantling is not argumentative in the argumentative sense; it is structural. Each verse removes one support of the polytheistic framework. The verse at 21:17 removes the support that depends on divine need. Without divine need, there is no reason to imagine that God took a consort, begot a child, or set up partners. The polytheistic worldview loses its foundation; the rest of the passage clears away the remaining structures. The verse is therefore not just a denial; it is a demolition that allows the construction of the next argument.
verses.18:
> In fact, We hurl the truth against falsehood, leaving it crushed, and it quickly vanishes. And woe be to you for what you claim

**The Image of Truth Against Falsehood**

The verse offers one of the Qur'an's most compact images. *Naqdhifu al-ḥaqqa ʿalā al-bāṭili* — We hurl the truth against falsehood. The verb *naqdhifu* names a forceful, casting motion. The truth is not presented; it is cast. The casting is against falsehood, and the result is the crushing of falsehood. The Arabic *yadmaghuhu* — to crush, to smash — is unusually violent. The same root appears in the word for the brain (*dimāgh*); the verb conveys the image of breaking a skull open to reach the brain. The verse is saying: when the truth is cast at falsehood, the falsehood is not gently displaced; it is destroyed at its core.

This is the Qur'an's fundamental ontology of the relationship between truth and falsehood. They are not co-equal forces that balance each other; they are not complementary perspectives that can both be true.

**The Closing Woe — "Woe Be to You for What You Claim"**

The verse ends with *wa waylun lakum mimmā taṣifūn* — and woe to you for what you claim. The verb *waṣafa* — to describe, to claim, to ascribe — is the same verb that appears in the audience's accusations of witchcraft and fabrication in 21:3 and 21:5. The closing line therefore returns to the audience. The audience had accused the Prophet of producing confused dreams, fabricated speech, and poetry. The verse is now saying: the truth has been cast at the falsehood, and the falsehood has vanished; woe to you for the descriptions you have been making.

**The Verse's Relation to Other Passages**

The relationship between truth and falsehood is a recurring theme in the Qur'an. 17:81 says: *Truth has come, and falsehood has vanished.* 8:8 says: *So that He may verify the truth and prove falsehood to be false.* 34:49 says: *Truth has come. Falsehood originates naught, nor restores.* 42:24 says: *God wipes out falsehood and verifies the truth through His Words.* The verse at 21:18 is the most violent of these images. The verb *damaghahu* — to crush — is not present in any of the other passages. The violence of the image is appropriate to the moment. The audience has been called to confess; the audience has refused; the casting of truth against falsehood is the divine response to the refusal. The response is not gentle.

**A Woe That Precedes the Woes That Follow**

The verse ends with the first of a series of woes in this sūrah. The audience will hear *waylun* again at 21:46, 54:8, and many other places. The woe is the Qur'an's standard word for the divine verdict pronounced on those who have refused the truth. The verse at 21:18 introduces the word into the sūrah; the audience is warned that the verdict is being prepared. The woe will come; the question is whether the audience will hear it as a warning in time, or as a verdict after the time. The verse at 21:18 is the warning; the verses that follow will determine which kind of hearing the audience has.
verses.19:
> To Him belong all those in the heavens and the earth. And those nearest to Him are not too proud to worship Him, nor do they tire

**"Those Nearest to Him" — The Proximity That Is Worship**

The second half of the verse specifies a particular group: *wa alladhīna ʿindahu* — those who are with Him, those in His presence, those nearest to Him. The phrase has been understood by al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī to refer to the angels — the beings whose existence is the most direct response to the divine presence. The verse is therefore making a claim about the highest order of created beings. If even the highest order worships, the implication for lower orders is firm.

**"Not Too Proud" — The Refusal of a Specific Vice**

The Arabic *lā yastakbirūna* — they do not behave with arrogance, they are not too proud — names a specific vice. Pride is not the only obstacle to worship; fear, fatigue, confusion, and distraction are also obstacles. The verse names the most theologically dangerous obstacle, which is the refusal to acknowledge the order of being. The beings nearest to God could, if they wished, claim a status that exempted them from worship. They could claim to be too exalted to prostrate, too close to the source to need to express gratitude. The verse says they do not.

The verses will return to the refusal by humans (Iblīs in 21:22 is not named here, but the contrast is implicit). The audience is invited to consider which side of the contrast they are on.
verses.20:
> They glorify ˹Him˺ day and night, never wavering

**"Never Wavering" — The Unfailing Continuation**

The phrase *lā yafturūn* — they do not cease, they do not interrupt, they do not waver — closes the verse. The verb *fatra* names a gap or interruption in an otherwise continuous activity. The verse says there is no such gap in the angelic worship. The worship is uninterrupted; the angels do not take a break; they do not alternate between glorification and other activities; the glorification is the steady state of their existence.

This is the second time the verse has emphasised the continuity of the angelic worship. The previous verse (21:19) said they do not tire; this verse says they do not waiver. The two claims are related but distinct. Not to tire is to have the energy for the activity; not to waiver is to remain committed to the activity. The angels are not just able to continue; they continue without interruption. The combination of the two claims is what makes the angelic worship a model of the permanent posture that the verse is describing.

**The Relation to 41:38**

The verse echoes 41:38, which says: *Those who are near to Him do not boast against each other, and they do not tire.* The two passages together form one of the Qur'an's recurring descriptions of the highest order of created beings. The echo is not accidental; the Qur'an returns to the same description because the description is foundational. The point is not to give biographical information about the angels; the point is to describe a permanent feature of the moral order. The moral order includes beings whose worship is the steady state of their existence.
verses.21:
> Or have they taken gods from the earth, who can raise the dead

**Why Resurrection Is the Litmus Test**

The verb *baʿatha* — to send forth, to raise, to bring back to life — names the central divine act that no created being can perform. The Qur'an elsewhere describes the challenge of the resurrection explicitly: *And they say, "When we are bones and crumbled dust, will we be raised as a new creation?"* (17:49; 17:98); *They say, "Will we indeed be returned to the original state of creation?"* (79:10). The Meccan audience had struggled with the teaching about bodily resurrection; the verse at 21:21 is built around the same struggle. The audience doubted that God would raise the dead; the audience is now being asked whether their gods could do what they doubted God would do.

**"From the Earth" — The Origin That Disqualifies**

The phrase *ālihatan min al-arḍi* — gods from the earth — specifies the origin of the gods the audience has taken. They are not transcendent; they are terrestrial. They came from the earth; they are made of the earth; they will return to the earth. The gods of the Meccan pantheon were often stones, trees, or statues carved from materials of the earth. The verse's specification of "from the earth" is the description of their origin and a quiet dismissal of their status. Gods that are from the earth are part of the earth's furniture; they are not its rulers.

This is also a refusal of the polytheistic worldview on a metaphysical level. The polytheists had imagined that the gods were at a distance from the world, sometimes intervening. The verse is saying that the gods they have taken are not at a distance; they are from the same place they inhabit. The gods are part of the world; they do not transcend it; they cannot raise anyone from the world because they are part of the world. The audience's framework has assigned transcendence to beings that have none.

The commentators note that the imagery of biological renewal — the revival of dead land by rain — is treated elsewhere as a symbol of resurrection (35:9). The verse at 21:21 fits within a wider Qur'anic argument that takes the revival of dead land as a small-scale model of the larger resurrection. The audience that sees land die and revive every season has a sign of the resurrection before its eyes. The verse's question — *who can raise the dead?* — is therefore not addressed to a community that lacks the data for an answer. The community has the data; the community has been watching the earth die and revive; the community has been told that the same hand that revives the land will revive the dead.
verses.22:
> Had there been other gods besides Allah in the heavens or the earth, both ˹realms˺ would have surely been corrupted. So Glorified is Allah, Lord of the Throne, far above what they claim

**The Argument from Corruption**

The verse makes a structural argument for monotheism. *Law kāna fīhimā ālihatun illā Allāhu la-fasadatā* — if there were in them gods other than God, they would have been corrupted. Any system with multiple independent authorities would not hold together. Each god would have a will; each will would seek to implement itself; the implementation of multiple wills would result in contradiction, and the contradiction would tear the system apart.

**The Closing Declaration of Transcendence**

The verse closes with *subḥāna Allāhi rabbi al-ʿarshi ʿammā yasifūn* — glory be to God, Lord of the Throne, above what they ascribe. The declaration of divine transcendence is the response to the ascriptions of partners, consorts, and children that the polytheists have made. The verb *sabbaha* — to declare transcendent, to glorify — is the same verb used of the angels' continuous worship (21:20). The audience is being asked to join the angels in declaring divine transcendence against the false ascriptions.

The phrase *rabb al-ʿarsh* — Lord of the Throne — names God in one of His most exalted titles. The Throne (*al-ʿarsh*) is, in the Qur'anic vocabulary, the seat of divine governance; the Lord of the Throne is the one in whose governance the heavens and the earth are held. The verse is therefore not just naming God in the abstract; it is naming God as the one whose governance is the condition of the heavens and the earth being intact. The Throne is the locus of the oneness that has just been argued for.

**The Verse As the Centre of the Anti-Polytheistic Argument**

The verse is the centre of the sūrah's anti-polytheistic argument. The verses before it (21:19–21) established that the heavens and the earth belong to God, that those nearest to Him worship without wavering, and that gods from the earth cannot raise the dead. The verse at 21:22 makes the structural argument that follows from these premises: if there were gods other than God, the order of the world would have been corrupted. The verses after it (21:23 onward) will draw the consequences: God is not questioned, but all others will be questioned; the audience is challenged to bring its proof; the messengers have always proclaimed the same monotheistic message.
verses.23:
> He cannot be questioned about what He does, but they will ˹all˺ be questioned

**The Asymmetry of Accountability**

The verse establishes a fundamental asymmetry. *Lā yuʾsalu ʿammā yafʿalu wa hum yuʾsalūn* — He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned. The verb *suʾāl* — to question, to hold to account — is the same verb that has appeared in 21:13 and 21:14; here it is given its sharpest application. God is not answerable to any external authority; creatures are answerable to Him. The asymmetry is not an arbitrary preference; it is the structural feature of the relationship between the Creator and the created.

**The Reverse Asymmetry — They Will Be Questioned**

The verse's second half — *wa hum yuʾsalūn* — but they will be questioned — restores the asymmetry the first half has established. The creatures will be questioned; the questioning will be done by the One who is not questioned. The forum is therefore not symmetric; the forum is one-sided. The creature stands before the Creator and is questioned; the Creator does not stand before the creature and answer.

The verse does not specify what the creatures will be questioned about. The commentators have inferred that the questioning will be about the deeds, the words, the intentions, the moments of life, and the choices made. The Qur'an elsewhere specifies some of the content of the questioning (the five greater things in the hadith tradition; the moments of standing before God in 36:65; the recording of every word and deed in 36:12; the weighing of deeds in 21:47). The verse at 21:23 is the general principle of which these specifications are applications.

The audience of al-Anbiyāʾ had not been engaged in philosophical questioning; they had been engaged in practical refusal. The verse at 21:23 addresses the arguments at their root.

**A Verse That Makes the Subsequent Demands Coherent**

The verse is the foundation for what the rest of the sūrah will demand of the audience. The audience will be challenged to bring proof of their claims (21:24); they will be told that messengers have always proclaimed the same message (21:25); they will be told that the things they have taken as partners are servants, not gods (21:26–29). None of these demands would be coherent if the creature could question the Creator. The demands are coherent only because the forum has been set by the verse at 21:23. The audience is being asked to recognise that the forum is not theirs; the forum is God's; the audience will be the ones questioned in it.

This is one of the most important religious moves in the Qur'an. The verse refuses to enter the creature's forum. The creature has imagined that the appropriate response to the message is to question the message's source. The verse says: the source is not to be questioned; you are. The forum is therefore the forum of accountability, not the forum of intellectual debate. The audience is invited to recognise the forum and to act accordingly. The recognition is the work the verse is asking for.
verses.24:
> Or have they taken other gods besides Him? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Show ˹me˺ your proof. Here is ˹the Quran,˺ the Reminder for those with me; along with ˹earlier Scriptures,˺ the Reminder for those before me.” But most of them do not know the truth, so they turn away

**"The Reminder for Those Before Me" — The Earlier Scriptures**

The second *dhikr* is the Reminder for those before the Prophet. The verse is referring to the Torah, the Gospel, and the other revealed books that preceded the Qur'an. The *dhikr* is the same function in a different community; the function is universal. The earlier communities also had a Reminder; the Reminder for them is the same kind of book as the Reminder for the present community.

This is part of the broader Qur'anic argument that the previous religious communities had been informed, in their own Scriptures, of the coming of the Prophet. The verse at 21:24 is not making that argument in detail; it is making the general claim that the Reminder is one and that the present Reminder is the same kind of thing as the previous Reminder. The detail of the argument is elsewhere; the principle is here.

**A Verse That Refuses to Enter the Audience's Forum**

In context, the verse functions as the argument counterpart to 21:23. The verse at 21:23 refused to allow the audience to question God; this verse refuses to allow the audience to make unsupported claims about gods. The two refusals together close the avenues by which the audience might have tried to continue its position. The audience is left with the position, but without the forum in which to defend it. The closure is the work of the verse.
verses.25:
> We never sent a messenger before you ˹O Prophet˺ without revealing to him: “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Me, so worship Me ˹alone˺.”

**The Unchanging Message Across Messengers**

The verse makes one of the Qur'an's most theologically significant claims: every messenger has been sent with the same essential message. *Wa mā arsalnā qablaka min rasūlin illā nūḥī ilayhi annahu lā ilāha illā ana fa-ʿbudūnī* — We did not send any messenger before you except that We revealed to him that there is no god except Me, so worship Me. The verse uses the conditional structure *illā* — except that — to make the claim absolute. Every messenger; every revelation; the same message.

**"There Is No God Except Me" — The First-Person Voice**

The verse puts the message in the first person of God. *Lā ilāha illā ana* — there is no god except I. The first-person speech is the speech of the One who is being addressed. The structural ambiguity of the Arabic is significant: *ana* — I — refers back to the One speaking in the verse, who is God. The saying of the message is the saying of the divine utterance; the message is not the Prophet's composition; it is the divine self-disclosure.

**The Uniform Content, the Varied Forms**

The Qur'an elsewhere acknowledges that the laws given to different communities were different (5:48). The uniformity of the verse at 21:25 is not an uniformity of all the details; it is an uniformity of the central message. The details are the work of the *sharīʿah*; the message is the work of the *dīn*. The verse is about the *dīn*.

The distinction is important for understanding the rest of the Qur'an's treatment of other religions. The Qur'an can say, at the level of the *dīn*, that all messengers brought the same message. The Qur'an can also say, at the level of the *sharīʿah*, that the specific commands given to different communities differed. The two claims are not contradictory. The verse at 21:25 is making the first claim; the verses that follow will work out the implications of both claims together.
verses.26:
> And they say, “The Most Compassionate has offspring!” Glory be to Him! In fact, those ˹angels˺ are only ˹His˺ honoured servants

**The Audience's Most Theologically Specific Accusation**

The verse records an accusation of particular precision: *The Most Compassionate has taken a child*. The Arabic *ittakhadha waladan* — has taken a child — is the same construction used in 21:17 of taking amusement. The accusation is therefore placed alongside the previous argument. The audience had accused God of having offspring; the verse responds with the same kind of refusal it has been making throughout.

**"Glory Be to Him!" — The Transcendence Refused**

The verse replies with *subḥānahu* — glory be to Him — declaring divine transcendence against the ascription. The verb is the same one used by the angels in their continuous worship (21:20). The audience is being asked to join the angels in declaring that God is utterly transcendent over the ascription. The declaration is the response; the ascription is the error.

**The Multiple Targets of the Verse**

The verse addresses two distinct religious errors. The first is the Arabian polytheistic belief that the angels are the daughters of God. The second is the Christian doctrine that Jesus is the Son of God. Both errors are forms of divine filiation; both involve the ascription of offspring to God; both are addressed by the same verse. The Qur'an does not typically single out one error at a time; it often addresses multiple errors in a single verse, because the verses are about categories of error rather than specific historical instances.

The verse is the next move in the sūrah's argument against polytheism. The audience had taken partners; the partners had been given of being status they did not have. The verse at 21:26 names the partners: the angels. The recognition is the conversion the verse is asking for.
verses.27:
> who do not speak until He has spoken, ˹only˺ acting at His command

**"Acting at His Command" — The Source of the Angels' Action**

The verse continues *wa bi-amrihi yaʿmalūn* — and they act at His command. The verb *yaʿmalu* — to act, to do — names the active dimension of the angels' service. The angels act; the acts are at God's command; the command is the source. What the verse describes, in other words, is a chain of obedience: God commands; the angels act; the acts follow from the command. The chain does not run in the other direction; the angels do not command and have God act.

The chain refuses a particular kind of piety that imagines the angels as intercessors who can independently intervene in the divine economy.

**The Relation to 21:19–20**

The verse continues the description of the angels begun at 21:19. The angels are nearest to God (21:19); they do not tire of worshipping God (21:19); they glorify God continuously (21:20). What 21:27 adds is a specific feature of their conduct: they do not speak before God speaks. That feature is the source of the appropriateness of their worship. The angels' worship is appropriate because it follows the divine initiative; the angels do not worship on their own initiative and then expect God to ratify it. The order is the other way around.

**A Refusal of Independent Intercession**

The verse is one of the Qur'anic foundations for the teaching about intercession. the teaching about intercession in the Qur'an is carefully bounded. Intercession can occur only with God's permission; the permission is specified in 21:28; the permission cannot be assumed. On their own initiative, the angels never intercede. They do not have an independent store of intercessory power. Their action, including any intercessory action, follows from the divine command. The verse is the foundation for the careful Qur'anic treatment of intercession: the angels are honoured servants; their honour does not include the right to intercede independently; the intercession is a matter of divine permission.

That foundation is one of the most distinctive features of the Qur'anic doctrine of intercession. The doctrine is not a denial that intercession can occur; the doctrine is a careful specification of when and how it can occur. The verse at 21:27 is one of the specifications: the angels do not start; they do not precede God in any act; they wait for the command. The intercession, when it occurs, follows the same pattern.

**The Verse That Frames the Angels' Service**

What 21:27 frames is what the angels' service looks like in practice. The previous verses had described the angels as those nearest to God and as those who glorify without tiring. The verse at 21:27 specifies the practical form of that service. The practical form is what makes the angelic service possible. A service without the waiting would not be service; it would be initiative. A service without the acting would be silent witness; the angels act as well as wait. The combination of the two is the form of the honoured service.
verses.28:
> He ˹fully˺ knows what is ahead of them and what is behind them. They do not intercede except for whom He approves, and they tremble in awe of Him

**The Scope of God's Knowledge of the Angels**

The verse specifies the scope of God's knowledge of the angels. *Yaʿlamu mā bayna aydīhim wa mā khalfahum* — He knows what is before them and what is behind them. The phrase *mā bayna aydīhim* — what is before them — names the future; the phrase *mā khalfahum* — what is behind them — names the past. The verse is therefore saying that God encompasses the entire temporal existence of the angels. The future and the past are both within God's knowledge.

Either reading reinforces the verse's central claim: the angels are not outside God's knowledge in any dimension of their existence. The future is not hidden from God; the past is not preserved only in the angels' memory; the Hereafter is not beyond the divine scope. The angels are within God's knowledge at every point. The knowledge is total; the angels are not exempt.

**The Verse As a Model for Human Posture**

The verse is one of the most explicit Qur'anic descriptions of how the highest created order responds to God. The response is the combination of two features: obedience to the divine command (21:27), and awe of the divine majesty (this verse). The combination is what honoured service looks like. The angels serve because they are commanded; they tremble because they recognise the majesty of the one who commands. The two features are not contradictory; the two features together constitute the honoured service.

**The Connection to the Argument Against the Audience's View of the Angels**

The verse is the third in a passage describing the angels (21:26–29). The passage has been dismantling the audience's view of the angels as divine partners or as beings who can be invoked independently. The verse at 21:28 contributes to the dismantling by specifying the limitations on angelic intercession. The limitation places the intercession within the divine economy; the intercession does not escape the economy.
verses.29:
> Whoever of them were to say, “I am a god besides Him,” they would be rewarded with Hell by Us. This is how We reward the wrongdoers

**A Hypothesis, Not an Event**

The verse states that if any of them — the angels, named in the line before — should say, "I am a god besides Him," that one would be requited with Hell. The construction is a hypothesis, not a report that any angel has said such a thing. It establishes a rule: the claim to divinity belongs to God alone, and no created being, however exalted, is exempt from judgement for making it.

Al-Ṭabarī and al-Qurṭubī record the view that the verse refers to Iblīs, who is sometimes counted among the angels before his refusal. The reference is possible, but the verse does not need it. A rule stated in general terms is stronger than a single example, because it covers every case rather than one. The sentence that follows closes the thought: "This is how We reward the wrongdoers." The wrongdoing is not the claim considered in the abstract; it is the claim made by a creature against its Maker, and the closing phrase puts it in the same category as every other act of injustice.

The argument these verses close began at 21:19, and the angels have just been described as honoured servants who do not speak before God and whose intercession is bounded by His approval (21:26, 21:27, 21:28). A creature so placed, if it claimed divinity, would be judged like any other wrongdoer. *Wrongdoers* is the sūrah's own thread: it is used of the townspeople who confessed when it was too late (21:14) and of those who will be judged on the scales with justice (21:47).
verses.30:
> Do the disbelievers not realize that the heavens and earth were ˹once˺ one mass then We split them apart? And We created from water every living thing. Will they not then believe

**A Question About Whether the Audience Has Noticed**

The verse opens with a question that contains its own accusation. *Awa lam yara alladhīna kafarū* — have the disbelievers not seen, not noticed, not realised? The verb *raʾā* — to see, to notice, to perceive — is the verb of empirical observation. The verse is asking whether the audience has failed to notice something that should have been obvious. The verse is not asking whether the audience has heard the news; the verse is asking whether the audience has looked at the sky.

**The Single Mass That Was Split Apart**

The verse specifies what the audience should have noticed. *An al-samāwāti wa al-arḍa kānatā ratqan fa-fataqnāhumā* — the heavens and the earth were a single mass, then We split them apart. The verb *ratq* names a closed, sealed, joined state; *fataqa* names the act of splitting open. The verse is describing an original state of unity and a subsequent act of separation. The description corresponds to one of the most theologically significant images in the Qur'anic the order of the universe: the heavens and the earth were joined, and God split them apart.
verses.31:
> And We have placed firm mountains upon the earth so it does not shake with them, and made in it broad pathways so they may find their way

**Mountains That Stabilise What Could Not Hold Itself**

The verse extends the cosmic argument begun at 21:30. The heavens and the earth were split apart (21:30); now the earth has been given stabilising mountains and the pathways that make it habitable. The verse names a specific feature of the earth's design: *rawāsiya* — firm, fixed, anchored mountains — that prevent the earth from shaking its inhabitants. The verb *a taḥīfa* — to shake, to totter, to be in motion — names a state the verse says the earth is protected from by the mountains.

The image is not a poetic flourish; it is a geophysical claim. The earth is described as needing anchors. The mountains are the anchors. Without the anchors, the earth would shake; with the anchors, the earth is stable. The Qur'an returns to this image at 16:15, 31:10, and elsewhere, treating the mountains as a structural feature of the earth's design that allows life to continue. The image is consistent with what geology describes: the continents ride on tectonic plates whose behaviour is shaped in part by the mountainous regions along their margins. The commentators, including al-Rāzī, preserve an image in which the earth floats upon water and would move about as if it were a ship at sea, were it not for the firm mountains anchoring it. The image is cosmic in the premodern sense, but it expresses something that survives the change of cosmic framework: the earth is held in place by features of its design, and those features are part of what makes life possible. The mountains are not accidents of geology; they are the stabilising elements without which the surface of the earth would not be a fit place for sustained life.

The verse continues the empirical argument begun at 21:30. The verse asks the audience to look at the world and to draw the conclusion. The mountains are there; the pathways are there; the design is observable. The verse is asking the audience to integrate the observation with the inference. The integration is the substance of belief. The refusal to integrate is the substance of the disbelief the verse is addressing.

The empirical argument is cumulative. 21:30 named the splitting of the heavens and the earth and the dependence of life on water; 21:31 names the stabilising features of the earth's surface and the pathways that make the surface habitable. The verses are not isolated observations; they are cumulative evidence for a designed order. The design is the evidence; the designer is the inference; the inference is the substance of the belief the verses are asking for.

**A Verse That Asks for Gratitude**

The empirical observation is offered; the inference is drawn; the audience is asked to respond. The response is gratitude; the gratitude is the form of worship that the verse at 21:25 has already demanded. The empirical verses and the demanding verses are not separate; they are part of the same argument. The argument is the unity of the designed order; the appropriate response to the unity is the worship of the designer.
verses.32:
> And We have made the sky a well-protected canopy, still they turn away from its signs

**The Sky As a Ceiling, Protected**

The verse offers a single, compact image. *Wa jaʿalnā al-samā'a saqfan maṣūnān* — and We made the sky a protected ceiling. The verb *jaʿala* — to make — is the same verb used throughout the cosmic passage. The sky is one of the things that has been made. The verse names what the sky has been made into: a ceiling, a roof, a canopy. The image is architectural. The sky is the upper boundary of the inhabited world; the sky covers the earth; the sky is the canopy under which life is possible.

The Arabic *maṣūn* — protected, preserved, guarded — names a specific feature of the canopy. The canopy is not just a covering; it is a protected covering. The commentators, including al-Rāzī, note that the protection is from the satans; the heavens are protected from demonic incursion. Al-Ṭabarī reads the protection as physical: the sky is held in place, prevented from falling down to the earth. The two readings are not exclusive; the verse can be describing both kinds of protection. The canopy protects what is below it from what is above; the protection is both physical and moral.

**"Still They Turn Away from Its Signs"**

The verse's second half records the audience's response. *Wa hum ʿan āyātihā muʿriḍūn* — and they, from its signs, turn away. The signs of the sky include the sun, the moon, the stars, the alternation of night and day, the rain, the colour of the sky at different times. The verse says the audience turns away from these signs. The turning away is a recurring theme in the sūrah (21:1, 21:24). The audience has refused to look at what is in front of them; the audience continues to refuse.

**The Image of a Canopy Is Both Literal and Architectural**

The Arabic *saqf* — ceiling, roof — is an architectural word. The sky is being described in the language of the building arts. The image is consistent with the rest of that picture: the sky is above; the earth is below; the design is that of a covered space in which life is possible. The image is not mythological; the image is the description of what the inhabitant of the earth sees when the inhabitant looks up. The inhabitant sees a covering. The question is whether the covering is recognised as part of a design.

The verse is one in a sequence that begins at 21:30 and continues through 21:33. The verses are presenting a cumulative case for the designed order of the world.
