The heavens and the earth were split apart (21:30); the earth has stabilising mountains and pathways (21:31); the sky is a protected canopy (21:32); the night, day, sun, and moon move in their orbits (21:33). The verses are not isolated claims; they are a cumulative demonstration. The demonstration is what the audience has been asked to look at.
verses.33:
> And He is the One Who created the day and the night, the sun and the moon—each travelling in an orbit

**"Each Travelling in an Orbit"**

The verse specifies a feature of the celestial bodies: *kullun fī falakin yasbāḥūn* — each swimming, gliding, travelling in an orbit. The verb *sabaḥa* names a kind of motion that is steady and continuous; the noun *falak* names the path or sphere of the motion. The verse is describing the celestial bodies as moving along trajectories that are not random and not arbitrary. The motion is regular; the regularity is the signature of design.

**The Cosmology the Verse Implies**

The commentators have noted that premodern Islamic astronomy often pictured the heavenly bodies as moving within spheres of an ethereal or subtle substance. The verse does not require this picture; the verse requires only that the motion is along trajectories. Some commentators, such as al-Ḍaḥḥāk, have read the verse more simply as saying that the celestial bodies move along their trajectories through the heavens. The reading is consistent with what the verse says; the verse does not require a specific cosmic model. The verse requires the design; the design is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

**The Verse As a Recurrence of an Earlier Pattern**

The verse's pairing of night and day, sun and moon, is one of the most common Qur'anic formations. The same combination appears at 36:40, 39:5, 71:16, and other places. The recurrence is not redundancy; it is the consistent application of a method. The method is to ask the audience to look at what is most familiar and to recognise the design in the familiarity. The audience has been looking at the night and the day for an entire life; the verse is asking the audience to see the design in what they have been looking at.
verses.34:
> We have not granted immortality to any human before you ˹O Prophet˺: so if you die, will they live forever

**The Prophet's Mortality As a Sign**

The verse makes a structural claim: *We have not granted immortality to any human being before you*. The Arabic *khuld* — immortality, perpetuity, everlastingness — is the same word used elsewhere for the state of the inhabitants of Paradise or Hellfire. What 21:34 sets out is that the Prophet, like every human being before him, has not been given the kind of perpetuity that would exempt him from death. The Prophet is mortal. The mortality is not a deficiency; it is the human condition.

The verse functions as a sign for the audience. The audience had hoped, or feared, that the Prophet's death would either vindicate or invalidate the message. What the verse is preparing the audience for is an event that will, in fact, occur — the death of the Prophet. The preparation is part of the verse's task; the task is to remove the symbolic weight the audience had loaded onto the Prophet's death.

**Question That Reframes the Audience's Hope**

The question's force is therefore not in the question itself but in the answer the question assumes. The answer is no. The audience will die. The death of the Prophet is the death of one mortal among mortals; the death of the audience will be the death of others. The two deaths are part of the same human condition; neither death has the symbolic weight the audience had hoped to load onto it.

**The Word "Khuld" As a Theological Category**

The Arabic *khuld* — perpetuity, immortality — is one of the Qur'an's most theologically loaded words. The same word is used for the state of the inhabitants of Paradise (3:15, 4:57, 5:119) and the inhabitants of Hell (7:36, 43:74). The verse's use of *khuld* for the kind of life the Prophet has not been given is therefore precise: the Prophet has not been given the Last-Day perpetuity that belongs to the next world; the Prophet has been given the mortality that belongs to this world. The two are different orders; the verse is making the distinction explicit.

The Prophet is not a divine being exempted from death; the Prophet is a human being who has been given a message. The message is not dependent on the Prophet's perpetual life; the message is dependent on the Prophet's transmission. The transmission has occurred; the transmission does not require the perpetuity of the transmitter. The perpetuity belongs to the message; the mortality belongs to the messenger.

**Junayd's Spiritual Reading**

The Sufi commentator Junayd offered a striking reading: *Whosoever is between the two vanishings is now vanishing*. The two vanishings are the state of nonexistence that precedes earthly life and the death at the end of earthly life. Between them, the human being is in a constant state of dying. The reading extends the verse into the interior life. The interior life is a constant process of letting go of what has been, in anticipation of what is to come. The letting go is the form the vanishing takes.
verses.35:
> Every soul will taste death. And We test you ˹O humanity˺ with good and evil as a trial, then to Us you will ˹all˺ be returned

**The Universality of Death**

The verse opens with one of the Qur'an's most insistent universal claims. *Kullu nafsin dhāʾiqatu al-mawti* — every soul will taste death. The word *kull* — every — is the words's most emphatic universal. The verb *dhāqa* — to taste — names an experiential encounter; the noun *al-mawt* — death — names the encounter's content. The verse is saying that every soul, without exception, will experience death. The universality is not qualified by rank, by piety, by prophetic office, by divine election. Every soul will die.

This is one of the Qur'an's most theologically significant universals. The verse at 21:34 said that no human being had been granted immortality; this verse extends the same observation to every soul. The audience cannot exempt itself from the observation; the audience is part of the universality. The death that will take the Prophet will take the audience; the death will take the believers; the death will take the disbelievers. The universality is total.

The use of *dhāqa* is also a way of saying that death is not annihilation.

**"Then to Us You Will Be Returned"**

The venue of the return is not specified in this verse; the venue is described in 21:47, where the scales of justice are set up. The scales will weigh what was done in the testing; the return will be the moment when the testing is finally evaluated. The verse at 21:35 is the principle of which 21:47 is the application. The principle is that the testing has a purpose; the purpose is the return; the return is the moment when the testing is resolved.
verses.36:
> When the disbelievers see you ˹O Prophet˺, they only make fun of you, ˹saying,˺ “Is this the one who speaks ˹ill˺ of your gods?” while they disbelieve at the mention of the Most Compassionate

**The Scene at the Encounter**

The verse records a recurring scene: the Prophet encounters the disbelievers; the disbelievers mock him. *Wa idhā raʾāka alladhīna kafarū* — when those who disbelieve see you. The verb *raʾā* — to see — names the visual encounter. The scene is not hypothetical; the verse is reporting what happens when the audience sees the Prophet. The reporting is part of the verse's task. The audience is being shown itself as the audience appears when it sees the Prophet.

The verse's use of the verb *raʾā* is also argumentative. The audience has been introduced to a cosmic argument (21:30–33) and to the universal fact of mortality (21:34–35). The audience has been asked to look at the world and to recognise the design. Now the audience is shown in the act of looking at the Prophet and of mocking. The two acts of looking are placed side by side. The contrast is the verse's argument.

**"While They Disbelieve at the Mention of the Most Compassionate"**

The use of *al-Raḥmān* — the Most Compassionate — is significant. The verse uses the most beautiful name of God, the name that emphasises mercy. The audience disbelieves at the mention of mercy. The verse is asking the audience to consider the contrast: the audience is sensitive about being mocked about its gods, but the audience mocks the mention of the Most Compassionate. The asymmetry is the verse's argumentative force.

The verse connects back to the sūrah's opening argument. In 21:5, the audience had accused the Prophet of being a poet, a fabricator, a producer of confused dreams. The posture is the audience's settled disposition toward the message; the disposition is what the verses have been describing from the opening of the sūrah.

The verse is asking the audience to consider what it would mean to receive the mention of the Most Compassionate with belief instead of disbelief.
verses.37:
> Humankind is made of haste. I will soon show you My signs, so do not ask Me to hasten them

**The Composition of the Human Being**

The verse makes a claim about the composition of the human being. *Al-insānu khuliqa min ʿajal* — the human being was created of haste, from haste. The Arabic *ʿajal* — haste, hurry, speed — names a quality of the human constitution. The verse is saying that the human being is constituted in such a way that haste is part of what the human being is. The haste is not a moral failing; the haste is a feature of the human makeup.

The commentators have read the verse in several ways. Al-Qurṭubī notes that the verse is similar to 30:54 — *God is He Who created you from weakness* — and 4:28 — *Man was created weak*. The verses are part of a Qur'anic pattern that describes the human being as created with a particular constitutional feature that the human being must learn to manage. The management is part of the moral task. The Qur'an does not deny the constitutional feature; the Qur'an names it so that the management can begin.

**"I Will Soon Show You My Signs"**

The Arabic *sawfa* — soon, before long — marks a near future. The verse is saying that the signs will be shown in the near future, not in some remote horizon. The nearness is part of the address's force. The audience had been asking for signs (21:5); the audience is now being told that signs will be shown in the near future. The audience does not need to demand the signs; the signs are already on the way. The demanding is therefore unnecessary.

**The Signs That Will Be Shown**

The verse's promise — *I will soon show you My signs* — does not specify which signs. The commentators have noted that the verse could refer to signs in this world, signs in the Last-Day sense, or both. The waiting is the substance of the verse's call.
verses.38:
> They ask ˹the believers˺, “When will this threat come to pass if what you say is true?”

**The Question That Is Its Own Refusal**

The verse records the audience's challenge. *Wa yaqūlūna matā hādha al-waʿdu in kuntum ṣādiqīn* — and they say, when will this promise come to pass, if you are truthful? The challenge is one of the recurring Qur'anic refrains. The audience had been making the same demand throughout the sūrah; the verse is now recording the most explicit form of the demand. The audience wants the promise to come to pass in a time the audience can see.

**The Verb of Refusal — "Yaqūlūna"**

The verse begins with *wa yaqūlūna* — and they say. The verb is in the simple past; the saying has already happened. The verse is reporting the saying as a fact. The audience has made the challenge; the challenge is recorded; the recording is part of the verse's argument. The recording is also part of the larger Qur'anic project of documenting the audience's refusals so that future generations can see what the audience said and how the messenger responded.

The saying is past tense from the perspective of the recitation. The recitation is reporting what the audience said; the audience's saying is now part of the historical record. The verse is reminding the audience that its refusals are not private; the refusals are part of what the verse has been recording.

**A Verse That Returns to the Earlier Argument**

The verse returns to the sūrah's earlier argument against the audience's demand for signs. In 21:5, the audience had asked for a tangible sign like those sent before; in 21:6, the Qur'an had responded with the empirical observation that no community that had received the signs had believed after receiving them. In 21:38, the audience is again asking for a sign — this time asking when the promised sign will come. The verse is therefore not breaking new ground; the verse is recapitulating the demand in a new form. The recapitulation is the recurrent pattern of the sūrah's argument.
verses.39:
> If only the disbelievers knew that a time will come when they will not be able to keep the Fire off their faces or backs, nor will they be helped

**The Conditional That Has No Sound Completion**

The verse opens with a conditional whose conclusion is implied rather than stated. *Law yalʿamūna* — if they knew. Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī note that the verse's completion is implicit: "if they knew, they would not act as they are acting." The conditional names the condition that would change the audience's behaviour; the verse does not specify the change. The specification is left to the audience's imagination. The imagination is part of the verse's work.

**"Nor Will They Be Helped"**

The verse adds *wa lā hum yuṣarūn* — and they will not be helped. The verb *naṣara* — to help, to support — names an action the verse says will be unavailable. The audience's expectation that someone will come to their aid is named and refused. The refusal is part of the verse's argument. The audience had been postponing the reckoning; the postponement had implicitly assumed that someone would intervene on the audience's behalf. The verse is saying: no one will intervene. The reckoning will not be postponed by intervention; the reckoning will arrive.

This is one of the most demanding moments in the Qur'anic treatment of the Last-Day punishment. What the audience is hearing in this verse is that there is no escape, no intervention, no help.

**The Recognising That Would Change the Behaviour**

The verse's opening conditional — *if they knew* — implies that knowledge would change the audience's behaviour. What the verse is pointing toward is the audience's current behaviour — the behaviour of those who do not know. The audience mocks (21:36); the audience demands hastening (21:37); the audience demands to know when the promise will come (21:38). All of these behaviours are the behaviours of those who do not know.

**A Verse That Returns to the Universal Mortality of 21:35**

The verse implicitly connects to the previous claim that every soul will taste death (21:35). The audience will die; the audience will be returned to God (21:35); the audience will face the reckoning. The description is concrete; the concreteness is part of the verse's argument. The audience is being asked to recognise what 21:35 named in universal terms; the verse is naming what the universal terms will look like in practice.
verses.40:
> In fact, the Hour will take them by surprise, leaving them stunned. So they will not be able to avert it, nor will it be delayed from them

**The Suddenness of the Hour**

The verse names the suddenness of the Hour. *Bal taʾtīhim baghtatan* — rather, it will come upon them suddenly, unexpectedly. The Arabic *baghta* — suddenness, unexpectedness — names the form of the arrival. The Hour will not announce itself; the Hour will arrive in the way that the audience has been postponing. The arrival is the form the postponement takes when the postponement is exhausted.

The verse's use of *bal* — rather — marks a contrast. The audience had asked when the promise will come (21:38); the verse is saying that the request itself is based on a false premise. The premise is that the Hour will come in a way the audience can predict; the verse is denying the premise. The Hour comes suddenly. The coming cannot be predicted. The audience's request for a date is therefore a request for the impossible. The verse is refusing the request by describing what the actual arrival will be like.

**"Nor Will It Be Delayed From Them"**

The verse closes *wa lā hum yunẓarūn* — and they will not be given respite. The verb *anẓara* — to grant respite, to delay — names an action the verse says will be refused. The audience that had been hoping for postponement is being told that the postponement will not come. The postponement is what the audience has been counting on; the verse is removing the count.

This is one of the most devastating moments in the sūrah. The audience's strategy of postponement — the strategy of refusing now and then saying they will consider later — has been the audience's main posture throughout the sūrah.

**The Connection to Other Verses on Suddenness**

The verse is one of several in the Qur'an that describe the suddenness of the Hour. 6:31 says: *If only you could see when they are set before the Fire and say, "Would that we could be returned and not deny the signs of our Lord!"* 7:95 says: *Then We shall turn them out from wherever they were, just as We brought forth the first creation.* 22:55, 26:202, 29:53, 39:55, 43:66, 47:18 — each of these verses describes the suddenness in a different phrase. The recurrence is the consistent application of a method: the audience that has been postponing is being told, in many forms, that the postponement will not be granted.

**The Verse As a Refusal of the Audience's Posture**

The verse is the climax of the sūrah's treatment of the audience's postponement. The previous verses (21:37–39) had warned against hastening and named what the audience would face if they knew; this verse names what the actual arrival will be like. The arrival is sudden; the arrival is confounding; the arrival cannot be averted; the arrival cannot be delayed. The audience that has been building a worldview on the postponement is being told that the worldview is built on a refusal that will not be granted.

The refusal is the substance of the verse's call. The audience is being asked to recognise that the postponement is the basis of the audience's behaviour; the postponement is being removed; the audience is being asked to consider what the behaviour will look like without the postponement. The behaviour without the postponement is what the verse is naming. The naming is the verse's argument; the recognition is the verse's call.
verses.41:
> ˹Other˺ messengers had already been ridiculed before you ˹O Prophet˺, but those who mocked them were overtaken by what they used to ridicule

**A Pattern Repeated Before**

The verse tells the Prophet that he is not the first messenger to face mockery. *La-qad istuhziʾa bi-rusulin min qablika* — messengers were certainly mocked before you. The verb *istahzā'a* — to mock, to ridicule, to make fun of — names the form the earlier refusals took. The pattern is the same pattern the audience has been following in Mecca. The Prophet is being reminded that the pattern is not original; the pattern has been tried before. The reminder is part of the verse's consolation and part of its argument.

**"Overtaken by What They Used to Ridicule"**

The second half of the verse specifies the consequence: *fa-aḥāṭa bi-alladhīna sakhirū minhum mā kānū bihi yastahziʾūn* — so there surrounded those who mocked of them what they used to mock. The verb *aḥāṭa* — to surround, to encompass, to beset — names the form the consequence takes. The mockery is overtaken by the very thing the mockers mocked. The audience that mocked the promise of punishment is overtaken by the punishment; the audience that mocked the warning is overtaken by the warning's fulfilment.

This is one of the most theologically pointed patterns in the Qur'an. The recurrence is at 6:10, 11:8, 16:34, 39:48, 40:83, 45:33, 46:26. The pattern is the same in each case: those who mock are overtaken by what they mocked. The pattern is the form the moral order takes when the mockers have refused to recognise what they were mocking. The mockers thought they were dismissing a possibility; the dismissal became the very mechanism by which the possibility became real. The substance of the pattern is that the mockers cannot keep their mockery at a distance from themselves. The mockery was meant to be at the messenger; the mockery ends up being about the mocker. The thing the mockers mocked is the thing that overtakes them.

**The Verse As a Recurrence of an Earlier Theme**

The verse is one of several in the Qur'an that connect the Prophet's experience to that of earlier messengers. 13:32 says: *Messengers before you were mocked, but I gave respite to those who disbelieved, then I seized them*. 15:11 says: *There did not come to them any messenger except that they used to mock him*. 36:30 says: *How many a generation have We destroyed before them, and they cried out when it was too late for escape*. The recurrence is the consistent application of a method: the Prophet is not alone in his experience; the experience is part of the prophetic calling.

The recurrence is also a teaching about the nature of the prophetic calling. The calling is to deliver a message that will be mocked; the message is delivered knowing that it will be mocked; the mocking is part of the test. The Prophet who knows the pattern has been started into the meaning of the calling. The audience that hears the pattern is being invited to recognise that the message is genuine — even the rejection of it follows the pattern. The pattern is evidence for the message as much as it is evidence against the audience.
verses.42:
> Ask ˹them, O Prophet,˺ “Who can defend you by day or by night against the Most Compassionate?” Still they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord

**A Question That Closes Off Every Escape**

The verse asks a question whose answer is rhetorically predetermined. *Man yajiruukum min al-Raḥmāni* — who will protect you from the Most Compassionate? The verb *jāra* — to protect, to take refuge with, to defend — names a specific form of action. The verse is asking who, if anyone, will defend the audience against the Most Compassionate. The answer is no one; the verse is constructed to make the answer obvious. The question is therefore not a genuine inquiry; it is an argumentative move. The argument is to close off the escape routes the audience had been imagining.

The specification of *al-Raḥmān* — the Most Compassionate — is significant. The name that emphasises divine mercy is the name under which the protection is being asked. The audience might have imagined that mercy exempts them from consequences; the verse is saying that mercy does not exempt; mercy is the very attribute under which the protection must be sought. The audience that refuses to seek protection cannot assume that the mercy will operate without the seeking.

**"Still They Turn Away from the Remembrance of Their Lord"**

The verse's closing observation is sharp. *Bal hum ʿan dhikri rabbihim muʿriḍūn* — rather, they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord. The verb *ʿaraḍa* — to turn away — is the same verb used throughout the sūrah (21:1, 21:24, 21:32). The audience has been turning away from the very remembrance that would constitute the answer to the question. The audience's turning away is the source of the audience's vulnerability; the audience has refused the protection because the audience has refused the one from whom the protection comes.

**The Name "The Most Compassionate" As Argument**

The verse's use of *al-Raḥmān* is one of the most theologically pointed choices in the sūrah. Al-Rāzī notes that the name is used here because it causes one to reflect on the fact that God encompasses all things with His mercy. The name is the name of mercy; the mercy is what the audience is being asked to seek refuge from; the paradox is the verse's argument. The audience that has been calling on God as the Most Compassionate has been assuming that the mercy is protection; the verse is saying that the mercy is also the source of consequences, because the mercy is part of a structure in which the merciful One is also the just One.

The argument is not a denial of mercy. The argument is a refusal to allow mercy to be reduced to a comfortable idea. The mercy of the Most Compassionate is operative in the entire moral order; the mercy is not an exemption from the order.

**A Verse That Returns to the Audience's Posture**

The verse is a return to the diagnosis the sūrah has been making of the audience's posture. The audience has been turning away from the remembrance (21:1); the audience has been listening jokingly (21:2); the audience has been mocking (21:36). The verse at 21:42 is the diagnosis of all those postures in a single line. The turning away is the consistent feature; the consistent feature is what the verse is naming. The naming is the diagnostic.
verses.43:
> Or do they have gods—other than Us—that can protect them? They cannot ˹even˺ protect themselves, nor will they be aided against Us

**A Question About Other Gods**

The verse returns to the question of gods other than God. *Am lahum ālihatun min dūninā* — or do they have gods besides Us, that can protect them? The construction *min dūninā* — other than Us, besides Us — is the Qur'an's standard way of referring to the supposed partners of God. The verse is asking whether the audience's supposed partners have the capacity to defend them. The question is constructed so that the answer is no.

The verse is a continuation of the argument begun at 21:21 and 21:22. The audience had been asked about gods that could raise the dead (21:21); the audience was told that multiple gods would corrupt the heavens and the earth (21:22). The verse at 21:43 is asking about a different capacity — the capacity to protect. The protection is what the audience's supposed partners are supposed to provide.

**"Nor Will They Be Aided Against Us"**

The verse adds *wa lā hum minnā yuṣḥabūn* — and they will not be aided against Us. The verb *yuṣḥabūn* is from *ṣaḥiba* — to be a companion, to accompany, to be present with. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī note that the phrase can be read as "they will not have Us as their Companion" or "they will not be given protection against Us." Either reading reinforces the verse's argument. The idols will not be aided by God against God. The reading refuses the polytheistic assumption that the idols have some standing in the divine economy that would protect them.

**A Verse That Names the Powerlessness of the Idols**

The verse is one of the clearest Qur'anic statements of the powerlessness of the supposed partners. The same point is made at 7:192, 7:197, and elsewhere. The repetition is the consistent application of a method: the idols are not what the audience has imagined them to be. The idols cannot protect themselves; the idols cannot protect the audience; the idols will not be aided against God. The idols are not part of the protective framework the audience has constructed; the idols are part of what the audience has been mistaken about.

The verse is therefore part of the diagnostic project the sūrah has been pursuing.

The verse connects back to the sūrah's earlier argument against the supposed partners. The partners were unable to raise the dead (21:21); the partners would have corrupted the heavens and the earth (21:22); the partners are honoured servants who do not speak first (21:27). The verse at 21:43 adds that the partners cannot protect themselves or the audience. The cumulative picture is one of partners who are unable to do any of the things the audience had been expecting of them. The picture is the form the audience's polytheism takes when examined; the examination is the work the verses have been doing.

The examination is not a defeat of the audience. The examination is an invitation to recognise the picture and to reconsider the framework that produced it. The reconsideration is the work the verses are asking for; the work is the substance of the response the verses are calling for. The audience that does the work has begun the change the verses have been calling for. The audience that refuses to do the work has refused the verses. The refusal is what the verses have been recording throughout.
verses.44:
> In fact, We have allowed enjoyment for these ˹Meccans˺ and their forefathers for such a long time ˹that they took it for granted˺. Do they not see that We gradually reduce ˹their˺ land from its borders? Is it they who will then prevail

**Enjoyment That Becomes Self-Evident**

The verse opens with an observation about the audience's history. *Bal mattaʿnā hāʾulāʾi wa ābāʾahum ḥattā ʿāla ʿalayhim al-ʿumuru* — rather, We gave enjoyment to these and their fathers, until time grew long upon them. The verb *mattaʿa* — to give enjoyment, to provide with the means of enjoyment — names what the audience has been given. The audience has been given enjoyment; the enjoyment has continued; the continuation has become the substance of the audience's life.

The audience has been receiving the enjoyment so long that the receiving has become invisible. The enjoyment has ceased to be recognised as a gift and has become recognised as a fact.

**Multiple Interpretations of "Reduction"**

The commentators have offered several interpretations of the reduction. Some read it as a reference to the loss of territory through military conquest — a reading that fits the Meccan context if the verse is read as anticipating the Muslim conquests. Others read it as the loss of the population and blessings of a community — a general reading that fits any period of decline. Still others read it as the loss of the learned sages of a community, citing a hadith about God removing knowledge by removing the learned. The interpretations are not exclusive; the verse can be read in any of the ways, and the verse can be read in all of them at once.

This is one of the recurring moves in the sūrah's argument. The audience is asked to consider what its actual position is, in light of the verses that have been describing the moral order.
verses.45:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “I warn you only by revelation.” But the deaf cannot hear the call when they are warned

**The Prophet's Task Defined**

The verse defines the Prophet's task in a single line. *Innamā undhirukum bi-l-waḥyi* — I warn you only by revelation. The verse is putting words in the Prophet's mouth; the words describe what the Prophet does. The Prophet warns; the warning is by revelation; the warning is not by personal opinion, not by inference from nature, not by deduction from moral principles. The warning is by revelation. The verse is therefore a statement about the source of the warning.

The verb *waḥy* — revelation — is the Qur'anic technical term for the act by which God communicates with the Prophet. The term is used throughout the Qur'an to describe the Prophet's reception of the message.

**The Reading That Addresses the Prophet**

Some commentators, including al-Qurṭubī and al-Rāzī, read the verb in the second person: *Thou canst not cause the deaf to hear when they are warned*. The reading addresses the Prophet directly and is consistent with other verses that remind the Prophet that his task is to deliver the message, not to make the audience hear (2:272; 16:35). The reading is not exclusive of the first reading; the two readings are compatible. The two statements describe the same situation from two angles.

The reading that addresses the Prophet is also a comfort. The Prophet is not failing; the audience's deafness is not the Prophet's responsibility. The Prophet's task is to deliver; the audience's hearing is the audience's responsibility. The verse is reminding the Prophet that the responsibility has limits. The limits are the limits of the prophetic task; the limits are part of what the prophetic calling is.

**A Verse That Closes Off One Form of Audience Demand**

The audience had been demanding that the Prophet produce signs (21:5); the audience had been demanding that the Prophet show his credentials (21:24); the audience had been demanding the timing of the promise (21:38). The verse at 21:45 is a refusal of one of those demands in particular: the demand that the Prophet's warning come with something other than revelation. The Prophet warns by revelation; the revelation is what the Prophet has; the audience's demand for something other than revelation is a demand for something the Prophet does not have.

The refusal is not arbitrary. The Prophet's warning by revelation is the appropriate form of the warning. The asking is not answered; the asking is the form the audience's refusal takes.

**The Deafness As a Spiritual Category**

The verse's treatment of deafness is part of the broader Qur'anic category of spiritual deafness, which is invoked at 2:18, 5:71, 6:25, 31:7, and elsewhere. The category names a state of being in which the senses operate but the inner reception has been blocked. The blocking is a chosen state; the chosen state is what the verse is naming. The audience has chosen to refuse the warning; the choice has produced the deafness; the deafness is what the warning encounters.
verses.46:
> If they were touched by even a breath of your Lord’s torment, they would certainly cry, “Woe to us! We have really been wrongdoers.”

**The Conditional and Its Implied Completion**

The verse opens with a conditional whose completion is implicit. *Wa la-in massahum nafḥatun min ʿadhābi rabbika* — if there touched them a breath of your Lord's torment. The conditional is completed by what follows: they would certainly cry out. The construction is one of the Qur'an's recurring patterns for describing what would happen if the audience were to experience the consequences. The consequences are described as hypothetical; the hypothesis is constructed so that the audience can recognise what it would be.

The Arabic *nafḥa* — breath, whiff, puff — is a precise term. It does not name the full force of the torment; it names what comes from the torment at a distance.

**"Woe to Us! We Have Been Wrongdoers"**

The verse records the cry that would come. *Ya waylanā innā kunnā ẓālimīn* — woe to us, we have indeed been wrongdoers. The cry is the same cry that the wrongdoers of 21:14 uttered when the punishment arrived. The verse is connecting the hypothetical cry to the cry that was recorded earlier; the connection is part of the verse's argument. The cry that the audience would utter in the hypothetical is the same cry the wrongdoers actually uttered. The audience and the wrongdoers are the same kind of people; the cry is the cry that the kind of people utter when the consequences arrive.

The verb *ẓalama* — to wrong — is the same verb used throughout the sūrah (21:14, 21:29). The wrongdoers are those who have put something in the wrong place; the wrong is specific; the wrongdoers know what the wrong is. The cry is therefore not a general expression of distress; the cry is the specific acknowledgement that the cry-er has been a wrongdoer.

**"If Only the Wrongdoers Knew"**

The verse is one of several in the Qur'an that connect the hypothetical experience of punishment to the recognition that would come. 67:10–11 says: *And they will say, "We would have been better off if we had listened and used our reason."* 39:48 says: *The evil of what they sent before them will appear to them. They will be encompassed by what they used to mock.* Each of these passages describes the recognition that comes when the consequences arrive. The recognition is too late; the consequences are not reversed; the recognition is part of the consequences.

The verse at 21:46 is therefore part of the Qur'an's consistent treatment of the belated recognition. The recognition is real; the lateness is the substance of the recognition's inadequacy. The audience that recognises too late has not recognised in time. The recognising in time is what the verse is asking for; the audience is being shown what the recognising in time would look like by contrast with the recognising too late.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Belated Recognition**

The verse is the second time the sūrah has recorded the cry *ya waylanā*. The verse at 21:46 is the hypothetical version of the same cry. The hypothetical is what the actual would have looked like before it became actual; the hypothetical is the warning; the warning is the substance of the verse's call.
verses.47:
> We will set up the scales of justice on the Day of Judgment, so no soul will be wronged in the least. And ˹even˺ if a deed is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as a ˹vigilant˺ Reckoner

**The Scales of Justice**

The verse names the apparatus of the Last-Day reckoning. *Wa naḍaʿu al-mawāzīna al-qista li-yawmi al-qiyāmati* — and We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection. The verb *waḍaʿa* — to set up, to place, to establish — names the act of establishing the scales. The noun *mawāzīn* is the plural of *mīzān* — scale, balance. The adjective *qist* — justice, equity, fairness — qualifies the scales. The reckoning will be done with just scales; the scales will be the apparatus of the reckoning.

**"Even if it be the Weight of a Mustard Seed"**

The verse continues *wa in kāna miṣqāla ḥabbatin min khardalin aṭaynā bihā* — and if it be the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. The mustard seed is the smallest object often known in the ancient world; it is used here to represent the smallest possible unit of action. No deed, no matter how small, will escape the reckoning. The mustard seed is the threshold; the threshold is so small that no deed can fall below it. The reckoning will catch everything.

The verse is connected to a recurring Qur'anic theme. 31:16 says: *If a mustard seed were hidden in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth, God would bring it forth*. 99:7–8 says: *Whoever has done an atom's weight of good will see it; and whoever has done an atom's weight of evil will see it*. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that no deed is too small to be reckoned.

**The Verse As a Refusal of the Idols' Mediation**

The correction is part of the sūrah's larger argument. The sūrah has been removing the supports of the polytheistic framework one by one. The verse at 21:47 removes the support that depends on the supposed insufficiency of the divine Reckoner. The removal is precise; the sufficiency of the Reckoner is the substance of the removal.

The verse is connected to 21:35, which stated that every soul will taste death and will be returned. The verse at 21:47 specifies what the return will involve. The return will be a reckoning; the reckoning will be done with scales of justice; no deed will escape the reckoning. The return is therefore not an arbitrary event; the return is the moment when the universal mortality is followed by the universal reckoning. The verse at 21:47 is the specification of what the return means in practice. The specification is the substance of the verse's call; the call is the audience's invitation to take the specification seriously.
verses.48:
> Indeed, We granted Moses and Aaron the standard ˹to distinguish between right and wrong˺—a light and a reminder for the righteous

**The Furqān Given to Moses and Aaron**

The verse announces the giving of the *furqān* — the criterion, the standard, the means by which truth is distinguished from falsehood. *Wa la-qad āṭaynā Mūsā wa Hārūna al-furqān* — and We gave Moses and Aaron the criterion. The use of *la-qad* — certainly, indeed — marks the verse as a decisive declaration. The criterion was given; the giving is part of the divine economy. The giving is to two specific messengers — Moses and Aaron — who are mentioned together here as elsewhere in the Qur'an (23:45; 25:35; 37:114).

The Arabic *furqān* comes from the root *f-r-q* — to divide, to separate, to distinguish. The criterion is the means of distinguishing. The Qur'an uses the term to refer to what distinguishes truth from falsehood in revelation itself. The Torah is described elsewhere as the criterion (2:53). The verse is therefore naming the Torah as the criterion given to Moses and Aaron; the naming is part of the verse's argument against the audience who would deny that God has given such criteria to His messengers.

**The Identification of the Criterion**

The commentators have offered different identifications of the *furqān*. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as referring to the Torah itself. Al-Rāzī reads it as referring to the help that God gave Moses in his mission — the parting of the sea, the destruction of Pharaoh, and other signs. The two readings are not exclusive. The Torah is the criterion in the sense that it distinguishes truth from falsehood; the help that God gave is the criterion in the sense that it showed the truth of Moses' message.

The Qur'an elsewhere describes itself as a criterion (25:1). The verse at 21:48 is therefore part of a broader Qur'anic argument that God has given criteria to His messengers; the criteria are what the messengers have; the messengers have been using the criteria to distinguish truth from falsehood in their respective communities.

**"A Light and a Reminder"**

The pairing of light and reminder is a recurring Qur'anic theme. The Qur'an itself is described as a light (5:15; 7:157; 64:8) and as a reminder (15:9; 21:2, 21:10). The verse at 21:48 is therefore part of the Qur'anic self-presentation that places the Qur'an in continuity with the Torah. The two revelations have the same function; the function is what the verse is naming.

**A Verse That Begins a New Section**

The verse is the first in a series of verses (21:48–91) that narrate the stories of various prophets. The series begins with Moses and Aaron, then moves to Abraham (21:51–73), Lot (21:74–75), Noah (21:76–77), David and Solomon (21:78–82), Job (21:83–84), Ishmael, Enoch, and Dhu'l-Kifl (21:85–86), Jonah (21:87–88), and Zachariah, John, and Mary (21:89–91). The series of stories is one of the longest in the Qur'an.

The verse is therefore a transition. The previous verses (21:1–47) have been the sūrah's argument against the Meccan audience and its view of the world. What the verse at 21:48 does here is introduce the new section that will narrate the prophetic histories. The criterion given to Moses and Aaron is the bridge: the criterion is what the messengers have; the messengers are the ones whose stories the sūrah is about to tell. The criterion is the doorway into the prophetic histories.
verses.49:
> who are in awe of their Lord without seeing Him, and are fearful of the Hour

**Two Features of the God-Fearing**

The verse describes the God-fearing whom the previous verse mentioned. The description has two parts. First, *alladhīna yukhshawna rabbahum bi-l-ghaybi* — who fear their Lord in the unseen, who are in awe of their Lord without seeing Him. Second, *wa hum min al-sāʿati mushfiqūn* — and they are wary of the Hour. The verse is therefore specifying two qualities of the God-fearing: the fear of God in the absence of visible confirmation, and the fear of the Last-Day reckoning. The two qualities together describe the inner posture of those for whom the criterion is intended.

**"Bi-l-Ghaybi" — The Meaning of "In the Unseen"**

The commentators have offered two readings of *bi-l-ghaybi*. Al-Rāzī reads it as referring to the God-fearing being absent from other people, praying in seclusion. Al-Qurṭubī reads it as referring to the fact that the God-fearing are not present before God and the realities of the Hereafter; they cannot perceive God directly, but they know Him through faith and reflection.

**The Verse As a Connection to the Earlier Cosmological Argument**

The verse connects to the cosmic argument of 21:30–33. The argument was that the heavens and the earth are designed; the audience is invited to recognise the design. The verse at 21:49 is asking for the recognition to issue in a specific kind of posture: the fear of God in the unseen. The posture is what the recognition is supposed to produce. The audience that recognises the design but does not develop the posture has not yet integrated the recognition with the response. The integration is what the verse is asking for.
verses.50:
> And this ˹Quran˺ is a blessed reminder which We have revealed. Will you ˹pagans˺ then deny it

**The Qur'an As a Blessed Reminder**

The verse names the Qur'an as a blessed reminder. *Wa hādha dhikrun mubārun unazzalnāhu* — and this is a blessed reminder We have revealed. The Arabic *dhikr* — reminder, remembrance — is one of the Qur'an's self-designations (15:9; 21:2, 21:10, 21:48). The verse is using the Qur'an's own word for itself. What is offered here is a blessed reminder; the blessed reminder has been revealed.

The use of *dhikr* — remembrance, reminder — is significant. The word is the same word used in 21:2 for the previous reminders; the word is the same word used in 21:24 for the Reminder of those before the Prophet; the word is the same word used in 21:48 for the Torah given to Moses and Aaron. The Qur'an is therefore being placed in a continuous series: each revelation is a reminder; each reminder is in continuity with the others; the continuity is what the verse is naming.

**"Blessed" — The Arabic "Mubārak"**

The Arabic *mubārak* — blessed — is a word that means not only "full of blessing" but also "a source of blessing." What is offered is not just blessed; it is a source of blessing. The verse is therefore not just making a claim about the Qur'an; the verse is making a claim about the audience's relationship to the Qur'an. Whoever receives the Qur'an will be blessed; whoever refuses will have refused the source of blessing.

The word *mubārak* also has connotations of being sustained and perpetuated. A blessed thing is a thing whose effects continue beyond the moment of its origin. The effects are what the audience is being asked to consider.

**"Will You Then Deny It?"**

The verse closes with *afa-antum lahu munkirūn* — will you then deny it? The verb *ankara* — to deny, to refuse to acknowledge, to be ungrateful — names the form the audience's refusal would take. The audience is being asked whether it will be ungrateful for the reminder; the asking is the verse's call. The call is rhetorical; the verse expects the audience to recognise the ungratefulness as ungratefulness and to change.

The use of *anta* — you — is in the second person plural.

**A Verse That Returns to the Sūrah's Central Theme**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's central themes. The sūrah has been asking the audience to recognise what has been given: the messengers (21:7–9); the criterion (21:48); the reminder (21:2, 21:10, 21:24, 21:48). The verse at 21:50 adds the Qur'an itself to the list. What is presented here is a blessed reminder; it has been revealed; the audience is being asked whether it will deny what has been revealed.

This is one of the most focused moments of the sūrah's argument. The argument has been building; the focus is now on the Qur'an itself. The question is the verse's call.
verses.51:
> And indeed, We had granted Abraham sound judgment early on, for We knew him well ˹to be worthy of it˺

**Sound Judgment Before the Office**

The verse announces a gift that preceded the prophetic office. *Wa la-qad āṭaynā Ibrāhīma rushdahu min qablu* — and We had given Abraham his sound judgment before. The Arabic *rushd* — right guidance, sound judgment, mature comprehension — names a quality of the intellect and the will. The gift is the gift of being rightly oriented before the formal office of prophethood was conferred.

The commentators, including al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī, have offered different readings of the timing. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as referring to Abraham's right guidance before Moses and Aaron; al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī read it as referring to Abraham's right guidance even as a child, before the formal conferral of prophethood.

**A Transition Verse**

The verse is the door into the longest narrative section of the sūrah. The verses that follow (21:52–73) narrate the story of Abraham's confrontation with his people and the idols. The verse at 21:51 prepares the audience for the story by naming Abraham's qualification. The qualification is the sound judgment; the sound judgment is what will enable Abraham to recognise the absurdity of the idols and to express it. The recognition and the articulation are what the rest of the narrative describes.

**The Sound Judgment As Intellectual and Moral**

The Arabic *rushd* names more than the correct opinion. It names the sound judgment that includes the intellectual capacity to recognise the truth, the moral disposition to act on the recognition, and the practical capacity to implement the action. The gift is therefore comprehensive; the gift touches the whole person. The whole person is what God has given Abraham; the giving is what the verse is naming.

This comprehensive reading is consistent with the rest of the Abraham narrative. What the verse at 21:51 is offering is the gift that produces all three.

**A Refusal of the Inheritance Argument**

The verses that follow will record the audience of Abraham's complaint: "We found our fathers worshipping them" (21:53). The complaint is the argument from inheritance. The complaint says that the worship is justified because the fathers did it. The verse at 21:51 is implicitly a refusal of the inheritance argument. The sound judgment that Abraham received was given to him before he inherited anything from his fathers; the judgment came from God, not from inheritance. The inheritance is what produced the error; the gift from God is what produced the truth.
verses.52:
> ˹Remember˺ when he questioned his father and his people, “What are these statues to which you are so devoted?”

**The Question That Begins the Argument**

The verse opens the Abraham narrative. *Idh qāla li-abīhi wa qawmihi mā hādhihi al-tamāthīlu allatī antum lahā ʿākidūn* — when he said to his father and his people, what are these statues to which you are devoted? The Arabic *tamāthīl* — statues, likenesses, images — names the objects of the audience's worship. The verb *ʿakada* — to cleave to, to be devoted to, to adhere to — names the form the worship takes. The verse is asking what these objects are and why they are the objects of such devotion.

The question is the form the Abraham narrative takes. The narrative is not presented as a long philosophical disproof of idolatry; the narrative is presented as a question. The question is the substance of the argument. The argument is the form the invitation takes.

The reconsideration is the substance of the verse's call.

**Connection to Other Qur'anic Versions of the Abraham Narrative**

The same question appears in other Qur'anic accounts of Abraham. 6:75 says: *And so We showed Abraham the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, that he might be of those possessing certainty*. 19:42 says: *Mention in the Book Abraham; he was a man of truth, a prophet*. 26:70 says: *And when he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"* 37:85 says: *When he said to his father and his people, "What do you worship?"* 43:26 says: *And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"*

The recurrence of the same question is part of the Qur'anic treatment of the Abraham narrative. The same question is asked in slightly different forms in different sūrahs; the differences are part of the variations in the narratives. The asking is consistent; the audience is being asked the same question in many forms. The asking is what the Qur'an is doing throughout; the asking is the substance of the call to Abraham; the call is what the audience is being invited to share.

**A Verse That Begins the Argument the Audience Will Continue**

The verse begins an argument that the Abraham narrative will continue. The argument is not just Abraham's; the argument is the form the divine economy takes in this sūrah. The argument will proceed through the smashing of the idols (21:58), the dialogue with his people (21:59–67), and the command to burn him alive (21:68). Each move in the argument is part of the larger argument against the audience's worship of idols. The argument is what the narrative is about; the narrative is what the sūrah is doing.

The argument is also a model for the audience's situation. The audience of the Qur'an is in a position analogous to Abraham's audience. The audience has been worshipping what has no right to be worshipped. The audience is being asked to consider the worship; the asking is the form the call takes. The call is the substance of the response the sūrah is asking for; the response is the same response Abraham's audience was asked to give. The asking continues; the audience is being invited to respond.
verses.53:
> They replied, “We found our forefathers worshipping them.”

**The Argument from Inheritance**

The verse records Abraham's people's reply. *Qālū wajadnā ābāʾanā lahā ʿābidīn* — they said, we found our fathers worshipping them. The Arabic *wajadnā* — we found — names the form of the report. The worship was not invented by the audience; the worship was inherited. The audience is therefore presenting the worship as something they received, not something they chose. The argument is the argument from inheritance: we do what we were taught to do.

This is one of the most common arguments the Qur'an has been refuting throughout. 5:104 records the same defence: *We found our fathers doing this*. 7:28 says: *And when they commit an immorality, they say, "We found our fathers doing this."* 31:21 says: *And when it is said to them, follow what God has revealed, they say, "Rather, we will follow that which we found our fathers doing."* The recurrence is the consistent application of the Qur'anic refusal: the inheritance argument is not a defence against the truth.

**A Refusal Without Argument**

The reply is not an argument; the reply is a report. The audience does not offer reasons for the worship; the audience offers the historical fact of the worship. The fact is being offered as a substitute for reasons. The substitution is the form the refusal takes. The audience is saying: we do not need to give reasons because the practice is established. The saying is the form the audience's resistance to thinking takes.

The verse is therefore asking the audience to do something the audience is not willing to do: to give reasons. The reasons would require examining the practice; the examination would require looking at the statues and considering what they are.

**A Bridge to the Rest of the Abraham Narrative**

The dialogue will continue in 21:54 with Abraham's reply: *Certainly you and your fathers have been in manifest error*. The reply will refuse the inheritance argument; the refusal will be the form the prophetic argument takes. The argument will proceed through the smashing of the idols and the trial. The trial is the culmination of the argument; the argument is the substance of the narrative.

The verse is therefore a bridge between Abraham's question (21:52) and Abraham's reply (21:54). The bridge is the audience's refusal to think; the refusal is what the narrative is documenting. The recognition is the substance of the response the sūrah is asking for.

The Qur'an records similar arguments from inheritance in multiple places. 43:22–23 records the polytheists' response to the Prophet: *We found our fathers following a religion, and we are, upon their footsteps, rightly guided*. 2:170 records: *And when it is said to them, follow what God has revealed, they say, "Rather, we will follow that which we found our fathers doing."* The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the inheritance argument is the argument of those who have refused to think for themselves.
verses.54:
> He responded, “Indeed, you and your forefathers have been clearly astray.”

**The Direct Refusal of the Inheritance Argument**

The verse is Abraham's reply to the inheritance argument. *Qāla la-qad kuntum antum wa ābāʾukum fī ḍalālin mubīn* — he said, indeed you and your fathers have been in manifest error. The reply is direct; the directness is the form the prophetic speech takes. Abraham does not soften the diagnosis; he states it. The heirs of a wrong practice are wrong; the fathers were wrong; the wrong has been transmitted.

The Arabic *ḍalāl* — error, misguidance, going astray — names the kind of error the verse is naming. The error is not a minor misstep; the error is *mubīn* — manifest, clear, evident.

**A Refusal of the Imitation Argument**

The verse is implicitly a refusal of the imitation argument that 5:104 records: *We found our fathers doing this*. The imitation is the substance of the inheritance argument. The verse is saying that imitation does not validate what is imitated.

The Qur'an refuses to accept the imitation of error as a defence. The audience that imitates is responsible for the imitation; the responsibility cannot be transferred to the imitated model. The audience is asked to consider what it is doing, not what its fathers did. The consideration is the form the verse's call takes; the call is the substance of the response the verse is asking for.

The verse is part of the broader Qur'anic treatment of the inheritance argument. 7:28 records: *And when they commit an immorality, they say, "We found our fathers doing this." God has certainly enjoined immorality and disbelief to them.* 31:21 records: *And when it is said to them, follow what God has revealed, they say, "Rather, we will follow that which we found our fathers doing."* 43:23 records: *And We found our fathers following a religion, and we are, in their footsteps, rightly guided.*

The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle: the inheritance argument is not a defence against the truth. The principle is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise. The recognition is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for.

**A Verse That Begins the Argument That Will Continue**

The verse begins the argument that will continue through 21:55–73. The argument will include the smashing of the idols (21:58), the dialogue about who smashed them (21:59–67), and the try to burn Abraham alive (21:68). The argument will end with Abraham being saved by the fire (21:69). The argument is the form the Abraham narrative takes; the form is what the verse is beginning.

The audience has been asked a question (21:52); the audience has offered a defence (21:53); Abraham has refused the defence (21:54). The argument is what the narrative is about; the narrative is what the sūrah is using to address its own audience. The audience of the Qur'an is being asked to consider the Abraham narrative as a mirror. The mirror is what the verse is offering; the considering is what the response requires.

The argument that follows will also be a model for the audience's situation. The audience of the Qur'an is in a position analogous to Abraham's audience. The audience has been worshipping what has no right to be worshipped; the audience is being asked to consider the worship.
verses.55:
> They asked, “Have you come to us with the truth, or is this a joke?”

**The Audience's Reclassification**

The verse records Abraham's people's response to his diagnosis. *Qālū a-jīʾtanā bi-l-ḥaqqi am anta min al-lāʿibīn* — they said, have you brought us the truth, or are you among those who jest? The verse shows the audience reclassifying what Abraham has said. The earlier accusation (in the sūrah's argument against the Meccan audience) was that the message is play (21:2). The same reclassification is happening here. Abraham has said something that does not fit the audience's framework; the audience is responding by reclassifying it as either truth (which the audience would not want to accept) or play (which the audience can dismiss).

**Truth or Play — The Audience's Binary**

The binary — truth or play — is the binary the audience has been using throughout the sūrah. The audience had earlier accused the Prophet of producing confused dreams, fabricated speech, or poetry (21:5). The accusations were ways of avoiding the truth of the message. The reclassification at 21:55 is doing the same work. The audience is offering Abraham the choice: admit you are jesting, or claim to be telling the truth and be dismissed as making extraordinary claims. The choice is rigged; the rigging is the form the audience's defence takes.

The rigging is what the verse is exposing. What we see here is the audience working with a binary that excludes the possibility that the messenger is telling the truth and the audience is mistaken. The exclusion is the substance of the audience's resistance. The audience is being asked to consider whether the binary is appropriate; the consideration is the form the verse's call takes.

**"Or Are You Among Those Who Jest?"**

The question — *am anta min al-lāʿibīn* — is one of the most theologically pointed in the Abraham narrative. The audience is accusing Abraham of jesting because the audience cannot fit what Abraham has said into the framework. The diagnosis is therefore reclassified as jest; the reclassification is what allows the dismissal.

The audience is being asked to consider what the dismissal has cost. The cost is the cost of refusing to hear the diagnosis; the cost is the form the resistance takes when it has been sustained for a long time.

**A Verse That Reframes the Sūrah's Theme of Play**

The verse returns to the theme of play that has been running through the sūrah. 21:2 described the audience as listening jokingly; 21:15 asked whether the destruction of the wrongdoers was divine amusement; 21:16 stated that God did not create the heavens and the earth in play. The verse at 21:55 is the audience's return to the theme of play. The audience is accusing Abraham of playing; the audience is using the vocabulary of play to dismiss what cannot be dismissed.

The Qur'an has been refusing the vocabulary of play throughout. The vocabulary is the form the audience's resistance takes; the vocabulary cannot accommodate the truth. The refusal is the form the sūrah's argument takes. What the vocabulary does is shut the audience off from the recognition the verse is calling for; the call requires the recognition to be freed.
verses.56:
> He replied, “In fact, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, Who created them ˹both˺. And to that I bear witness.”

**The Direct Affirmation**

The verse is Abraham's reply to the question of truth or play. *Qāla bal rabbukum rabbu al-samāwāti wa al-arḍi alladhī faṭarahunna wa anā ʿalā dhālika min al-shāhidīn* — he said, rather, your Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, who originated them, and I am among those who bear witness to this. Abraham is not answering the question as posed; he is reframing the entire conversation. The reframing is the substance of the reply.

The Arabic *bal* — rather — is the same particle that overturns an earlier claim. The earlier claim was "truth or play"; the *bal* refuses both alternatives and proposes a third. The third is that God is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. The third is what Abraham has been trying to communicate; the refusal of the binary is the form the communication takes.

**"Your Lord Is the Lord of the Heavens and the Earth"**

The verse names the Lord as the Lord of the heavens and the earth. The naming is an argumentative move. The audience had been worshipping statues (21:52); the statues are not the Lord of the heavens and the earth. The Lord of the heavens and the earth is the One who originated them; the originating is the form the Lordship takes. The worship of statues is therefore not just a different choice; it is a refusal of the actual Lord.

The verse is also a repetition of the theme that has been running through the sūrah. 21:19 said: *To Him belong all those in the heavens and the earth*. 21:22 said: *If there had been gods other than God in them, they would have been corrupted*. 21:30 said: *Do they not see that the heavens and the earth were a single mass, then We split them apart*. The verse at 21:56 is Abraham's form of the same theme. The form is what the verse is asking the audience of the Qur'an to recognise.

**"And to That I Bear Witness"**

The verse closes with *wa anā ʿalā dhālika min al-shāhidīn* — and I am among those who bear witness to this. Abraham places himself among those who witness to the Lordship. The witnessing is the form the prophetic calling takes. Abraham is not just stating the truth; Abraham is testifying to it. The testimony is what makes his speech prophetic.

**The Witness Who Stands Inside the Truth**

The argument is therefore not just about the content of the testimony; it is about the standing of the witness. The standing is the kind that comes from a direct encounter with what is being witnessed.
verses.57:
> ˹Then he said to himself,˺ “By Allah! I will surely plot against your idols after you have turned your backs and gone away.”

**"After You Have Turned Your Backs"**

The verse specifies the timing: *baʿda a tuwallū mudbirīn* — after you have turned your backs. The verb *wallā* — to turn — and the active participle *mudbirīn* — turning away — name the form the audience's departure will take. The audience will leave; the idols will be unattended; the plan can be executed. The plan depends on the departure; the departure is the form the timing takes.

**The Interiority of the Resolution**

The verse is one of the few in the Qur'an that records the private resolve of a prophet before the action is taken. The resolve is recorded because the resolve is part of what the narrative is teaching. The teaching is that the prophetic task involves both the verbal address and the interior preparation for what follows when the verbal address has been refused. The interior preparation is what 21:57 makes visible; the visibility is itself part of the verse's contribution. The audience of the Qur'an is being shown that the prophets are not just speakers; the prophets are also those who have prepared themselves for what speaking will cost. The preparing is part of the prophetic vocation.

---

The plan Abraham forms here is the one the sūrah then narrates: the idols smashed, the biggest left standing with the axe in its hand, and the townspeople's return to find the scene (21:58–61). The same scene is told in the sūrah of the Ranged, where he turns on them with a blow of his right hand and the people rush back (37:91–95), and the report that he acted at a festival when the town had gone out explains the timing the verse states: after you have turned your backs. What follows in this sūrah is the dialogue of the trial, so the plan is the hinge between the two halves of the story.
verses.58:
> So he smashed them into pieces, except the biggest of them, so they might turn to it ˹for answers˺

**"Save the Largest of Them"**

The exception is *kabīran lahum* — the largest of them. The largest idol was preserved. The preservation is the rhetorical centre of the demonstration. By preserving the largest idol while smashing the others, Abraham created a situation in which the audience would have to ask who smashed the idols. The answer could only be the largest idol. The audience would have to recognise that the largest idol, which they had treated as the most valuable, was the only candidate for the action. The asking is the form the demonstration takes; the answer is the substance of the demonstration.

**The Demonstration As Rhetoric**

This is one of the most sophisticated pieces of prophetic rhetoric in the Qur'anic narrative. The demonstration is not destructive; the demonstration is argumentative. The smashing is the form the argument takes; the argument is the form the prophetic speech takes when verbal argument has reached its limit. The limit is what 21:55 had recorded; the demonstration is the form the next step takes.
verses.59:
> They protested, “Who dared do this to our gods? It must be an evildoer!”

**The Rhetoric of the Outcry**

The audience's outcry is rhetorical even before it is rational. The Arabic word order in *man faʿala hādha bi-ālihatinā* — who has done this to our gods — places the audience's possessive relationship to the idols at the centre of the inquiry. The possessive pronoun has already done the interpretive work before any candidate is named. The gods are *ours*; the action against them is therefore an action against *us*. The framing is what prepares the audience to identify the perpetrator as an evildoer rather than as someone who has revealed something important about the gods.

The demonstration has produced the inquiry; the inquiry will produce the dialogue; the dialogue will produce the recognition. The dialogue will continue in 21:60–67.

The documenting is part of the sūrah's argument. The audience of the Qur'an is being shown how a demonstration works. The demonstration begins with an action; the action produces an inquiry; the inquiry produces a dialogue; the dialogue produces a recognition. The pattern is the form the prophetic demonstration takes. The audience is being asked to recognise the pattern. The recognition is what the verse is offering.

**The Audience's Premature Verdict**

The audience of the Qur'an is being asked to consider whether they have done the same thing. The audience that has been treating the message as wrong without examining the message has been doing what Abraham's audience is doing at 21:59. The verse is asking the audience to consider the parallel. The consideration is the form the call takes; the call is what the verse is offering.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Wrongdoing**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the wrongdoers. The verb *ẓalama* — to wrong — is the same verb used throughout the sūrah (21:14, 21:29, 21:47). The wrongdoers are those who have put something in the wrong place. The audience is using the word to condemn whoever smashed the idols. The verses that follow will show that the smashing was not the wrong; the wrong was the worship of things that cannot defend themselves. The framework of wrongdoing is being turned against the audience. The turning is the form the demonstration's argument takes.

**The Rhetoric of the Outcry**

The framing is the form the audience's commitment takes when it has been disturbed. The commitment cannot survive without framing the disturbance as wrongdoing. The framing is what the demonstration has provoked. The provocation is the form the demonstration's argument takes; the verses that follow will determine whether the provocation leads to reflection or to retaliation.
verses.60:
> Some said, “We heard a young man, called Abraham, speaking ˹ill˺ of them.”

**The Naming of the Perpetrator**

The verse records the identification of the perpetrator. *Qālū samiʿnā fatan yadhkuruhum yuqālu lahu Ibrāhīm* — they said, we heard a young man mentioning them; he is called Abraham. The verse is the second step in the demonstration: the audience has asked who did it (21:59); the audience is now naming who they think did it. The naming is the form the inquiry takes when the inquiry has reached its next stage.

The Arabic *fatan* — young man — is the term used for Abraham. The use of *fatan* is significant. The word can mean young man, servant, or one who is being tried. The polysemy is part of what the verse is doing. The audience is identifying Abraham as a young man; the audience is also, without knowing it, identifying him as one who is being tried. The trial is what the rest of the narrative will describe.

**"We Heard Him Mentioning Them"**

The verb *dhakara* — to mention — is the same verb used elsewhere in the sūrah for the Prophet's speech about the audience's gods. The verse is presenting the audience's report of what Abraham said. The audience heard Abraham mention the idols in a way that the audience considered insulting. The mentioning is what the verses earlier recorded (21:52, 21:54). The audience is now identifying the source of the mentioning.

**A Verse That Sets Up the Trial**

The verse is the setup for what will follow. The audience has identified the perpetrator; the audience is now demanding that the perpetrator be brought for the public confrontation. The confrontation will be the climax of the Abraham narrative; the narrative is what the verses are setting up.

The trial will be a confrontation between Abraham's argument and the audience's framework. The confrontation will culminate in Abraham's sarcastic suggestion that the largest idol had smashed the others (21:63). The suggestion will expose the audience's framework; the exposure is the form the prophetic argument takes when it has reached its climax. The trial is the form the demonstration takes when it has been pushed to its limit.

**The "Mentioning" That Is Already a Argument**

The audience reports Abraham as *yadhkuruhum* — mentioning them. The same root *dhikr* is what the Qur'an elsewhere calls itself (21:50). The audience uses the word in a pejorative sense: Abraham has been speaking against the gods. The pejorative sense is the audience's; the pejorative sense assumes the gods deserve defending. The assumption is what the demonstration has begun to disturb. The disturbance will continue as the dialogue unfolds; the unfolding is what the narrative is about.
verses.61:
> They demanded, “Bring him before the eyes of the people, so that they may witness ˹his trial˺.”

**Bring Him Out Where Everyone Can See**

The crowd's demand is to bring Ibrāhīm before the people so that they can witness it. The Arabic used for bringing him out, *bi-ṣirāḥin*, carries the sense of openly, in the daylight, for all to see. Al-Ṭabarī notes that the demand has a double edge: they want the case proved in public, and they want the punishment to be public too.

The purpose clause the verse adds — "so that they may witness" — is the crowd's own reasoning, and it shows how they understood what they were doing. The trial is not the private settling of a question; it is a spectacle the town has chosen, so that the outcome will be known and remembered. That choice shapes everything that follows. In the next verses the same crowd becomes the audience for Ibrāhīm's reply, and their verdict turns on themselves in front of everybody. The public form they asked for is the form the reversal takes.

The argument has run from the diagnosis of the town's practice (21:54) to the demonstration (21:58), and the surrounding verses set the demand in its place: the verdict had already been reached (21:59), and the trial that begins here ends with the attempt to burn Ibrāhīm alive and his rescue (21:68–69). The chapter's own audience is addressed in the same terms — they had asked the Prophet for a sign (21:5) and asked when the promise would come (21:38) — so a crowd demanding a public demonstration is not a story about the distant past only.
verses.62:
> They asked, “Was it you who did this to our gods, O Abraham?”

**The Direct Confrontation**

The verse is the formal confrontation. *Qālū a-antum faʿalta hādha bi-ālihatinā yā Ibrāhīm* — they said, was it you who did this to our gods, O Abraham? The verse is the moment the inquiry becomes a direct accusation. The audience has identified the perpetrator (21:60); the audience has demanded a public trial (21:61); the audience is now addressing the perpetrator directly. The addressing is the form the trial takes.

The Arabic *a-antum* (here *anta*) — was it you? — is a question that demands a yes or no answer. The verse is asking Abraham to confirm or deny. The asking is the form the public trial takes; the trial will determine the audience's verdict. The verdict will not be a recognition of what Abraham has showed; the verdict will be the verdict the audience had already reached before the trial began.

**"O Abraham" — The Naming That Frames the Question**

The address — *yā Ibrāhīm* — is the formal naming of the accused. The audience is no longer speaking about the young man who mentioned them (21:60); the audience is now addressing Abraham by name. The naming is the form the trial takes. The trial is no longer about an anonymous perpetrator; the trial is about a named person. The person is being asked to take responsibility for what he has done.

The naming is also part of the argument. The audience that has named the perpetrator has done the work that the demonstration was designed to produce. The demonstration forced the naming; the naming is the form the demonstration's first phase takes. The naming will lead to the trial; the trial will lead to the climax; the climax is what the narrative is about.

**The Question That Is Not Neutral**

The question is not neutral. The audience is not genuinely asking whether Abraham did it; the audience is accusing Abraham and demanding a confession. The form of the question assumes the answer. The audience has decided that Abraham did it; the question is the form the decision takes. The decision has been made before the trial began; the trial is the public confirmation.

**A Verse That Begins the Trial's Verbal Phase**

The verse is the opening of the trial's verbal phase. The trial will proceed through the question here, Abraham's reply in 21:63, the audience's momentary recognition in 21:64, their retreat in 21:65, Abraham's final argument in 21:66–67, and the verdict in 21:68. The progression is the form the trial takes. The trial will move from the direct accusation through Abraham's reductio ad absurdum, through the audience's brief recognition, through the retreat into the framework, to the verdict of burning.

The verse connects to the broader sūrahic argument against the audience of the Qur'an. The Meccan audience had been asking the Prophet questions; the questions were forms of accusation. The questions had been answered by the Qur'anic verses; the answers were forms of the prophetic argument. The verse at 21:62 is part of the same structure. The questions and the answers are the form the prophetic confrontation takes.

The confrontation will end with the audience's inability to defend its framework. The inability is what the dialogue is producing. The producing is the form the demonstration's argument takes. The argument is what the sūrah is offering the audience of every age; the offering is the substance of the verse's call.
verses.63:
> He replied ˹sarcastically˺, “No, this one—the biggest of them—did it! So ask them, if they can talk!”

**The Answer That Turns the Question Around**

Asked who had smashed the idols, Ibrāhīm answers: "No — this one, the biggest of them, did it. Ask them, if they can speak." The particle *bal* turns the accusation back on the question, and the reply is deliberately absurd. He had left the largest idol standing, and he now names it as the culprit. The absurdity is the argument.

If the idols are gods, able to act and to answer, then ask them. Their silence answers for them, and the town's own question — who did this? — becomes the demonstration that the things they worship cannot act at all. The commentators note that Ibrāhīm's aim is not to escape but to make his people test their own claim. He hands them the method: ask.
