The verse ends with the condition that decides everything, "if they can speak," and the crowd's inability to meet it is recorded in the next verse.

This is one of the three occasions recorded of Ibrāhīm's ironic speech: his saying "I am sick" (37:89), his answer about Sarah (Genesis 20:2), and this reply about the largest idol. The argument has run from the diagnosis of the town's practice (21:54) to the demonstration (21:58) to the inquiry (21:59) and now to this answer, which leads to the brief recognition of 21:64, the relapse in 21:65, and the sentence of burning in 21:68.
verses.64:
> So they came back to their senses, saying ˹to one another˺, “You yourselves are truly the wrongdoers!”

**The Moment They Turn Against Themselves**

"So they came back to themselves and said, 'You yourselves are truly the wrongdoers.'" The Arabic *rajaʿū ilā anfusihim* means they returned to their own minds, and the phrase describes a moment when a crowd stops and looks at what it has been doing. For an instant the argument lands. The people who had been demanding that the culprit be found and punished admit that the fault is their own — worshipping what cannot answer.

The moment is one of the most striking reversals in the Qur'anic story, and it is worth noticing what produces it. Not a miracle and not a threat: a question they cannot answer without convicting themselves. The confession follows. Then, in the very next verse, it is gone. The narrative keeps the two beats apart to show that the recognition was real, and that its being real makes the relapse worse. They saw it, said it in their own words, and turned away from it.

*Wrongdoers* is the sūrah's word for those who know better: the townspeople confess too late (21:14), the verse before used it of a hypothetical claim to divinity (21:29), the scales of justice will expose it (21:47), the verdict had already formed (21:59), and the verbal diagnosis (21:54) had done what it could. Their recognition lasts only until the next verse, where they fall back into the worship the argument had just refuted (21:65).
verses.65:
> Then they ˹quickly˺ regressed to their ˹original˺ mind-set, ˹arguing,˺ “You already know that those ˹idols˺ cannot talk.”

**Turned Upside Down Again**

"Then they were turned upside down, and said: 'You already know that these cannot speak.'" The Arabic *nukisū ʿalā ruʾūsihim* pictures a person toppling head over heels. The image matches what the verse describes: the recognition of the previous verse is overturned within a breath, and the crowd returns to the belief it had just abandoned.

What makes the relapse so telling is that their own sentence concedes the whole argument. "You already know that these cannot speak" — that is exactly Ibrāhīm's case against them, and they use it as an answer to him. They admit the idols have no power to act and then go back to worshipping them anyway. The passage, read to its end, is about how people hold a belief for reasons they themselves cannot state without refuting it. The next verses give Ibrāhīm's closing line: do you worship, besides God, what can neither benefit nor harm you?

Read with the verse before it (21:64), the passage is a study of a belief that cannot survive being examined but survives being abandoned. The scene closes with the town's decision to burn Ibrāhīm alive (21:68).
verses.66:
> He rebuked ˹them˺, “Do you then worship—instead of Allah—what can neither benefit nor harm you in any way

**The Final Argument Before the Verdict**

The verse is Abraham's final argument before the audience pronounces its verdict. *Qāla afa-taʿbudūna min dūni Allāhi mā lā yanfaʿukum shayʾan wa lā yaḍurrukum* — he said, do you worship besides God that which neither benefits you in anything nor harms you? The verse is the climax of the verbal phase of the trial. The argument is reduced to its essentials; the essentials are the question.

The question — *afa-taʿbudūna* — do you worship? — is one of the most direct in the Abraham narrative. The verb *ʿabada* — to worship — names the action the audience has been performing; the question is asking the audience to consider what the action has meant. The meaning is what the question is exposing. The exposure is the form the argument takes.

**"What Can Neither Benefit Nor Harm You"**

The Arabic *nafaʿa* and *ḍarara* — benefit and harm — name the two basic forms of agency a worshipper would expect from a god. The audience's gods can do neither. The gods cannot benefit; the gods cannot harm. The gods are not gods; the gods are nothing. The verse is naming the nothing.

**Connection to Other Qur'anic Statements**

The verse echoes similar statements throughout the Qur'an. 5:76 says: *You have taken idols besides God in vain; between yourselves in the life of this world; but on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another*. 6:71 says: *We have been warned against this; and woe to those who associate others with God*. 10:18 says: *They worship besides God that which neither harms them nor benefits them*. 13:16 says: *They have taken besides Him gods; they do not create anything, but are themselves created*. 22:12 says: *He calls, besides God, that which neither harms him nor benefits him*. 25:55 says: *They serve, besides God, that which neither benefits them nor harms them*.

**A Verse That Returns to the Sūrah's Central Argument**

The verse is part of the sūrah's argument against the polytheistic framework. The audience of Abraham had been treating the idols as partners of God; the verse is denying that the idols have the agency that would make them partners. The denying is the form the argument takes. The argument is what the sūrah has been doing since 21:19. The verse at 21:66 is the Abrahamic form of the argument; the form is what the audience of the Qur'an is being asked to recognise.

**A Verse That Precedes the Final Argument**

The verse is the second-to-last of Abraham's arguments. The next verse (21:67) will be the final argument — *fie upon you and upon what you worship besides God*. The climax is what the trial has been building toward; the climax is what the verses that follow will respond to. The response will be the verdict of burning (21:68). The verdict is what the audience has chosen in preference to the recognition. The choosing is what the verse is documenting; the documentation is part of the sūrah's argument.

The audience of the Qur'an is being shown what the choice looks like when it has been made fully. The choosing is what the verses are asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the verse's call takes; the call is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.
verses.67:
> Shame on you and whatever you worship instead of Allah! Do you not have any sense?”

**The Final Argument**

The verse is Abraham's final argument before the verdict. *Uffun lakum wa limā taʿbudūna min dūni Allāhi afalā taʿqilūn* — fie upon you and upon what you worship besides God; have you no sense? The verse is the climax of the verbal argument; the argument is being closed. The closing is the form the prophetic speech takes when the speech has done what it can do.

The Arabic *uff* — fie, an exclamation of annoyance and disgust — is unusually strong language in the Qur'an. The same word appears in 17:23 in the verse that forbids even saying *uff* to one's parents. The use of *uff* here, against the idols the audience worships, is a striking rhetorical move. The rhetorical move is meant to communicate the intensity of Abraham's reaction to what the audience has been doing. The intensity is the form the argument takes.

**"You and Whatever You Worship Instead of God"**

The phrase *min dūni Allāhi* — besides God, other than God — is the standard Qur'anic way of referring to the supposed partners of God. The phrase has been used throughout the sūrah (21:43, 21:53, 21:55, 21:57, 21:58, 21:66). The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the partners are not partners. The principle is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise; the recognition is the form the response takes.

**"Do You Not Have Any Sense?"**

The closing question — *afalā taʿqilūn* — have you no sense? — is the same kind of question that has appeared throughout the sūrah. 21:10 asked: *Will you not then understand?* 21:30 asked: *Will they not then believe?* The question is the form the sūrah's call takes. The call is the audience's invitation to use the minds they have. The minds are what the audience is being asked to exercise; the exercise is what the question is offering.

The question is also the recognition that the audience has not been using the minds they have. The minds have been subordinated to the framework; the framework has been operating without examination; the examination is what the question is asking the audience to do. The doing is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for.

**A Verse That Closes the Verbal Phase of the Trial**

The verse closes the verbal phase of the trial. The next verse (21:68) will record the audience's verdict: *Burn him, and help your gods*. The transition from argument to verdict is the form the trial takes when the argument has been completed. The completing is what the verse is documenting; the documenting is part of the sūrah's argument.

**A Verse That Returns to the Sūrah's Refusal of the Inheritance Argument**

The verse implicitly returns to one of the sūrah's recurring refutations. The audience had argued that they were worshipping because their fathers had worshipped (21:53). The verse's question — *do you not have any sense?* — is asking the audience to consider whether the inherited practice is justified by any sense they can recognise.

The verse is therefore not just an expression of disgust; the verse is an appeal to the intellect. The appeal is the last thing the argument has to offer. The appeal is what the verse is asking the audience to take seriously.
verses.68:
> They concluded, “Burn him up to avenge your gods, if you must act.”

**"Help Your Gods"**

The verb *naṣara* — to help, to support — is being used here in its basic sense. The audience is being asked to help the gods; the gods cannot help themselves. The asking is the form the audience's continued commitment to the framework takes. The commitment has survived the entire argument; the commitment is now being asked to express itself in action against the messenger.

**A Refusal of the Accusation of Nimrod**

The commentators, including al-Rāzī, note that the popular stories attached to this incident — particularly the assertion that it was Nimrod who ordered the burning — have no direct basis in the Qur'an. The Qur'an does not name the king; the Qur'an only records the audience's verdict.

**A Verse That Sets Up the Miracle**

The verse is the setup for the miracle at 21:69. The audience has pronounced its verdict; the verdict will be the occasion for the divine intervention. The argument has not just been verbal; the argument has been moving toward the moment when the divine power will be visibly showed.
verses.69:
> We ordered, “O fire! Be cool and safe for Abraham!”

**The Divine Intervention**

The verse records the divine intervention. *Qulnā yā nāru kūnī bardan wa-salāman ʿalā Ibrāhīm* — We said, O fire, be coolness and peace for Abraham. The verb *qāla* is in the first person plural — We said — and the address is to the fire itself. The fire is being addressed as an agent; the fire is being commanded to do something contrary to its nature. The command is the form the divine intervention takes.

The verse is one of the most famous in the Qur'an. The intervention has become a pattern of divine deliverance; the deliverance is what the verse is recording. The recording is part of the sūrah's larger treatment of the prophets; the treatment is what the verses have been preparing for. The preparation is what the argument has been doing; the argument is what the previous verses have been building toward.

**"Be Coolness and Peace for Abraham"**

The constructive — *kūnī bardan wa-salāman* — be coolness and peace — names the form the command takes. The fire is commanded to be two things: coolness and peace. The coolness removes the heat; the peace removes the harm.

Al-Ṭabarī records that without the peace, the coolness would have been so extreme that Abraham would have been harmed by the cold. The peace is what makes the coolness safe; the safety is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

**A Verse That Returns to the Sūrah's Theme of Deliverance**

The verse is one of several in the sūrah that record divine deliverances. 21:9 promised: *Then We fulfilled Our promise to them, saving them along with whoever We willed*. 21:71 will record: *They had sought to harm him, but We made them the worst losers*. The verse at 21:69 is the specific instance of the promise; the instance is what the verse is recording.
verses.70:
> They had sought to harm him, but We made them the worst losers

**The Reversal of the Verdict**

The verse completes the reversal. *Wa arādu bihi kaydan fa-jaʿalnāhum al-akhsarīn* — they intended against him a plan, but We made them the greatest losers. The verb *arāda* — to intend, to plan — names the audience's action. The verb *jaʿala* — to make — names God's response. The response is the form the verse's argument takes; the argument is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

**Connection to 21:9**

The verse echoes the promise made earlier in the sūrah: *Then We fulfilled Our promise to them, saving them along with whoever We willed and destroying the transgressors*. The verse at 21:70 is the specific instance of the general promise. The destruction of the transgressors is now recorded as the greatest losers. The recording is what the sūrah has been preparing for; the preparation is what the earlier verses have been doing.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Scheming**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: scheming. The Arabic *kaid* — scheming, plotting, planning — is the same word that Abraham used for his own plan against the idols (21:57). The audience is now doing what Abraham had done: planning against something. The planning is the form the resistance takes; the resistance is what the verses are documenting.

**A Verse That Closes the Abraham Narrative of the Sūrah**

The verse closes the Abraham narrative within the sūrah. The verses that follow will move to Lot (21:74–75) and then to other prophets. The closure is the form the Abraham narrative takes; the narrative has moved from the verbal diagnosis to the demonstration to the trial to the verdict to the deliverance. The progression is what the narrative is about. The about-ness is the substance of the sūrah's argument.

The audience of the Qur'an is being asked to integrate the Abraham narrative into their understanding of the divine economy. The integrating is the form the response takes; the response is what the verses are asking for.
verses.71:
> Then We delivered him, along with Lot, to the land We had showered with blessings for all people

**The Deliverance to the Blessed Land**

The verse records Abraham's deliverance along with Lot. *Wa najjaynāhu wa Lūṭan ilā al-arḍi allatī bāraknā fīhā lil-ʿālamīn* — and We delivered him and Lot to the land that We blessed for all peoples. The verb *najjā* — to deliver, to save — is the same verb used throughout the sūrah for divine deliverance. The deliverance has brought Abraham and Lot to a specific land; the land has been blessed for all peoples.

The commentators differ on which land is meant. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as the Levant (Shām); al-Qurṭubī reads it as Mecca, where Abraham went to build the Kaʿbah with Ishmael (2:127). The land from which they were delivered is reputed to be Mesopotamia. The reading is part of the commentators' effort to place the Abraham narrative in a specific geography; the geography is not essential to the verse's argument, but the blessing is.

**"Blessed for All Peoples"**

The phrase *allatī bāraknā fīhā lil-ʿālamīn* — that We blessed for all peoples — names the form the blessing takes. The blessing is not for Abraham alone; the blessing is for all peoples. The blessing is therefore an universal blessing; the universality is part of what the verse is asking the audience to recognise. The land has been made a place of blessing for the entire human community; the recognition of the blessing is part of the response the verse is asking for.

The same vocabulary appears elsewhere in the Qur'an in connection with other prophets and other lands. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that divine blessing has been placed on specific lands for the benefit of all peoples. The principle is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

**Lot's Companionship in Deliverance**

Lot is mentioned here as a companion in the deliverance. *Lūṭan* — Lot — is the nephew of Abraham in the Qur'anic narrative (11:74–81); his wife was a disbeliever who stayed behind when the cities were destroyed. The companionship of Lot in the deliverance shows that the divine deliverance is not reserved for one person; the deliverance extends to those who have aligned themselves with the messenger.

**A Verse That Returns to the Sūrah's Theme of Deliverance**

The verse returns to the sūrah's theme of divine deliverance. The deliverance has been promised (21:9); the deliverance has been manifested in Abraham's case (21:69–70); the deliverance has now been extended to a specific land. The progression is what the sūrah is documenting. The documenting is the form the divine economy takes; the economy is what the verses are asking the audience to consider.

**A Verse That Sets Up the Following Narrative**

The verse is the bridge between the Abraham narrative and the verses that will follow. The next verses will describe Abraham's descendants (21:72), his role as imam (21:73), Lot's deliverance (21:74–75), Noah's deliverance (21:76–77), David and Solomon's judgment (21:78–80), and the rest of the prophetic narratives. The bridge is what the verse is providing; the providing is the form the narrative's coherence takes.

The coherence is part of what the sūrah is doing. The sūrah is not just listing prophets; the sūrah is showing how the prophetic calling has continued from one messenger to the next. The recognition is the substance of the response the verses are asking for; the asking is the form the call takes.
verses.72:
> And We blessed him with Isaac ˹as a son˺ and Jacob ˹as a grandson˺, as an additional favour—making all of them righteous

**The Gift of Descendants**

The verse records the gift of descendants. *Wa wahabnā lahu Isḥāqa wa Yaʿqūba nāfilatan* — and We bestowed upon him Isaac and Jacob as an additional gift. The verb *wahaba* — to bestow, to grant as a gift — names the form the giving takes. The giving is not earned; the giving is gift. The gift is the substance of the verse's announcement; the announcement is what the verse is making.

The Arabic *nāfila* — additional gift, supererogatory gift — is a precise term. The commentators differ on what it modifies. Al-Ṭabarī reads it as referring to Jacob alone, on the reasoning that Abraham had prayed for Isaac (37:100) but not for a grandson. Al-Qurṭubī reads it as applying to both: the initial gift was Isaac, and the additional gift was Jacob. The reading is not essential to the verse's argument; the additionalness is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The gift is bigger than what was prayed for.

**"Making All of Them Righteous"**

The verse continues *wa jaʿalnāhum salihīn* — and We made them righteous. The verb *jaʿala* — to make — names the act of making. The gift is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

The making of the prophets and their descendants righteous is one of the most theologically significant features of the Qur'anic narrative. The righteousness is not produced by the prophets themselves; the righteousness is given by God. The giving is the form the divine economy takes; the economy is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

**A Verse That Returns to the Sūrah's Theme of Divine Gifts**

The verse returns to the sūrah's recurring theme of divine gifts. 21:51 said: *And We had given Abraham his sound judgment before*. 21:48 said: *We gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion*. The verse at 21:72 is the next instance of the same theme. The gifts are what God has given to the prophets; the giving is what the sūrah is documenting; the documenting is part of what the verses are asking the audience to consider.

**A Verse That Extends the Abrahamic Narrative**

The verse extends the Abrahamic narrative by adding his descendants. The narrative had focused on Abraham himself (21:51–71); the verse now extends to Isaac and Jacob.

The extension is also part of the broader Qur'anic argument about the continuity of the prophetic calling. The calling has been passed from one messenger to the next; the calling is the form the divine economy takes. The verses that follow (21:73) will extend the argument further by making Abraham and his descendants imams who guide by God's command. The extension is what the sūrah is doing; the doing is part of what the verses are asking the audience to recognise.
verses.73:
> We ˹also˺ made them leaders, guiding by Our command, and inspired them to do good deeds, establish prayer, and pay alms-tax. And they were devoted to Our worship

**The Making of Imams**

The verse records the making of the prophetic descendants into leaders. *Wa jaʿalnāhum aʾimmatan yahdūna bi-amrinā* — and We made them imams guiding by Our command. The noun *imam* — leader, one who is followed — names the role; the verb *jaʿala* — to make — names the act. The making is divine; the leading is the form the role takes; the role is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

The commentators, including al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī, note that the making into imams means that they were the ones who were followed and imitated. They taught and guided people in matters of religion and good deeds. The guidance is the substance of the role; the role is what the divine economy produces. The producing is the form the verse's argument takes.

**"Guiding by Our Command"**

The phrase *yahdūna bi-amrinā* — guiding by Our command — specifies the form the guidance takes. The guidance is not by personal opinion or by inherited tradition; the guidance is by divine command. The guidance is therefore authoritative in a way that human guidance cannot be. The authority is the form the guidance takes; the guidance is what the verse is offering the audience to consider.
verses.74:
> And to Lot We gave wisdom and knowledge, and delivered him from the society engrossed in shameful practices. They were certainly an evil, rebellious people

**Lot's Gifts**

The verse returns to Lot. *Wa ilā Lūṭin āṭaynāhu ḥukman wa ʿilman* — and to Lot We gave judgment and knowledge. The verb *āṭā* — to give — is the same verb used throughout the sūrah for the gifts given to the prophets. The gifts to Lot are judgment and knowledge; the gifts are what the verse is recording.

The Arabic *ḥukm* — judgment, the ability to decide between disputants — is one of the recurring descriptions of what prophets are given. 3:79 says: *It is not for any human being to whom God has given the Book, the judgment, and prophethood to then say to the people, "Be worshippers of me besides God."* 12:22 says: *And when he reached maturity, We gave him judgment and knowledge*. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the prophets are given the capacity to judge and to know. The principle is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

**"And We Delivered Him from the Society"**

The verse continues *wa najjaynāhu min al-qaryati allatī kānat taʿmalu al-khabāʾith* — and We delivered him from the town that was committing vile deeds. The verb *najjā* — to deliver — is the same verb used for the deliverance of Abraham (21:71). The deliverance is the form the divine protection takes; the protection is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

The town is described as one that was committing *khabāʾith* — vile deeds, shameful practices. The Arabic word names acts that are morally repugnant. The town is not just generally immoral; the town is committed to specific kinds of immoral acts. The commitment is what the verse is recording; the recording is part of the sūrah's argument.

**"They Were Certainly an Evil, Rebellious People"**

The description is part of the Qur'an's larger treatment of Lot's people. 7:80–84, 11:77–83, 15:57–77, 26:160–73, 27:54–58, 29:28–35, and 54:33–38 all describe the same story with various emphases. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the actions of Lot's people were beyond the pale of what a community could tolerate; the tolerance is what the divine deliverance is responding to.

**The Transition from Lot to Noah**

The verse is the bridge to the next narrative, which will be Noah's story (21:76–77). The verse itself is mostly about Lot; the next verses will be about Noah. The transition is what the sūrah is doing; the doing is part of the prophetic narratives that will continue through 21:91. The continuation is what the sūrah is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.

The audience of the Qur'an is being asked to consider the cumulative picture the narratives present. The picture is one of messengers sent to communities that refused the message; the refusal produced divine deliverance for the messengers and destruction for the refusing communities. The picture is what the verses are asking the audience to integrate; the integration is the form the response takes.
verses.75:
> And We admitted him into Our mercy, ˹for˺ he was truly one of the righteous

**Entry Into God's Mercy**

The verse records Lot's admission into God's mercy. *Wa adkhalnāhu fī raḥmatinā* — and We admitted him into Our mercy. The verb *adkhala* — to admit, to cause to enter — names the form the action takes. The admission is divine; the mercy is the substance of the admission. The verse is asking the audience to consider what it means to be admitted into the divine mercy.

The verse is one of several in the Qur'an that use the image of being admitted into God's mercy. 4:175 uses the same image for the believers. 7:151 says: *And We admitted them into Our mercy from Us*. 9:99, 42:8, 45:30, 48:25, 76:31 all use the same or related images. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the divine mercy is a place that one can enter. The entry is the substance of the verse's announcement; the announcement is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise.

**"He Was Truly One of the Righteous"**

The verse closes *innahu min al-ṣāliḥīn* — he was truly among the righteous. The Arabic *ṣāliḥīn* — the righteous — is one of the Qur'an's most theologically loaded terms. The righteous are those who have aligned their lives with the divine order; the alignment is the form the righteousness takes. Lot is being affirmed as one of the righteous; the affirmation is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

The use of *innahu* — truly, indeed — is emphatic. The verse is making a strong claim about Lot's status. The strength is part of what the verse is asking the audience to recognise. The recognition is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for.

**A Verse That Closes the Lot Narrative**

The verse closes the Lot narrative within the sūrah. The next verses will move to Noah (21:76–77). The closure is the form the narrative takes; the narrative has moved from Lot's gifts (21:74) to his deliverance to his admission into mercy. The progression is what the narrative is about; the about-ness is what the sūrah is offering the audience. The offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.

The audience of the Qur'an is being asked to consider how the Lot narrative fits into the larger picture. The picture is one of messengers sent, communities refusing, divine deliverance following, and the messengers being admitted into mercy. The admitting is the form the divine economy takes; the economy is what the verses are asking the audience to recognise.

The admission into mercy is not a vague hope; the admission is the specific form the divine response takes to a life of righteousness. The life is what the verse is describing in Lot; the describing is part of the model the verse is offering. The offering is what the audience of every age is being asked to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.
verses.76:
> And ˹remember˺ when Noah had cried out to Us earlier, so We responded to him and delivered him and his family from the great distress

**The Cry and the Response**

The verse records Noah's earlier cry to God. *Wa Nūḥun idhā nadā min qablu* — and Noah, when he cried out before. The verb *nadā* — to call, to cry out — names the form the prayer takes. The cry is one of supplication; the supplication is the substance of what Noah did. The verse is asking the audience to consider what it means to cry out to God in distress.

**"We Responded to Him"**

The verse continues *fa-istajabnā lahu* — and We responded to him. The verb *istajāba* — to respond, to answer — names the form the divine response takes. The response is to the cry; the response is what the verse is recording. The recording is part of the sūrah's pattern of showing how God responds to those who call.

The Arabic *karb* — distress, anguish — is a strong term. The word is used elsewhere in the Qur'an for the experience of being overwhelmed by circumstances beyond one's capacity.

**A Verse That Returns to the Sūrah's Theme of Deliverance**

The verse returns to the sūrah's recurring theme. The deliverance has been promised (21:9); the deliverance has been manifested in Abraham and Lot (21:69–71, 21:74–75); the deliverance has now been manifested in Noah. The recurrence is what the sūrah is documenting; the documenting is part of what the verses are asking the audience to consider.

**A Verse That Sets Up the Flood Narrative**

The verse is the setup for the flood narrative that follows in 21:77. The cry and the response are the prelude; the flood is the consequence. The verse is therefore not just describing a past event; the verse is preparing the audience for what the next verse will describe. The preparing is the form the narrative takes; the narrative is what the sūrah is offering.

The audience of the Qur'an is being asked to integrate the Noah narrative into their understanding of the divine economy. The economy includes cry, response, deliverance, and consequence. The integrating is the form the response takes; the response is what the verses are asking for.
verses.77:
> And We made him prevail over those who had rejected Our signs. They were truly an evil people, so We drowned them all

**Noah's Prevailing Over the Rejecters**

The verse records Noah's prevailing over those who rejected God's signs. *Wa najaynāhu min al-qawmi alladhīna kadhhabū bi-āyātinā* — and We helped him prevail against the people who denied Our signs. The verb *najā* is being used here in a slightly different sense — not just to deliver but to make prevail. The making prevail is the form the divine support takes; the support is what the verse is recording.

**"So We Drowned Them All"**

The verse closes *fa-aghraqnāhum ajmaʿīn* — so We drowned them all. The verb *aghraqa* — to drown — names the specific form the divine punishment took. The verb is used in the first person plural — We drowned them — and the object is *ajmaʿīn* — all of them. The totality of the punishment is what the verse is recording; the recording is the form the argument takes.

**A Verse That Closes the Noah Narrative**

The verse closes the Noah narrative within the sūrah. The next verses will move to David and Solomon (21:78–82). The closure is the form the narrative takes; the narrative has moved from the cry to the response to the prevailing to the punishment. The progression is what the narrative is about; the about-ness is what the sūrah is offering the audience. The offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.
verses.78:
> And ˹remember˺ when David and Solomon passed judgment regarding the crops ruined ˹at night˺ by someone’s sheep, and We were witness to their judgments

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Wisdom and Knowledge**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the divine gifts of wisdom and knowledge. Lot was given judgment and knowledge (21:74); David and Solomon are shown exercising the gifts in a specific case. The exercising is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**A Specific Case of Prophetic Judgment**

The verse names a specific case the prophets had to adjudicate. The animals had wandered into a cultivated area and damaged it. Two prophets were asked to decide; they decided. The deciding is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the consideration is the form the response takes.

**Two Versions of the Decision**

The verse's silence about the specific outcome is itself a teaching. The teaching is that the prophetic judgment is grounded not in human cleverness but in divine assistance. The assistance is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise; the recognition is the form the response takes.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Wisdom and Knowledge**

The consideration is the substance of the response the verses are asking for; the asking is the form the call takes. The verse is part of the broader Qur'anic narrative about David and Solomon, which is told most fully in Sūrah 27 and Sūrah 38. The narratives agree on the basic gifts given to David and Solomon; the verses differ in which aspects they emphasise. The verse at 21:78 emphasises the practical exercise of the prophetic office in community disputes.
verses.79:
> We guided ˹young˺ Solomon to a fairer settlement, and granted each of them wisdom and knowledge. We subjected the mountains as well as the birds to hymn ˹Our praises˺ along with David. It is We Who did ˹it all˺

**Solomon's Better Judgment**

The verse makes a specific claim: Solomon's judgment was the fairer one. *Fafahhamnāhā Sulaymāna* — and We made Solomon to understand it (the case). The verb *fahhama* — to make understand — is a precise term. The making-understand is what God did for Solomon; the making is the substance of the verse's announcement.

The commentators have offered two main ways of reading this. One reading takes the verse to mean that Solomon's judgment was the better of the two; David accepted Solomon's judgment when Solomon explained it. Another reading treats the verse as recording a case in which both judgments were valid but the later one (Solomon's) superseded the earlier one — a form of divine abrogation. The two readings need not be exclusive; the verse can be showing that prophetic judgments can be refined through further insight.

**"Each of Them We Granted Wisdom and Knowledge"**

The verse continues *wa kullan āṭaynāhu ḥukman wa ʿilman* — and unto each of them We gave judgment and knowledge. The Arabic *ḥukm* and *ʿilm* — judgment and knowledge — are the same terms used for Lot (21:74). The recurrence is part of the Qur'anic pattern of describing the prophets as those who have been given the wisdom to govern and the knowledge to teach. The recurrence is what the verse is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.

**The Mountains and Birds Glorifying with David**

The verse continues *wa sakhkharnā maʿa Dāwūda al-jibāla yusabbiḥna wa al-ṭayra* — and We subjected the mountains with David to glorify, and the birds. The verb *sakhkhara* — to subject, to subdue — names the form the divine action takes. The mountains and the birds are described as joining David in glorification; the joining is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

The same image appears in 27:16, 34:10, and 38:19. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that David was given a special relationship with the natural world; the natural world joined him in glorifying God.

**"It Is We Who Did It"**

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The verse is claiming that the entire prophetic phenomenon is the work of God. The work is not the prophets' achievement; the work is God's gift.
verses.80:
> We taught him the art of making body armour to protect you in battle. Will you then be grateful

**David's Art of Armour**

The verse records that David was taught a specific craft. *Wa ʿallamnāhu ṣanʿata labūsin lakum li-tuḥṣinakum min baʾsikum* — and We taught him the craft of garments for you, to protect you from your violence. The verb *ʿallama* — to teach — names the form the divine action takes. The action is teaching; the teaching is what the verse is recording. The recording is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

The Arabic *labūs* — garment, covering — is the same word used in 34:11, where God says to David: *Make coats of mail, and measure well the links of it*. The reference is to the practical craft of making armour. The craft is what David was taught; the teaching is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"To Protect You from Your Violence"**

The phrase *li-tuḥṣinakum min baʾsikum* — to protect you from your violence — specifies the purpose of the craft. The Arabic *baʾs* — violence, battle, harm — names the kind of threat the armour is meant to address. The threat is human; the threat is what the armour protects against. The protection is the substance of the verse's argument.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The protection is not from a divine threat; the protection is from human violence. The divine teaching is in the service of human protection. The protection is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"Will You Then Be Grateful?"**

The verse closes *afalā tashkurūn* — will you then be grateful? The verb *shakara* — to thank, to be grateful — names the form the response should take. The response should be gratitude; the gratitude is what the verse is asking the audience to offer. The asking is the form the call takes.

The closing question is one of the recurring rhetorical moves in the sūrah. The question is asking the audience to consider what response they have given to what they have received. The response is what the verses have been asking for throughout.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Divine Gifts**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine gifts. The gifts include sound judgment (21:51), the criterion (21:48), wisdom and knowledge (21:74, 21:79), and now the craft of making armour. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that God has given specific gifts for specific purposes. The principle is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise; the recognition is the form the response takes.
verses.81:
> And to Solomon We subjected the raging winds, blowing by his command to the land We had showered with blessings. It is We Who know everything

**Solomon's Command Over the Wind**

The verse records Solomon's dominion over the wind. *Wa li-Sulaymāna al-rīḥa ʿāṣifan tajrī bi-amrihi ilā al-arḍi allatī bāraknā fīhā* — and to Solomon the wind, running violent by his command to the land We had blessed. The verb *sakhkhara* — to subject — names the form the divine action takes. The wind has been subjected to Solomon; the subjecting is what the verse is recording.

This is one of the most famous miracles of the Qur'anic Solomon narrative. 34:12, 38:36, and the longer narrative in 27:17–44 all expand on the same theme: Solomon was given dominion over the wind; the wind ran by his command; the running was the form the divine gift took. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that God gives specific gifts to specific messengers; the giving is the substance of the verse's announcement.

**"The Land That We Had Blessed"**

The phrase *al-arḍi allatī bāraknā fīhā* — the land We had blessed — names the destination of the wind's running. The destination is the same blessed land that was mentioned in 21:71. The recurrence of the blessing is part of the sūrah's argument that divine blessing has been placed on specific lands; the lands are what the verses are asking the audience to recognise.

The wind runs to the blessed land by Solomon's command. The running is the form the divine gift takes; the gift is what the verse is recording. The recording is part of the sūrah's argument about the prophetic office; the office is what the verses are asking the audience to consider. The considering is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for.

**"It Is We Who Know Everything"**

The verse closes *wa kunnā bi-kulli shayʾin ʿālimīn* — and We are knowers of all things. The verb *ʿalima* — to know — is being used here in the divine sense. The knowing is comprehensive; the comprehension is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The verse is saying that the divine knowledge encompasses everything, including the running of the wind to the blessed land by Solomon's command. The encompassing is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the consideration is the form the response takes.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Prophetic Gifts**

The verse returns to the sūrah's recurring theme of divine gifts. The gifts have included sound judgment (21:51), the criterion (21:48), wisdom and knowledge (21:74, 21:79), and now the wind's subjection. The principle is what the verse is asking the audience to recognise; the recognition is the form the response takes.

The audience of the Qur'an is being asked to consider the range of gifts the prophets have been given.

The verse is implicitly addressing the audience of the Qur'an. The audience is being asked to consider how God has given specific gifts to specific people for specific purposes. The consideration is the form the verse's call takes. The audience of every age is being invited to consider what gifts they have received; the consideration is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.
verses.82:
> And ˹We subjected˺ some jinn that dived for him, and performed other duties. It is We Who kept them in check

**Jinn Subjected to Solomon**

The verse records that some of the jinn were subjected to Solomon. *Wa min al-shayāṭīni man yaʿūṣūna lahu wa yaʿmalūna ʿamalan dūna dhālika* — and among the demons were those who dived for him and did work other than that. The verb *yaʿūṣa* — to dive — names one of the tasks; the diving is part of what the jinn were doing for Solomon. The doing is the form the subjection takes; the subjection is what the verse is recording.

The verse is part of the longer Solomon narrative in Sūrah 27 and Sūrah 34, where the jinn's subjection is described in greater detail. The jinn worked for Solomon; they built, they dived, they performed other tasks; the performing was the form the divine gift took. The gift is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"It Is We Who Kept Them in Check"**

The verse closes *wa kunnā lahum ḥāfiẓīn* — and We were guarding over them. The verb *ḥafiẓa* — to guard, to keep — names the form the divine action takes. The action is guarding; the guarding is the substance of the verse's claim.

The commentators explain that the guarding ensured that the works of the jinn would not be corrupted. The corruption would have come from the jinn's own tendency to do something apparently good and then make it bad. The guarding is what prevented the corruption; the preventing is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The considering is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Subjected Forces**

The verse returns to the sūrah's recurring theme of forces subjected to the prophets. The wind was subjected to Solomon (21:81); the jinn were subjected to Solomon (21:82); the mountains and birds joined David in glorification (21:79). The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the natural and supernatural orders can be subjected to the prophetic office; the subjecting is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the Qur'anic treatment of the prophetic office. The office is not just a matter of words; the office includes the power to command forces that are normally beyond human control. The commanding is the form the divine gift takes; the gift is what the verses are offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.

**A Verse That Closes the Solomon Narrative**

The verse closes the Solomon narrative within the sūrah. The next verses will move to Job (21:83–84), Ishmael, Idrīs, and Dhu'l-Kifl (21:85–86), Jonah (21:87–88), and Zachariah (21:89–90). The closure is the form the narrative takes; the narrative has moved from Solomon's wind (21:81) to his jinn (21:82). The progression is what the narrative is about; the about-ness is what the sūrah is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.
verses.83:
> And ˹remember˺ when Job cried out to his Lord, “I have been touched with adversity, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.”

**Job's Cry**

The verse records Job's cry to God. *Wa Ayyūb idhā nādā rabbahu annī massaniya al-ḍurru wa anta arḥamu al-rāḥimīn* — and Job, when he called his Lord, "Truly affliction has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful." The verb *nādā* — to call, to cry out — names the form the prayer takes. The prayer is the substance of the verse's announcement; the announcement is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

Job's prayer combines two movements. The first is the acknowledgment of affliction — *massaniya al-ḍurru*, affliction has touched me. The second is the acknowledgment of God's mercy — *wa anta arḥamu al-rāḥimīn*, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful. The two movements are not in tension; the two movements are part of the same prayer. The prayer acknowledges what has happened and asks for what can happen.

**"The Most Merciful of the Merciful"**

Job's title for God — *arḥamu al-rāḥimīn* — is the most intense form of the Arabic superlative. The construction places Job's address of God at the very peak of divine names.

The prayer combines the acknowledgment of affliction with the recognition of divine mercy. The combination is the form the prayer takes when it is offered in the right spirit; the spirit is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Prayer in Distress**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: prayer in distress. Noah cried out to God (21:76); Abraham pleaded with God in various ways; Zachariah will cry out to God (21:89); the prayer is the form the relationship with God takes when the relationship has been pressed. The pressing is what the verses are documenting; the documenting is part of what the sūrah is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.

The verse is part of the broader Qur'anic treatment of Job, which is told more fully in 38:41–44. The treatment in both sūrahs emphasises the prayer, the answer, and the restoration. The verse at 21:83 is the prayer; the next verse will be the answer. The verse is asking the audience to integrate the prayer and the answer; the integration is the form the response takes.
verses.84:
> So We answered his prayer and removed his adversity, and gave him back his family, twice as many, as a mercy from Us and a lesson for the ˹devoted˺ worshippers

**The Answer to Job**

The verse records God's answer to Job's prayer. *Fa-istajabnā lahu wa kashafnā mā bihi min ḍurrin wa āṭaynāhu ahlahu wa mithlahum maʿahum raḥmatan min ʿindinā wa dhikrā lil-ʿābidīn* — so We answered him and removed what was of affliction in him. We gave him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder to the worshippers. The verb *istajāba* — to answer — is the same verb used for the answer to Noah's prayer (21:76). The answering is the form the divine response takes; the response is what the verse is recording.

The prayer in 21:83 was brief; the answer in 21:84 is specific. The specific removes the affliction, restores the family, doubles the household, and gives the restoration as a mercy and a reminder. The specific is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the consideration is the form the response takes.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Divine Response**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine response to prayer. Noah prayed and was answered (21:76–77); Job prayed and was answered (21:83–84). The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the one who calls out to God in the right spirit will be answered. The answering is the form the divine economy takes; the economy is what the verses are asking the audience to consider.

The commentators noted the details the tradition preserved: the years of illness, the patience that became a proverb, and the restoration described as twice the number he had lost.
