verses.85:
> And ˹remember˺ Ishmael, Enoch, and Ⱬul-Kifl. They were all steadfast

**The Group of Patient Prophets**

The verse names three figures in a single sentence. *Wa Ismāʿīla wa al-Idrīsa wa Dhū al-Kifli kullun min al-ṣābirīn* — and Ishmael, and Idrīs, and Dhu'l-Kifl, each of them was among the patient. The verse is asking the audience to remember three specific prophets; the remembering is the form the call takes.

Ishmael's mention is significant. Ishmael is the son of Abraham and Hagar, the ancestor of the Arab peoples through whom the Prophet Muhammad would come. The Qur'an elsewhere mentions Ishmael with his father in the founding of the Kaʿbah (2:127). The mention here is in a list of patient prophets; the patience is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**Idrīs and Dhu'l-Kifl**

Idrīs is usually identified with the Biblical Enoch. The identification is consistent with what the Qur'an elsewhere says about Idrīs being raised to a high station (19:57). The mention here is brief; the brief is part of the verse's compression. The compression is what the verse is asking the audience to integrate with the longer treatments elsewhere.

Dhu'l-Kifl is a more obscure figure. He is also mentioned in 38:48. The traditional accounts identify him variously: as an Israelite entrusted with responsibility, as a prophet under various other names. Some Indian Muslim scholars have identified him with the Buddha. The Qur'an itself does not specify; the Qur'an only names him as one of the patient. The patience is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"Each of Them Was Among the Patient"**

The verse's specification — *kullun min al-ṣābirīn* — is one of the most pointed in the entire sūrah. The Arabic *ṣābirīn* — the patient — is an intensive form. The patience is not just the patience of those who happen to wait; the patience is the patience of those who have made endurance their defining characteristic.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of the Patient**

The verse returns to one of the Qur'an's recurring themes: the patient. The patient are those who endure what they are given; the enduring is the form the patience takes. The Qur'an elsewhere describes the patient as those who will be rewarded without measure (39:10). The verse at 21:85 is asking the audience to consider what the patience looks like in specific prophetic lives. The considering is the form the response takes.
verses.86:
> We admitted them into Our mercy, for they were truly of the righteous

**Admission Into Mercy**

The verse records the admission of the three prophets into God's mercy. *Wa adkhalnāhum fī raḥmatinā innahum min al-ṣāliḥīn* — and We admitted them into Our mercy; indeed they were of the righteous. The verb *adkhala* is the same verb used for Lot's admission (21:75); the admission is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

The admission is into the divine mercy; the mercy is the form the divine action takes. The action is what the verse is recording; the recording is part of the sūrah's argument that the prophets' lives are templates for the divine response to righteousness. The templates are what the verses are asking the audience to consider.

**"They Were Truly of the Righteous"**

The verse's specification — *innahum min al-ṣāliḥīn* — is one of the recurring descriptions in the sūrah. The righteous are those who have aligned their lives with the divine order; the aligning is the form the righteousness takes. The three prophets named in 21:85 are confirmed as being among the righteous; the confirmation is what the verse is offering the audience.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The righteousness is not just a description; the righteousness is the basis for the admission into mercy. The admission is grounded in the righteousness; the grounding is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The considering is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for.

**A Verse That Closes the Group of Three**

The verse closes the brief treatment of Ishmael, Idrīs, and Dhu'l-Kifl. The next verses will move to Jonah (21:87–88). The closure is the form the treatment takes; the treatment has named the three prophets and described them as patient and righteous. The description is what the verses are offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.

The audience of the Qur'an is being asked to integrate the description into their understanding of the prophetic tradition. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine mercy. The mercy has been invoked in many forms throughout the sūrah (21:25, 21:36, 21:42, 21:75, 21:83).
verses.87:
> And ˹remember˺ when the Man of the Whale stormed off ˹from his city˺ in a rage, thinking We would not restrain him. Then in the ˹veils of˺ darkness he cried out, “There is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except You. Glory be to You! I have certainly done wrong.”

**Jonah's Departure**

The verse records Jonah's departure in anger. *Wa Dhu al-Nūni idhā dhahaba mughaḍiban* — and the Man of the Whale, when he went away angry. Jonah — *Dhu al-Nūn* — is so named from the whale that swallowed him. The whale incident is not told in full here; the verse assumes the audience knows the story. The assuming is part of what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"Thinking We Would Not Restrain Him"**

The verse continues *fa-ẓanna a lan naqdira ʿalayhi* — and he thought We would not straiten him. The Arabic *naqdira* — from *qadara* — can mean either to have power or to straiten or to withhold. The commentators disagree on which sense is intended. Some read it as Jonah believing God would not punish him for his sins; others read it as Jonah not believing God could end the punishment he was already suffering.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Prayer in Distress**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: prayer in distress. Noah prayed (21:76); Job prayed (21:83); now Jonah prays. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that prayer is the form the relationship with God takes when the relationship has been pressed. The pressing is what the verses are documenting; the documenting is part of what the sūrah is offering the audience.
verses.88:
> So We answered his prayer and rescued him from anguish. And so do We save the ˹true˺ believers

**The Answer and the Pattern**

The verse records God's answer to Jonah's prayer. *Fa-istajabnā lahu wa najjaynāhu min al-ghammi wa kadhalika nunjī al-muʾminīn* — so We answered him and saved him from the anguish, and so We save the believers. The verb *istajāba* — to answer — is the same verb used for Noah (21:76) and Job (21:83). The answer is the form the divine response takes; the response is what the verse is recording.

The Arabic *ghamm* — anguish, distress, that which covers the heart — is a precise term. The distress Jonah experienced was not just physical; the distress was the kind that covers the heart. The covering is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the consideration is the form the response takes.

**"And Thus Do We Save the Believers"**

The shift from the specific (Jonah) to the general (the believers) is one of the most theologically significant moves in the verse. The same form of divine action that saved Jonah is the form the divine action always takes when the believers are in distress. The always is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The divine saving is not reserved for the prophets alone; the saving extends to all believers. The extending is what the verse is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for. The response is the audience's recognition that the divine saving is available; the recognition is what the verse is asking for.
verses.89:
> And ˹remember˺ when Zachariah cried out to his Lord, “My Lord! Do not leave me childless, though You are the Best of Successors.”

**Zachariah's Prayer**

The verse records Zachariah's prayer for a heir. *Wa Zakarīyā idhā nādā rabbahu rabbi lā tadarnī fardan wa anta khayru al-wārithīn* — and Zachariah, when he called his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone, and You are the best of inheritors." The verb *nādā* — to call, to cry out — names the form the prayer takes. The prayer is the substance of the verse's announcement; the announcement is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

Zachariah's prayer has two parts. The first is the request — *lā tadarnī fardan* — do not leave me alone, childless. The second is the doxological affirmation — *wa anta khayru al-wārithīn* — and You are the best of inheritors. The two parts together are the prayer; the prayer is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"The Best of Successors"**

The Arabic *khayru al-wārithīn* — the best of inheritors — is one of the most pointed phrases in the verse. The phrase can be read as a simple affirmation of God as the ultimate heir: if there is no heir, God will be the heir. The verse is therefore asking the audience to consider what it means to entrust one's legacy to God.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Prayer**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: prayer. Noah prayed (21:76); Job prayed (21:83); Jonah prayed (21:87); Zachariah prays. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the prophets are not just those who speak; the prophets are also those who call out to God. The calling is the substance of the prophetic office; the office is what the verses are asking the audience to consider.
verses.90:
> So We answered his prayer, granted him John, and made his wife fertile. Indeed, they used to race in doing good, and call upon Us with hope and fear, totally humbling themselves before Us

**The Answer and the Restoration**

The verse records God's answer to Zachariah's prayer. *Fa-istajabnā lahu wa wahabnā lahu Yaḥyā wa aṣlaḥnā lahu zawjahu* — so We answered him and bestowed upon him John and made his wife sound for him. The verb *istajāba* is the same verb used throughout the sūrah for divine answering. The answering is the form the divine action takes; the action is what the verse is recording.

The Arabic *aṣlaḥnā* — we made sound, we made right — is being used here to mean making Zachariah's wife able to bear children. The commentators, including al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī, note that Zachariah's wife had been described as barren elsewhere (3:40). The verse is recording the reversal of the barrenness; the reversal is the substance of the divine answering.

**"They Used to Race in Doing Good"**

The verse continues *innahum kānū yusāriʿūna fī al-khayrāti* — indeed, they used to race in doing good. The verb *sāraʿa* — to race, to hasten — names the form the action takes. The action is racing; the racing is the substance of the verse's claim.

**"With Hope and Fear"**

The verse continues *wa yadʿūnānā raghaban wa rahaban* — and they used to call upon Us with desire and with fear. The Arabic *raghaban* — desire, hope, longing — and *rahaban* — fear, awe, trembling — name the two poles of the prophetic address to God. The address combines the two; the combining is the form the prayer takes when the prayer is offered in the right spirit.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The prayer is not just hope; the prayer is also fear. The fear is not the fear of punishment; the fear is the fear of awe. The awe is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"Totally Humbling Themselves Before Us"**

The verse is part of the broader Qur'anic treatment of Zachariah, which is told more fully in 3:37–41 and 19:2–11. The treatment in all three places emphasises the prayer, the answer, and the birth of John. The verse at 21:90 is unique in its emphasis on the family dynamic of racing in good deeds, calling upon God with both hope and fear, and humbling themselves.
verses.91:
> And ˹remember˺ the one who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her through Our angel, ˹Gabriel,˺ making her and her son a sign for all peoples

**The One Who Guarded Her Chastity**

The verse refers to Mary. *Wa allatī aḥṣanat farjaha* — and she who guarded her chastity. The Arabic *aḥṣana* — to guard, to preserve, to keep inviolate — names the form the guarding takes. The guarding is the substance of the verse's announcement; the announcement is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

The reference to Mary is brief here; the full story of Mary is told elsewhere (3:35–47, 19:16–35, 66:12). The brevity here is part of the verse's role in the larger sūrahic narrative. The narrative is what the verses are documenting; the documenting is part of what the sūrah is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.

**"We Breathed Into Her of Our Spirit"**

The verse continues *fa-nafakhnā fīhā min rūḥinā* — so We breathed into her of Our Spirit. The verb *nafakha* — to breathe, to blow — names the form the divine action takes. The action is the breathing; the breathing is the substance of the verse's claim. The claim is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The breathing into Mary is what produced the pregnancy without a father; the pregnancy is one of the most discussed events in the Qur'anic narrative. The commentators, including al-Rāzī, note that the breathing into Mary parallels the breathing into Adam (38:72); the parallel is part of what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"Making Her and Her Son a Sign for All Peoples"**

The verse closes *wa jaʿalnāhā wa ibnāhā āyatan lil-ʿālamīn* — and We made her and her son a sign for all the worlds. The noun *āya* — sign — names the form the divine action takes. The action is the making; the making is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the Qur'anic treatment of Mary and Jesus. They are presented together as a sign; the sign is for all peoples; the universality is part of what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The consideration is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Divine Signs**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine signs. The heavens and the earth were signs (21:30); the cosmic order is a sign (21:30–33); now Mary and her son are a sign. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the divine action produces signs that point beyond themselves. The pointing is what the verses are asking the audience to recognise; the recognising is the form the response takes.
verses.92:
> ˹O prophets!˺ Indeed, this religion of yours is ˹only˺ one, and I am your Lord, so worship Me ˹alone˺

**One Religion, One Lord**

The verse announces the unity of religion and the unity of lordship. *Inna hādhihi ummatukum ummatan wāḥidatan wa anā rabbukum fa-ʿbudūnī* — indeed, this community of yours is one community, and I am your Lord, so worship Me. The verse is addressed to the prophets; the address is the form the divine speech takes throughout the sūrah. The speech is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

The Arabic *ummatan wāḥidatan* — one community — names the unity of the religious community. The unity is not just numerical; the unity is the form the prophetic message takes when the message is received in its essence. The receiving is what the verse is asking the audience to integrate; the integrating is the form the response takes.

**"I Am Your Lord, So Worship Me"**

The structure is one of the most pointed in the Qur'an: identity, then demand. The identity is the Lord's; the demand is for worship; the worship is the substance of the response the verse is asking for.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The demand is grounded in the identity. The identity is what makes the demand appropriate; the appropriateness is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The considering is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for.

**A Verse That Returns to the Sūrah's Central Theme**

The verse returns to the sūrah's most central theme: the oneness of God and the call to worship Him alone. The theme has appeared throughout (21:25, 21:36, 21:42). The verse at 21:92 is the explicit declaration: the religion is one; the Lord is one; the worship is owed to one. The declaration is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the consideration is the form the response takes.

The verse is part of the broader Qur'anic treatment of the unity of religion. 23:52, 42:14, and other passages develop the same theme. The treatment is consistent across the Qur'an: the religion has always been one; the messengers have always brought the same essential message; the fragmentation that has occurred is the result of human disagreement, not of divine instruction.
verses.93:
> Yet the people have divided it into sects. But to Us they will all return

**The Fragmentation**

The verse records what has happened to the unified religion. *Wa taqṭaʿū amrahum baynahum thubūr* — and they have fragmented their affair among themselves into sects. The Arabic *taqṭaʿa* — to cut into pieces, to divide — names the form the action takes. The action is the fragmentation; the fragmentation is the substance of the verse's claim.

The verse is one of several in the Qur'an that addresses the divisions within religious communities. 2:213, 3:19, 5:48, and 42:14 all develop the same theme: the religion was one; the communities divided; the division is the form the human reception of the religion takes when the reception has been corrupted. The corruption is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"But to Us They Will All Return"**

The verse continues *wa ilaynā tarjiʿūn* — and unto Us they shall return. The verb *tarjiʿūn* — you will return — names the form the future takes. The future is the return to God; the return is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The fragmentation is not the final word; the return to God is the final word. The final word is what the verse is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for. The response is the audience's recognition that the fragmentation will be reversed at the return; the recognition is what the verse is asking for. The verse returns to the sūrah's previous declaration (21:92) that the religion is one. The declaration and the fragmentation are paired in the same passage: the religion is one (21:92); the people fragmented it (21:93). The pairing is the form the verse's argument takes; the argument is that the unity was given and the fragmentation happened.
verses.94:
> So whoever does good and is a believer will never be denied ˹the reward for˺ their striving, for We are recording it all

**The Guarantee of Reward**

The verse guarantees that the striving of the believer who does good will not be denied. *Wa man yaʿmalu ṣāliḥan min al-muʾminīn fa-lā yakfurru ʿamalahu* — and whoever works righteousness among the believers, their work will not be denied. The verb *kafara* — in this usage to deny, to be ungrateful for — names the form the denial would take. The denial will not occur; the verse is the announcement that the denial will not occur.

The verse is connected to a recurring Qur'anic theme. 17:19 says: *And whoever desires the Hereafter, and strives for it with the effort that is its due, and is a believer — those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated*. The verse at 21:94 is the explicit declaration that the striving will be appreciated. The declaration is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"We Are Recording It All"**

The verse continues *wa inna lanā la-hu kātibūn* — and indeed We are writing it down for him. The verb *kataba* — to write — names the form the divine action takes. The action is the writing; the writing is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The divine writing is the form the divine recording of deeds takes. The recording is consistent throughout the Qur'an: every deed is recorded (10:21, 36:12, 45:28–29, 78:29). The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine recording. 21:47 said: *If a deed is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth*. The verse at 21:94 is the same theme: every deed is recorded. The recording is the consistent application of the principle that nothing done is lost.

**A Verse That Closes the Long Prophetic Section**

The verse closes the long prophetic narrative section of the sūrah (21:51–94). The verses that follow will move to Last-Day themes: the destruction of the communities that refused the messengers, the unleashing of Gog and Magog, the coming of the true promise, the fuel of Hell. The closing is the form the narrative takes; the narrative has moved from the messengers to the consequences. The consequences are what the verses will next address; the addressing is what the sūrah is offering the audience.
verses.95:
> It is impossible for a society which We have destroyed to ever rise again

**The Forbidden Return**

The verse states that a destroyed community cannot return. *Wa ḥarramunnā ʿalayhi al-qaryata al-muhlikata annahum lā yarjiʿūn* — and We have forbidden unto those towns that We have destroyed that they shall not return. The verb *ḥarrama* — to forbid — names the form the divine action takes. The forbidding is what the verse is recording; the recording is the form the verse's announcement takes.

The verse has an apparent double negative that commentators discuss. Some read it as meaning that the destroyed communities will not return to the world. Others read it as meaning that they will inevitably return to God in the Hereafter. The two readings need not be exclusive; the verse can be showing both the absence of return to the world and the certainty of return to God.

**"Towns That We Have Destroyed"**

The Arabic *al-qaryata al-muhlikata* — towns that have been destroyed — is the technical term for the communities that have been destroyed by divine punishment. The verse is referring to all the communities mentioned in the sūrah's earlier narratives: the community of Noah, of Abraham, of Lot, of Moses. The destruction is the form the divine response took; the taking is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The destruction is final in this world; the destruction is the form the divine punishment takes. The finality is what the verses are offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for. The response is the audience's recognition that the destruction is final; the recognition is what the verse is asking for. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine punishment. The punishment has been promised throughout (21:11–15, 21:38, 21:46). The verse at 21:95 is the explicit declaration that the punishment is final. The declaration is what the verse is asking the audience to integrate; the integrating is the form the response takes. The verse is part of the broader Qur'anic treatment of the finality of divine punishment. 2:217, 3:144, and other passages develop the same theme: the punishment, when it comes, is final. The treatment is consistent across the Qur'an; the finality is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.
verses.96:
> until ˹after˺ Gog and Magog have broken loose ˹from the barrier˺, swarming down from every hill

**The Unleashing**

The verse names the unleashing. *Ḥattā idhā futiḥat Yajūj wa Majūj wa hum min kulli ḥadabin yansilūn* — until Gog and Magog are opened, and they rush down from every hill. The verb *fatiḥa* — to be opened — names the form the divine action takes. The action is the opening; the opening is the substance of the verse's announcement.

Gog and Magog (Yajūj wa Majūj) are described in the Qur'an in 18:94–99 as vicious and destructive beings locked away by the figure Dhu'l-Qarnayn behind a barrier of iron and copper. The unleashing is the form the Last-Day chaos takes; the chaos is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The unleashing has been promised throughout the sūrah; the promise is the form the divine economy takes; the economy is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"From Every Hill"**

The phrase *min kulli ḥadabin yansilūn* — they rush down from every hill — specifies the form the unleashing takes. The Arabic *hadab* — hill, high place — names the kind of place from which they descend. The descent is from heights; the descent is the form the chaos takes.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The unleashing produces a flood of descent; the descent overwhelms whatever is below. The overwhelming is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The hill is every elevated place; the elevated places will produce what they have been given to produce.

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Last-Day Chaos**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the chaos that will come at the end of time. The chaos has been described throughout the sūrah (21:40, 21:46). The verse at 21:96 is one of the most vivid descriptions; the description is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The chaos has been the recurring description throughout the sūrah (21:11, 21:30, 21:44); the recurrence is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

The verse is part of the broader Qur'anic treatment of the Last-Day chaos. 18:94–99, 27:82, and other passages develop the same theme. The treatment is consistent across the Qur'an; the chaos is what the verse is asking the audience to integrate; the integrating is the form the response takes. The broader treatment can be traced through 27:87, 39:67, and 69:13–16, all of which describe the cosmic transformation with similar imagery. The imagery is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.
verses.97:
> ushering in the True Promise. Then—behold!—the disbelievers will stare ˹in horror, crying,˺ “Oh, woe to us! We have truly been heedless of this. In fact, we have been wrongdoers.”

**The True Promise Drawing Nigh**

The verse records the arrival of the true promise. *Wa aqtaraba al-waʿdu al-ḥaqqu* — and the true promise has drawn nigh. The verb *aqtaraba* — to draw nigh, to come close — is the same verb used in the opening verse of the sūrah (21:1). The drawing nigh is the form the divine action takes; the action is what the verse is recording.

The Arabic *al-waʿdu al-ḥaqq* — the true promise — is a technical term for the Hour of Resurrection. The promise was given throughout the sūrah; the promise is now arriving. The arriving is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The promise is drawing nigh; the nearing is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"The Disbelievers Will Stare in Horror"**

The verse continues *fa-idhā hiya shākhiṣatun abṣaru alladhīna kafarū* — and behold, the stares of those who disbelieved are fixed. The Arabic *shākhiṣa* — to stare in horror — names the form the reaction takes. The form is the fixed stare; the stare is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most vivid descriptions in the Qur'an of the moment when the Hour arrives. 14:42, 80:34–37, and other passages develop the same theme. The description is consistent across the Qur'an; the form is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The staring is the form the denial takes when the denial meets what it had denied; the meeting is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"We Have Truly Been Heedless of This"**

The verse continues *yā waylanā qad kunnā fī ghaflatin min hādhā bal kunnā ẓālimīn* — woe to us, we have been in heedlessness of this; rather, we have been wrongdoers. The cry is one of recognition that comes too late; the recognition is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

The Arabic *ghaflah* — heedlessness — is one of the Qur'an's most theologically loaded terms. The heedlessness has been the form the audience's life has taken; the taking is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The heedlessness is what the verse is naming; the naming is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's most central themes: the arrival of the Hour. The arrival has been described throughout the sūrah (21:40, 21:46). The verse at 21:97 is the explicit description of what the arrival looks like: the stares of the disbelievers fixed in horror, the cry of recognition that comes too late.
verses.98:
> Certainly you ˹disbelievers˺ and whatever you worship instead of Allah will be the fuel of Hell. You are ˹all˺ bound to enter it

**The Worshippers and What They Worship as Fuel**

The verse makes a striking declaration. *Innakum wa mā taʿbudūna min dūni Allāhi ḥasabu jahannama antum lahā wāridūn* — indeed, you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell; you are bound to enter it. The verse is addressing the disbelievers and the objects they have been worshipping; both are described as fuel. The fuel is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most theologically pointed moments in the entire sūrah. The objects of worship become fuel; the worshippers become fuel. The fuel is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**Fuel, Burning, and the Direction of the Entering**

The Arabic *ḥasabu jahannama* — fuel of Hell — names what the disbelievers and their objects of worship have become. The Arabic *ḥasab* — fuel, firewood — is the substance that is burned. The burning is what awaits; the awaiting is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The disbelievers and their objects are not just named as going to Hell; they are described as what Hell will consume.

The verb *warada* — to enter, to arrive at, to descend into — names the form the action takes. The verb is in the plural active; the disbelievers are the subjects of the entering. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: Hell. Hell has been mentioned throughout (21:29, 21:39, 21:46). The verse at 21:98 is the specific description of what Hell is for and who will be in it.
verses.99:
> Had those idols been ˹true˺ gods, they would not have entered it. And they will be there forever

**The Hypothetical That Confirms the Verdict**

The verse offers a conditional that confirms the verdict. *Law kāna hāʾulāʾi ālihatan mā waradūhā wa kullun fīhā khālidūn* — had these been gods, they would not have entered it; but all of them shall abide in it. The conditional is structured to make the conclusion obvious: the objects of worship are not gods; the conclusion is that they will enter Hell.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The conditional tests the audience's assumption that the objects of worship are gods. The test shows that the assumption is false; the falsity is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

The clause *law kāna hāʾulāʾi ālihatan* — had these been gods — poses the hypothesis. The hypothesis is that the objects of worship are gods. The hypothesis is then denied by the consequence: the gods would not have entered Hell. The denial is the form the verse's argument takes; the argument is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the Qur'anic treatment of the supposed partners. The Qur'an tests the hypothesis by considering the consequence. The consequence fails the test; the failure is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

**"All of Them Shall Abide In it"**

The verse continues *wa kullun fīhā khālidūn* — and all of them shall abide in it. The verb *khālada* — to abide forever — names the form the punishment takes. The punishment is permanent; the permanence is the substance of the verse's claim.

The abide is forever; the forever is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The audience that recognises the permanence of the punishment has begun the response the verse is asking for; the audience that refuses to recognise has refused the verse.

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the punishment. The punishment has been promised throughout (21:11–15, 21:46, 21:98). The verse at 21:99 is the explicit declaration that the punishment is permanent. The declaration is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.
verses.100:
> In it they will groan, and will not be able to hear

**The Groaning**

The verse describes the punishment's form. *Lahum fīhā zafīrun wa hum fīhā lā yasmaʿūn* — theirs shall be groaning in it, and they shall not hear in it. The noun *zafīr* — groaning — names the form the punishment takes. The punishment produces groaning; the groaning is the substance of the verse's claim.

The Arabic *zafīr* is also used in 11:106 in connection with the punishment of those who have earned God's wrath. The recurrence is the consistent application of the principle that the punishment produces sounds of distress. The producing is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"And They Will Not Hear"**

The verb *samiʿa* — to hear — is negated; the negating names the form the punishment takes. The punishment includes an inability to hear; the inability is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The inability to hear is not just a physiological deficit; the inability is the form the punishment takes when the punishment has isolated the punished from everything else.

Some interpret the inability to hear as the experience of the punishment utterly alone; the punished cannot communicate with others in the punishment. Others interpret it as a literal deafness; the punished are resurrected deaf (17:97). The two interpretations are not exclusive; the verse can be showing both the literal and the figurative aspects of the punishment. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the specific form of the Last-Day punishment. The punishment has been described throughout the sūrah (21:29, 21:39, 21:98). The verse at 21:100 is the specific description of what the punishment will look and sound like.
verses.101:
> Surely those for whom We have destined the finest reward will be kept far away from Hell

**Those for Whom the Best Has Already Gone Forth**

The verse names those for whom the best has already gone forth from God. *La alladhīna ṣadawat ʿanhum al-sūʾā wa yujzawna al-ʿaẓīma mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — those whom the evil has gone forth from, and they shall be requited with the greatest [reward] for what they used to do. The verse is announcing the category of those who will be spared the punishment described in the previous verses.

The commentators have offered different interpretations of the announcement. Al-Ṭabarī understands it as a statement of predestination about those whose destination in the Garden has already been determined. Al-Rāzī understands it as referring to those objects of worship who were worshipped falsely but did not invite the worship themselves, such as Jesus and the angels. The Sufi tradition extends it to the saints who have been chosen for friendship with God. The interpretations are not exclusive; the verse can be read in any of these ways.

**"They Shall Be Kept Far from It"**

The verse's specification — *yujzawna al-ʿaẓīma mā kānū yaʿmalūn* — they shall be requited with the greatest reward for what they used to do — names the form the requital takes. The requital is the opposite of the punishment; the punishment and the requital are the two sides of the divine response. The response is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

The verse is offering a contrast: the previous verses have described the punishment; this verse is now describing the reward. The contrast is the form the divine economy takes; the economy is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine reward. The reward has been promised throughout (21:10, 21:48, 21:94). The verse at 21:101 is the specific announcement of who will receive the reward.
verses.102:
> not even hearing the slightest hissing from it. And they will delight forever in what their souls desire

**No Sound of Hell**

The verse records the silence of Hell for the righteous. *Lā yasmaʿūna ḥasīsahā wa hum fī mā ishtahat anfusuhum khālidūn* — they will not hear the slightest hiss of it, and they will abide in what their souls desire. The Arabic *ḥasīs* — the slightest sound — names what they will not hear. The not-hearing is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The righteous do not just escape Hell; the righteous do not hear Hell's sounds. The hearing is the form Hell's presence takes for those who have been spared. The sparing is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"Abide in What Their Souls Desire"**

The verb *ishtahā* — to desire, to long for — names the form the desiring takes. The desiring is for what they want; the wanting is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The vision of the righteous is what they themselves would want. The Qur'an elsewhere describes the inhabitants of Paradise as having what they ask for (16:31; 25:16; 36:57; 39:34; 42:22; 50:35; 77:41–42). The asking and the receiving are the same; the receiving is the form the divine response takes; the response is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine reward. The reward has been promised throughout (21:10, 21:48, 21:94, 21:101). The verse at 21:102 is the specific description of what the reward will be: not hearing Hell's sounds, and having what the soul desires.

The Sufi commentators, including al-Qushayrī, offer a striking reading of this verse that goes beyond the Last-Day surface. For those who have arrived at real knowing, the clamour of ordinary existence loses its grip; they are so taken up with the divine that nothing beside it draws their attention. The yearning of the spirit draws them toward nearness; the yearning of the heart draws them toward sight. The reading takes the verse into the inner life; the inner life is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.
verses.103:
> The Supreme Horror ˹of that Day˺ will not disturb them, and the angels will greet them, ˹saying,˺ “This is your Day, which you have been promised.”

**The Greatest Terror**

The verse announces that the greatest terror will not grieve the righteous. *Wa lā taḥzanuhumu al-fāzaʿatu al-akbaru wa talaqqāhumu al-malāʾikatu hādhika yawmukumu alladhī kuntum tūʿadūn* — and the greatest terror will not grieve them. The angels will receive them, saying, "This is your day which you have been promised." The Arabic *al-fāzaʿa al-akbar* — the greatest terror — names what will not grieve them. The not-grieving is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The greatest terror is the most extreme form of fright; the righteous are preserved from even being affected by it. The preservation is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**The Angels Will Receive Them**

The verse continues *wa talaqqāhumu al-malāʾikatu* — and the angels will receive them. The verb *talaqqā* — to receive, to greet — names the form the angels' action takes. The receiving is the form the divine welcome takes; the welcome is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The angels are not just present at the Last-Day transition; the angels are actively receiving the righteous.

**"This Is the Day You Have Been Promised"**

The angels say *hādhika yawmukumu alladhī kuntum tūʿadūn* — this is your day which you have been promised. The promise is fulfilled; the fulfilling is the substance of the verse's claim. The promise had been made throughout the sūrah (21:9, 21:103; cf. 21:48).

The angels address the righteous as those whose promise has come. The coming is the form the divine faithfulness takes; the faithfulness is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring references to the angels. The angels have appeared throughout the sūrah (21:26, 21:103, etc.). The verse at 21:103 is the specific description of the angels' role at the Last-Day transition.
verses.104:
> On that Day We will roll up the heavens like a scroll of writings. Just as We produced the first creation, ˹so˺ shall We reproduce it. That is a promise binding on Us. We truly uphold ˹Our promises˺

**The Sky Folded Like a Written Sheet**

The verse describes the cosmic transformation of the Day of Judgment. *Yawm naṭwi al-samāʾa ka-ṭayyi al-sijilli lil-kutub* — the day We shall fold the sky like folding a written sheet for writings. The Arabic *ṭayy* — to fold — names the form the action takes. The folding is the cosmic transformation; the transformation is the substance of the verse's claim.

The commentators have noted that the sky's being described as a scroll recalls 39:67 — the heavens will be enfolded in His right Hand. The two descriptions are the same vision from different angles; the angles are what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**The Arabic "Sijill"**

The Arabic *sijill* — scroll — is the noun that names what the sky is being compared to. Some commentators understand *sijill* to refer to rolled-up pages upon which one writes; others understand it as the proper name of an angel. The two interpretations are not exclusive; the verse can be showing both the literal and the figurative aspects of the cosmic ending.

**"Just as We Began the First Creation, So We Shall Repeat It"**

The verse continues *ka-mā badaʾnā awwala khalqin nuʿīduhu* — just as We began the first creation, We shall repeat it. The Arabic *nuʿīduhu* — We shall repeat it, We shall return it — names the form the divine action takes. The repeating is the form the divine power takes; the power is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The repeating is the same as the beginning; the beginning and the repeating are the same divine act. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the transformation of the cosmos at the Day of Judgment. The transformation has been promised throughout (21:30, 21:44). The verse at 21:104 is the specific description of what the transformation will look like.
verses.105:
> Surely, following the ˹heavenly˺ Record, We decreed in the Scriptures: “My righteous servants shall inherit the land.”

**The Psalms and the Record**

The verse points to the Psalms and to a prior record. *Wa laqad katabnā fī al-zabūri baʿda al-dhikri anna al-arḍa yarithuhā ʿibādiya al-ṣāliḥūn* — and We have already written in the Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants. The Arabic *al-zabūr* — the Psalms — names the scripture; the Arabic *al-dhikr* — the Reminder — names what the Psalms were written after.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The Qur'an is here pointing to the Psalms of David as a witness to the truth of the divine promise that the earth will be inherited by the righteous. The pointing is the form the cross-scriptural argument takes; the argument is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

The commentators have offered different interpretations of *al-dhikr*. Al-Ṭabarī understands it as what is in Heaven — the Mother of the Book — with God (3:7; 13:39; 43:4). Al-Rāzī follows the same reading. The Reminder is the heavenly archetype of all scripture; the archetype is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"My Righteous Servants Shall Inherit the Earth"**

The verb *yarithu* — to inherit — names the form the action takes. The inheriting is the form the divine promise takes; the promise is what the verse is asking the audience to consider.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The inheritance is not a metaphor; the inheritance is the actual possession of the earth by the righteous. The possession is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**Two Readings of What the Earth Signifies**

The commentators have offered two main readings of what the earth here names. One reading, associated with al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī, takes it as a figure for the soil of the Garden — a higher earth that belongs to the righteous only, since the lower earth is shared between those who refuse the message and those who accept it. Another reading, favoured by al-Rāzī, takes it as the actual lands of this world, which the community of Muhammad would come to inhabit after the earlier communities had been removed. The two readings are not mutually exclusive; the verse can be drawn into either. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the earth. The earth has been mentioned throughout the sūrah (21:16, 21:30, 21:44). The verse at 21:105 is the specific declaration that the earth shall be inherited by the righteous.
verses.106:
> Surely this ˹Quran˺ is sufficient ˹as a reminder˺ for those devoted to worship

**The Proclamation in the Qur'an**

The verse records that the Qur'an contains a proclamation for a worshipful people. *Wa mā arsalnāka illā raḥmatan lil-ʿālamīn* — and We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds. The Arabic *in fī hādhā la-bashāra li-ummatin yaʿbudūn* — surely in this there is good news for a worshipping people — names what the Qur'an contains. The containing is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The Qur'an is here described as containing a proclamation for a worshipping people. The proclamation is the form the divine address takes; the address is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**A People Marked by Devotion**

The verse names the audience of the proclamation: *ummatin yaʿbudūn* — a people who worship. The worshipping is the form the people's action takes; the action is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

The commentators have offered different interpretations of who these worshipping people are. Al-Qurṭubī and al-Ṭabarī read the phrase as naming those who hold the regular prayers and the month-long fast — that is, the community of the Prophet. The Sufi commentators, including al-Qushayrī, open the meaning outward: the verse names those whose worship is not bargained for paradise or bought to escape punishment, but offered out of love for the divine and the dignity of being a servant of God.

**Returning to the Theme of the Qur'an**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the Qur'an itself. The Qur'an has been mentioned throughout the sūrah (21:2, 21:10, 21:45). The verse at 21:106 is the specific description of what the Qur'an contains: a proclamation for a worshipping people. The description is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The verse returns to the sūrah's central concern with the worship of God. The worship has been the focus of the sūrah throughout (21:25, 21:36, 21:92). The verse at 21:106 is the specific announcement that the Qur'an is a proclamation for those who worship.
verses.107:
> We have sent you ˹O Prophet˺ only as a mercy for the whole world

**A Mercy to All the Worlds**

The verse is one of the most cited in the entire Qur'an: *Wa mā arsalnāka illā raḥmatan lil-ʿālamīn* — and We did not send you except as a mercy to all the worlds. The Arabic *raḥmah* — mercy, compassion, kindness, love, caring — names what the Prophet is. The naming is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The Prophet is not described as a warner, a teacher, a judge, or a ruler; the Prophet is described as a mercy. The mercy is the form the divine sending takes; the sending is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

The grammar allows two readings. On one reading, the sending of the Prophet is the merciful act. On another reading, the Prophet himself is the mercy. The two readings are not exclusive; the verse can be showing both aspects at once.

**The Concept of Raḥmah**

The Arabic *raḥmah* is one of the names of God (1:3). On *raḥmah* in relation to God, see 1:3c and 7:156c. The name is given to the Prophet here as the form the divine mercy takes for the worlds. The taking is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"All the Worlds"**

The verse continues *lil-ʿālamīn* — to all the worlds. The Arabic *ʿālamīn* — worlds — names the audience of the mercy. The audience is not just the Arabs or the believers or the people of the Prophet's time; the audience is all the worlds.

Some commentators restrict *ʿālamīn* to human beings and jinn. Others restrict it to believers only. The commentators frequently note that the Prophet was a mercy even to those who rejected him, in the sense that his adversaries were spared the catastrophic defeats that befell the enemies of earlier prophets. The sparing is the form the divine protection takes; the protection is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The verse closes the section of the sūrah that has been describing the Prophet's sending. The Prophet has been mentioned throughout the sūrah (21:5, 21:7, 21:10). The verse at 21:107 is the specific description of what the Prophet is: a mercy to all the worlds.
verses.108:
> Say, “What has been revealed to me is this: ‘Your God is only One God.’ Will you then submit?”

**One God**

The verse records the Prophet's call to one God. *Qul innamā yūḥā ilayya annamā ilāhukum ilāhun wāḥidun afalā tuslimūn* — say, it is only revealed to me that your God is one God; will you then submit? The Arabic *ilāhun wāḥidun* — one God — names what is revealed. The revealing is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The Qur'an consistently calls to the unity of God (cf. 2:163; 16:22; 22:34; 29:46; 41:6). The call is the form the divine address takes; the address is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The oneness is what the verse is naming; the naming is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"Will You Then Submit?"**

The verse continues *afalā tuslimūn* — will you then submit? The Arabic *aslama* — to submit — names the form the response takes.

The submission is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes; the response is what the verse is asking for. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's most distinctive themes: the unity of God. The unity has been the central argument of the sūrah throughout (21:22, 21:25, 21:29). The verse at 21:108 is the explicit call to submit to the one God. The polytheists had associated partners with God; the verse is now calling them to submit to the one God.
verses.109:
> If they turn away, then say, “I have warned you all equally. I do not know if what you are threatened with is near or far

**"If They Turn Away"**

The verse addresses the case of those who refuse the call. *Wa in tuwallaw yaqqul ʿalā sawāʾin innī undhītukum sawāʾa baynahu wa qarīb* — and if they turn away, say, I have warned you equally, and I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far. The conditional addresses the case of refusal; the refusal is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"I Have Warned You All Equally"**

The Prophet is commanded to say *innī undhītukum sawāʾan* — I have warned you all equally. The Arabic *sawāʾ* — equally, in a just way — names how the warning is delivered. The warning is delivered to everyone; the delivery is the form the warning takes; the warning is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the Qur'anic treatment of the Prophet's role. The Prophet is not given authority over hearts; he is given only the duty of delivery. The delivery is the form the Prophet's role takes; the role is what the verse is asking the audience to consider. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the Prophet's role. The Prophet's role has been described throughout (21:5, 21:10, 21:107). The verse at 21:109 is the specific description of what the Prophet can and cannot do.
verses.110:
> Allah surely knows what you say openly and whatever you hide

**What Is Said Openly and What Is Hidden**

The verse records God's knowledge of both the spoken and the concealed. *Wa Allāhu yaʿlamu mutajārahu wa khafiyyahu* — and God knows what is declared and what is hidden. The Arabic *mutajārah* — what is declared openly — and *khafiyy* — what is hidden — name the two aspects of what God knows. The knowing is the substance of the verse's claim.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. God knows both what is declared and what is concealed; the knowing is the form the divine omniscience takes; the omniscience is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The claim is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**The Two Spheres of Knowledge**

The verse names two spheres: the open and the hidden. The open sphere is what is said aloud; the hidden sphere is what is kept within. The two spheres cover the entirety of human speech and thought; the entirety is what God knows.

The Qur'an is consistent on this point. Public statements and secret thoughts are equally known by God (cf. 2:284; 4:149; 27:74; 33:54; 87:7).

**A Verse That Returns to the Theme of Divine Omniscience**

The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: divine omniscience. The omniscience has been the focus of the sūrah throughout (21:4, 21:81); the consistency of the focus is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes. The verse at 21:110 is the specific declaration that God knows what is declared and what is hidden; the declaration is what the verse is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for.

**A Verse That Closes the Section on Divine Knowledge**

The verse closes the section of the sūrah that has been describing God's knowledge of human speech and thought. The omniscience has been described throughout the sūrah (21:4, 21:81). The verse at 21:110 is the final declaration of God's knowledge in the sūrah. The section has been building across these verses (21:4 and 21:81 earlier, 21:110 here); the closing is the form the arc takes; the arc is what the verse is offering the audience; the offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for. The section has been building throughout the sūrah (21:4, 21:81, 21:110); the closing is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.
verses.111:
> I do not know if this ˹delay˺ is possibly a test for you and an enjoyment for a while.”

**"Perhaps It Is a Trial for You"**

The verse returns to the theme of delay. *Wa lā aʿlamu laʿallahu fitnatun lakum wa tamāṭun ilā ḥīn* — and I do not know; perhaps it is a trial for you and an enjoyment for a while. The Arabic *fitnah* — trial, test — names what the delay may be. The trial is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

This is one of the most distinctive features of the verse. The delay of the punishment can be a blessing or a trial; the meaning of the delay depends on how the one given the delay uses it.

**The Delay as Test**

The commentators understand the delay to be a test in the sense that the postponement of the punishment gives the disbelievers more time to commit evil and entrench themselves in denial. The Qur'an elsewhere makes the same point (cf. 26:205–7, where the Qur'an says that more time only gives the disbelievers more opportunity to commit evil).

The Arabic *fitnah* — trial — can also be read in the older sense of the word: a smelting, a refining by fire. The delay is the fire in which the metal is tested; the testing is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"Enjoyment for a While"**

The Arabic *tamāṭ* — enjoyment, pastime — and the Arabic *ḥīn* — a while, a time — name the form the postponement takes. The postponement is a brief enjoyment; the brief is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

This is one of the most theologically significant features of the verse. The verse returns to one of the sūrah's recurring themes: the delay of the punishment. The delay has been mentioned throughout (21:1, 21:109). The verse at 21:111 is the specific description of what the delay may be: a trial and an enjoyment for a while.
verses.112:
> ˹In the end,˺ the Prophet said, “My Lord! Judge ˹between us˺ in truth. And our Lord is the Most Compassionate, Whose help is sought against what you claim.”

**The Final Prayer**

The verse records the Prophet's final prayer. *Qāla rabbi aḥkum bil-ḥaqqi wa rabbunā al-raḥmānu al-mustaʿānu ʿalā mā taṣifūn* — he said, my Lord, judge with the truth; and our Lord is the Compassionate, the One Whose help is sought against what you describe. The Arabic *aḥkum* — judge — names the form the prayer takes. The prayer is the form the divine address takes; the address is what the verse is asking the audience to consider; the considering is the form the response takes.

**"Judge with the Truth"**

The verb can be read as an imperative, "Say: My Lord, judge with the truth!" Or as a past tense, "My Lord has judged with the truth." The two readings are not mutually exclusive; the verse can be drawn into either sense. A similar form is used elsewhere (cf. 7:89, where the prayer is for the Lord to decide between the servants and the people with the truth, for He is the best of deciders). The verse continues *wa rabbunā al-raḥmānu* — and our Lord is the Compassionate. The Arabic *al-raḥmān* — the Compassionate — names an attribute of God.

**The One Whose Help Is Called Upon**

The commentators offer different interpretations of what the description refers to. Some take it as the Prophet seeking God's help against the false accusations of magic and verse-making that had been levelled against him (vv. 3–5). Others take it as the Prophet seeking God's help against the things being said about God Himself — claims of offspring or partner that diminish the divine (cf. 19:35). The two readings are not mutually exclusive; the verse can be read in either way.

**A Verse That Closes the Sūrah**

The verse closes the entire sūrah. The sūrah has run from the question of the coming judgment (21:1) to the Prophet's prayer that God judge with the truth. The closing is the form the sūrah takes; the sūrah is what the verse is offering the audience. The offering is the substance of the response the verses are asking for; the asking is the form the call takes; the call is the substance of the sūrah.
